weeks.title: FAR U4·W4 — Pensions & Stock-Based Compensation (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — promising to pay employees later

Two forms of deferred employee pay get their own accounting: pensions (and other postretirement benefits) and stock-based compensation. Both recognize expense now for value delivered later, and both are heavy on estimates and on the income-versus-OCI distinction from earlier FAR units. If MBG offers a pension or grants equity to key staff, these standards govern the cost.

Defined contribution versus defined benefit

A defined-contribution plan (a 401(k)) promises only a contribution; the employer's expense each period equals the contribution, and the employee bears the investment risk — simple accounting. A defined-benefit plan promises a future benefit (often based on salary and years of service); the employer bears the investment and actuarial risk, and the accounting is complex because the obligation must be estimated and measured today.

The pension obligation and funded status

The key measure of a defined-benefit obligation is the projected benefit obligation (PBO) — the actuarial present value of benefits earned to date, using future salary levels. The plan's assets (held in a separate trust) are measured at fair value. The funded status = plan assets − PBO, and the net amount is reported on the balance sheet as a pension asset (overfunded) or liability (underfunded). The accumulated benefit obligation (ABO) uses current salaries and is a secondary measure.

Net periodic pension cost

The income-statement expense, net periodic pension cost, has several components — remembered as SIRAGE: Service cost (the PV of benefits earned this year, the only component in operating income), plus Interest cost on the PBO, minus the expected Return on plan assets, plus or minus Amortization of prior service cost, plus or minus amortization of Gains and losses, and amortization of any Existing net obligation. Worked example: service cost $200,000 + interest cost $90,000 − expected return $70,000 + prior-service-cost amortization $20,000 = $240,000 of net periodic pension cost.

Gains, losses, and OCI

Two items bypass net income and sit in other comprehensive income until amortized: prior service cost (from a plan amendment that grants credit for past service) and actuarial gains and losses (from changes in assumptions or differences between expected and actual asset returns). They accumulate in OCI and are amortized into pension cost over time — gains and losses only when they exceed a corridor (10% of the greater of the PBO or plan assets), spread over the average remaining service period. This OCI treatment smooths the volatile actuarial swings out of reported earnings.

Other postretirement benefits

Other postretirement benefit (OPEB) plans — chiefly retiree health care — follow a parallel model, but the obligation is the accumulated postretirement benefit obligation (APBO) and benefits are not salary-based. The cost is recognized over the period from hire to the date the employee is fully eligible for benefits, and like pensions the actuarial gains/losses and prior service cost flow through OCI. The common thread is accruing the cost of a promise over the service period that earns it.

Stock-based compensation

ASC 718 measures equity awards at their grant-date fair value and recognizes the cost as compensation expense over the service (vesting) period. For stock options, fair value comes from an option-pricing model (such as Black-Scholes) using the exercise price, stock price, expected term, volatility, risk-free rate, and dividends; the total is the fair value per option times the number expected to vest. Worked example: 10,000 options with a $9 grant-date fair value vesting over three years produce $90,000 of total compensation, expensed at $30,000 per year. Restricted stock units (RSUs) are measured at the grant-date share price. The offsetting credit is to additional paid-in capital (equity), so equity-classified awards do not create a liability.

Vesting, forfeitures, and modifications

Compensation cost is recognized only for awards that vest. An entity either estimates forfeitures up front or accounts for them as they occur (a policy election), truing up so that cumulative expense reflects awards that actually vest. Service conditions and performance conditions affect whether and how much expense is recognized, while market conditions (a target stock price) are built into the grant-date fair value and not reversed even if unmet. A modification (repricing underwater options) recognizes any incremental fair value. The principle throughout: recognize the grant-date value of awards expected to vest over the period employees earn them.

Pension obligation and asset rollforwards

The two pension accounts each roll forward. The PBO increases with service cost and interest cost and with actuarial losses, and decreases with benefits paid and actuarial gains; a plan amendment adds prior service cost. Plan assets increase with the actual return and employer contributions and decrease with benefits paid. The difference between the expected and actual return on plan assets is itself an actuarial gain or loss deferred in OCI — which is why net periodic cost uses the smoother expected return while the balance sheet reflects the actual asset value. Tracking these rollforwards is how the exam tests whether a plan is over- or underfunded and what the year's expense should be.

Liability awards and the tax angle

Not every stock award is equity-classified. An award that will be settled in cash (a cash-settled stock appreciation right) is a liability, remeasured to fair value each reporting period until settlement, so its expense fluctuates with the share price — unlike an equity award fixed at grant-date value. Stock compensation also creates a book-tax difference: the book expense (grant-date fair value over vesting) rarely equals the tax deduction (often the intrinsic value at exercise), producing deferred taxes and, on settlement, excess tax benefits or deficiencies that flow through the income-tax provision. The unifying idea across pensions and stock comp is that the accounting accrues the economic cost of deferred pay over the period it is earned, routing the volatile pieces through OCI or remeasurement rather than distorting operating income.

CMA bridge

Pension and stock-comp accounting reinforces the income-versus-OCI map from FAR Units 1 and 2: service and interest cost hit income while actuarial gains/losses wait in OCI, mirroring the AFS and hedge treatments. For a closely held contractor like MBG these may be modest, but the exam tests the mechanics — and the deferred-tax consequences tie back to ASC 740.

Practice and recap

  1. Expense a defined-contribution plan at the contribution; measure a defined-benefit obligation at the PBO and report funded status (assets − PBO) on the balance sheet.
  2. Compute net periodic pension cost (SIRAGE): service + interest − expected return ± amortizations.
  3. Route prior service cost and actuarial gains/losses through OCI, amortizing gains/losses outside the 10% corridor.
  4. Measure stock compensation at grant-date fair value and expense it over vesting; recognize cost only for awards that vest.

Recap: defined-benefit pensions report funded status (plan assets minus PBO) on the balance sheet and expense net periodic cost of service + interest − expected return ± amortizations (here $240,000), with prior service cost and actuarial gains/losses deferred in OCI; and stock-based compensation expenses grant-date fair value over the vesting period — 10,000 options worth $9 each over three years give $30,000 of expense per year — recognized only for awards expected to vest — and a cash-settled award is instead a liability remeasured to fair value each reporting period until settlement.

flashcards.back: DC: expense = the contribution (employee bears risk). DB: promises a future benefit; employer bears actuarial/investment risk; complex accounting.
Actuarial present value of benefits earned to date using FUTURE salary levels (ABO uses current salaries).

flashcards.front: Funded status on the balance sheet
flashcards.back: Plan assets (fair value) − PBO; reported as a net pension asset (overfunded) or liability (underfunded).
Service cost + Interest cost − expected Return on plan assets ± Amortization of prior service cost ± amortization of Gains/losses ± amortization of Existing net obligation.
Prior service cost and actuarial gains/losses bypass net income into OCI, then amortize (gains/losses only outside the 10% corridor).
Equity awards at GRANT-DATE fair value, expensed over the service (vesting) period; offset to additional paid-in capital.
10,000 options × $9 grant-date fair value = $90,000 over 3-year vesting = $30,000/year.
Market conditions are built into grant-date fair value (not reversed if unmet); service/performance conditions affect whether/how much expense is recognized.

questions.q: In a defined-contribution plan, the employer's annual pension expense equals:
questions.explain: Defined-contribution expense is simply the contribution; the employee bears investment risk.

questions.q: The funded status reported on the balance sheet equals:
choices: Plan assets at fair value − PBO
questions.explain: Funded status = fair value of plan assets minus the PBO.

questions.q: Service cost $200,000, interest cost $90,000, expected return $70,000, prior-service-cost amortization $20,000. Net periodic pension cost is:
Actuarial gains and losses on a defined-benefit plan are initially recognized in:
questions.explain: They flow through OCI and are amortized to pension cost (outside the 10% corridor).

questions.q: Under ASC 718, equity-classified stock compensation is measured at:
choices: Grant-date fair value, expensed over the vesting period
questions.explain: Equity awards use grant-date fair value recognized over the service/vesting period.

questions.q: 10,000 options with a $9 grant-date fair value vest over 3 years. Annual compensation expense is:
Compensation cost for stock awards is recognized:
choices: Only for awards that ultimately vest
For all granted awards regardless of vesting
questions.explain: Expense is recognized only for awards that vest, with forfeitures estimated or recognized as they occur.

units.title: FAR Unit 5 — Cash & Receivables, Liabilities/Contingencies, Fair Value & Consolidations

weeks.title: FAR U5·W1 — Cash, Receivables & Credit Losses (CECL)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the top of the balance sheet

The most liquid assets — cash and receivables — open every balance sheet, and they carry their own measurement rules. This week covers what counts as cash, the bank reconciliation that proves it, how accounts receivable are stated at net realizable value, and the modern current-expected-credit-loss (CECL) model that sets the allowance. For Meridian Building Group, where progress billings and retainage drive a large receivable balance, these accounts are where the audit and the financial statements begin.

Cash and cash equivalents

Cash includes coin, currency, and demand deposits available without restriction. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less (Treasury bills, money-market funds). Items that are not cash include restricted cash (a compensating balance or a sinking fund — disclosed or classified separately), post-dated checks, and IOUs. The classification matters because cash and cash equivalents are the reconciling total on the statement of cash flows from FAR Unit 3.

The bank reconciliation

A bank reconciliation ties the book balance to the bank balance, isolating timing differences and errors. On the bank side, add deposits in transit and subtract outstanding checks; on the book side, add items the bank recorded that the company has not (interest earned, note collections) and subtract bank charges and NSF checks. Only the book-side adjustments generate journal entries, because they represent transactions the company has not yet recorded. The reconciliation is both a control and the support for the cash figure reported.

Accounts receivable at net realizable value

Trade receivables are recorded at the amount expected to be collected — net realizable value — which is the gross receivable minus the allowance for credit losses and any anticipated sales discounts and returns. Cash (sales) discounts (e.g., 2/10, net 30) may be recorded by the gross or net method. Because some customers will not pay, the receivable cannot be carried at its face amount — the allowance bridges the gap between what is owed and what will realistically be collected, keeping the asset faithfully stated.

The CECL model

Under ASC 326, the allowance is set by the current expected credit loss (CECL) model, which replaced the old incurred-loss method. CECL requires recognizing lifetime expected credit losses at origination — a day-one reserve — based on historical experience, current conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts. The result is generally a larger, earlier allowance than the incurred model, because the entity no longer waits for a loss to become probable. The allowance is a contra-asset; the period's change runs through credit loss expense.

Estimating and recording the allowance

Two estimation approaches are common. The percentage-of-sales method (income-statement approach) sets credit-loss expense as a percentage of credit sales, ignoring the existing allowance balance. The percentage-of-receivables / aging method (balance-sheet approach) computes the required ending allowance — often via an aging schedule applying higher loss rates to older buckets — and the entry is the amount needed to adjust the allowance to that target. Worked example: if aging indicates a required allowance of $90,000 and the account already has a $20,000 credit balance, the entry debits credit-loss expense and credits the allowance for $70,000. A specific write-off later debits the allowance and credits the receivable — with no effect on net receivables or expense.

Notes receivable

A note receivable is a written promise bearing interest. It is recorded at present value; if the stated rate differs from the market rate, the note is recorded at a discount or premium amortized to interest income using the effective-interest method from FAR Unit 2. A non-interest-bearing note is recorded net of an implied discount. Interest accrues over time (principal × rate × time), and a note received for goods or services is measured at the fair value of what was exchanged when the rate is unrealistic.

Financing receivables: factoring and pledging

A company can convert receivables to cash early. Pledging uses receivables as collateral for a loan (the receivables stay on the books, with disclosure). Factoring sells the receivables: without recourse, the buyer absorbs credit losses and the sale is final (derecognize the receivable, record a loss/fee); with recourse, the seller retains some risk, and whether it is a sale or a borrowing turns on whether control transferred. Assigning specific receivables is a financing midpoint. For MBG, factoring progress receivables can be a deliberate working-capital tool — at the cost of the factor's fee.

Internal control over cash

Because cash is the most liquid and most stolen asset, it carries the strongest internal controls: segregation of the custody, recording, and reconciliation functions; daily deposit of receipts intact; payment by pre-numbered check or electronic transfer with dual authorization; and an imprest petty-cash system replenished only with documented receipts. A lockbox arrangement, in which customers remit directly to a bank, removes cash from employees' hands entirely. These controls are the operational counterpart to the bank reconciliation — together they make the reported cash figure both accurate and safeguarded.

Presentation and disclosure of receivables

Receivables require disclosure beyond the single net number. The notes separate trade from nontrade receivables, disclose amounts pledged or factored, and present the allowance and the credit-quality information CECL demands — including a rollforward of the allowance and the aging of past-due balances. Receivables expected to be collected beyond one year are classified noncurrent. For MBG, retainage — amounts withheld by owners until a job is complete — is a receivable whose timing of collection must be disclosed, because it can sit on the books well past the normal cycle.

Discounting and dishonored notes

A holder needing cash early can discount a note receivable at a bank: the bank advances the maturity value (principal plus interest) less a discount computed on that maturity value for the remaining term. Whether the transfer is a sale or a borrowing again depends on recourse and control. If the maker later dishonors the note, the holder reclassifies it to an account receivable at maturity value (plus any protest fee) and assesses it for collectibility. These mechanics extend the same financing-versus-sale judgment that governs factored accounts to interest-bearing notes.

CMA bridge

The CMA program managed MBG's receivable turnover and cash conversion cycle; FAR governs how those same receivables are measured — net realizable value, the CECL allowance, and the accounting when they are factored for cash. The day-one CECL reserve directly affects the working-capital ratios the CFO reports.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify cash and cash equivalents (original maturity ≤ 3 months); exclude restricted cash, post-dated checks, IOUs.
  2. Prepare a bank reconciliation (bank side: + deposits in transit, − outstanding checks; book side: + collections, − NSF/charges → journal entries).
  3. State receivables at net realizable value; set the CECL allowance (lifetime expected losses, day one) via percentage-of-sales (expense) or aging (adjust to required balance).
  4. Record notes receivable at present value (effective-interest); account for pledging (collateral) vs factoring (sale, with/without recourse).

Recap: cash equivalents are highly liquid investments maturing in three months or less (restricted cash excluded); a bank reconciliation isolates timing differences, with only book-side items journalized; receivables are carried at net realizable value using the CECL allowance, which books lifetime expected losses at origination and is estimated by percentage-of-sales (expense) or aging (adjust the allowance to a required balance, e.g., a $70,000 entry to reach $90,000); notes receivable are measured at present value with effective-interest amortization; and receivables are monetized by pledging (collateral) or factoring (a sale, with or without recourse).

flashcards.back: Short-term, highly liquid investments with ORIGINAL maturity ≤ 3 months (T-bills, money-market funds). Restricted cash, post-dated checks, and IOUs are NOT cash.
Only BOOK-side adjustments (interest/notes collected, NSF, bank charges) get journal entries. Bank side: + deposits in transit, − outstanding checks (no entry).
Gross receivable − allowance for credit losses − anticipated sales discounts/returns.

Current expected credit loss model: recognize LIFETIME expected credit losses at origination (day-one reserve) using history, current conditions, and reasonable/supportable forecasts. Replaced incurred-loss.
% of sales (income-statement): expense = % × credit sales, ignore existing allowance. Aging (balance-sheet): compute required ending allowance, adjust the allowance up/down to that target.
Required allowance $90,000, existing credit balance $20,000 → entry: Dr credit-loss expense / Cr allowance $70,000.
Dr allowance, Cr accounts receivable. NO effect on net receivables or expense (both gross A/R and allowance drop).
Pledging: receivables are collateral for a loan (stay on books). Factoring: sell receivables — without recourse (buyer bears loss, final sale) or with recourse (seller retains risk).

questions.q: To qualify as a cash equivalent, an investment must have an original maturity of:
questions.explain: Cash equivalents are highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less.

questions.q: In a bank reconciliation, which item requires a journal entry on the company's books?
choices: An NSF check returned by the bank
questions.explain: Only book-side items (NSF checks, bank charges, collections) are journalized; deposits in transit and outstanding checks adjust the bank side.

questions.q: The CECL model requires an entity to recognize:
choices: Lifetime expected credit losses at origination
Losses only when probable and incurred
questions.explain: ASC 326 (CECL) books lifetime expected credit losses on day one, replacing the incurred-loss model.

questions.q: Aging shows a required allowance of $90,000; the allowance has a $20,000 credit balance. The credit-loss entry is:
questions.explain: Under the balance-sheet (aging) approach, the entry adjusts the allowance to the target: $90,000 − $20,000 = $70,000.

questions.q: Writing off a specific uncollectible account:
choices: Has no effect on net realizable value
questions.explain: A write-off debits the allowance and credits A/R, leaving net receivables and expense unchanged.

questions.q: Selling receivables WITHOUT recourse means:
choices: The buyer absorbs credit losses and the sale is final
The seller still bears all credit risk
The receivables stay on the seller's books as collateral
questions.explain: Without recourse, credit risk transfers to the factor and the receivables are derecognized.

questions.q: A non-interest-bearing note receivable is initially recorded at:
choices: Present value (net of the implied discount)
questions.explain: Notes receivable are recorded at present value; a non-interest-bearing note carries an implied discount amortized to interest income.

weeks.title: FAR U5·W2 — Current Liabilities, Contingencies & Commitments
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the obligations side

The current-liabilities section reports what MBG owes within the year — payables, accruals, warranty reserves — plus the harder judgments of contingencies and commitments. The recognition question is sharp: some obligations are recorded, some are only disclosed, and some are ignored entirely. This week works the classification of current liabilities, the ASC 450 contingency framework, and the related estimates (warranties, compensated absences, asset retirement obligations) that turn uncertain future outflows into today's liabilities.

Defining current liabilities

A current liability is an obligation expected to be settled within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer, using current assets or by creating another current liability. The category includes accounts payable, accrued liabilities (wages, interest, taxes payable), the current portion of long-term debt, and unearned revenue. A short-term obligation expected to be refinanced on a long-term basis is classified as noncurrent only if the entity both intends to refinance and has the ability (a noncancelable agreement) to do so — otherwise it stays current.

Accruals: payroll and compensated absences

Several liabilities accrue as employees work. Payroll liabilities include amounts withheld from employees (income tax, the employee share of FICA) and the employer's own payroll taxes (the matching FICA, unemployment) — the withheld amounts are a liability until remitted. Compensated absences (vacation, sick pay) are accrued when the right vests or accumulates, the obligation relates to services already rendered, payment is probable, and the amount is estimable — so MBG records a vacation liability as employees earn the time, not when they take it.

Warranties

A product or service warranty creates a liability for the estimated future cost of honoring it. An assurance-type warranty (the product will work as promised) is not a separate performance obligation — the entity accrues the estimated warranty cost as an expense in the period of sale (matching). A service-type warranty (an extended or separately priced warranty) is a separate performance obligation under ASC 606, so its price is deferred and recognized as revenue over the coverage period. Worked example: if MBG estimates warranty costs at 2% of $5,000,000 in sales, it accrues a $100,000 warranty expense and liability, drawing the liability down as actual repairs occur.

Loss contingencies — the ASC 450 framework

A loss contingency — pending litigation, a product recall, a guarantee — is evaluated on two axes: the likelihood of the loss and whether it is reasonably estimable. The rule: if a loss is probable AND estimable, accrue it (record the liability and expense; use the best estimate, or the low end of a range when no amount is better than another). If it is only reasonably possible (or probable but not estimable), disclose it in the notes. If it is remote, generally ignore it (with narrow exceptions, like guarantees). This probable/reasonably-possible/remote matrix is one of FAR's most tested judgments.

Gain contingencies and commitments

Gain contingencies are treated conservatively: they are not accrued (to avoid recognizing income before it is realized) and are disclosed only when their realization is probable. Commitments — such as a noncancelable purchase commitment to buy materials at a fixed price — are generally disclosed, but if the market price has fallen below the contracted price by year-end, the entity recognizes a loss on the purchase commitment for the decline, paralleling lower-of-cost rules. The asymmetry — accrue probable losses, defer gains — reflects accounting conservatism.

Asset retirement obligations

An asset retirement obligation (ARO) under ASC 410 is a legal obligation to retire a long-lived asset — to dismantle a structure or restore a site at the end of its use. The entity recognizes the ARO at the fair value (present value) of the future cost when incurred, with a corresponding increase to the asset's carrying amount; the asset portion is then depreciated and the liability is accreted (accretion expense) up to its future settlement amount. For a contractor with site-restoration duties, the ARO puts the eventual cleanup cost on the balance sheet the day the obligation arises.

Other current liabilities

Several recurring items round out the section. Unearned (deferred) revenue — a customer deposit or advance — is a liability until the performance obligation is satisfied. Premiums and coupons (customer-incentive programs) require accruing the estimated cost of redemptions outstanding. Refundable deposits and sales-tax payable (collected from customers and owed to the government) are liabilities, not revenue. Each reflects the same principle: an inflow the entity has not yet earned, or an amount it holds on behalf of others, is an obligation rather than income.

Accruing bonuses and other estimated costs

Many obligations require estimating an amount tied to results. A bonus or profit-sharing liability is accrued when the entity has a present obligation from past service and the amount is estimable — sometimes computed as a percentage of income, which can be circular when the bonus is based on income after the bonus, requiring an algebraic solution. Property taxes are accrued ratably over the fiscal period they cover. The common thread is the accrual principle: an expense and liability are recorded in the period the obligating event occurs, not when cash is eventually paid.

Contingencies in practice: litigation and guarantees

The contingency rules are applied most often to litigation. The entity, with counsel, assesses the likelihood of an unfavorable outcome and the range of loss; a letter of audit inquiry to the client's attorney (from AUD) corroborates the assessment. Guarantees are a special case — even a remote guarantee of another's debt is disclosed, and a standby guarantee is initially recognized at fair value as a liability. These applications show the matrix is not mechanical: it requires judgment about probability and estimability, exactly the area where management bias is a risk.

Exit and disposal costs

One more accrual deserves note: a liability for exit or disposal activities (restructuring) — such as one-time termination benefits or the cost to vacate a facility — is recognized only when the obligation is incurred, not when management merely commits to a plan. A liability cannot be booked simply because a restructuring was announced; there must be a present obligation meeting the recognition criteria. This rule prevents the old practice of front-loading a large "big bath" restructuring reserve, and it reinforces that a liability requires a genuine present obligation, not just an intention.

CMA bridge

The CMA program forecasts MBG's payables and accrued costs for the cash budget; FAR decides which obligations are recognized versus merely disclosed. The contingency matrix is exactly the judgment a CFO faces with a pending construction-defect claim — accrue, disclose, or ignore — and it directly affects reported liabilities and equity.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify current vs noncurrent (≤ 1 year/operating cycle); keep a refinanceable short-term obligation current unless intent AND ability to refinance exist.
  2. Accrue payroll withholdings, compensated absences (vesting/accumulating), and assurance-type warranties; defer service-type warranty revenue.
  3. Apply ASC 450: probable + estimable → accrue (low end of a range if needed); reasonably possible → disclose; remote → ignore. Gain contingencies are not accrued.
  4. Record an ARO at present value with accretion + depreciation; treat unearned revenue, premiums, deposits, and sales tax as liabilities.

Recap: current liabilities settle within a year or the operating cycle, and a refinanceable short-term debt stays current absent both intent and ability to refinance; entities accrue payroll, compensated absences, and assurance-type warranties (2% of $5,000,000 sales = a $100,000 accrual) while deferring service-type warranty revenue; ASC 450 accrues a loss that is probable and estimable, discloses a reasonably possible one, and ignores a remote one, with gain contingencies never accrued; and an ARO is recorded at present value with later accretion and depreciation.

flashcards.back: Settled within one year or the operating cycle (whichever is longer) using current assets or by creating another current liability.
Classify as noncurrent ONLY if the entity intends to refinance AND has the ability (noncancelable agreement); otherwise it stays current.
Assurance (works as promised): accrue estimated cost as expense at sale (not a separate obligation). Service-type (extended/priced): a separate ASC 606 obligation — defer revenue over coverage.
Probable AND estimable → ACCRUE (best estimate; low end of range if none better). Reasonably possible (or not estimable) → DISCLOSE. Remote → ignore.
Never accrued (conservatism); disclose only if realization is probable.
A noncancelable fixed-price purchase commitment whose market price falls below contract price by year-end → recognize a loss for the decline.
Recognize legal retirement obligation at fair value (PV) when incurred + add to asset cost; later depreciate the asset and accrete the liability (accretion expense).
Accrue when the right vests or accumulates, relates to services already rendered, payment is probable, and the amount is estimable.

questions.q: A loss contingency is accrued when it is:
questions.explain: ASC 450 requires accrual when a loss is both probable and reasonably estimable; reasonably possible losses are disclosed.

questions.q: When a loss is probable and the estimate is a range with no better point in it, the entity accrues:
choices: The low end of the range
questions.explain: If no amount in the range is a better estimate, the minimum (low end) is accrued.

questions.q: A gain contingency is:
choices: Not accrued; disclosed only if probable
questions.explain: Conservatism prevents accruing gain contingencies; disclose only if realization is probable.

questions.q: An assurance-type warranty is accounted for by:
choices: Accruing estimated warranty cost as expense in the period of sale
Deferring revenue over the coverage period
Recording it only when claims are paid
questions.explain: Assurance warranties accrue estimated cost at sale; service-type warranties defer revenue under ASC 606.

questions.q: Warranty estimated at 2% of $5,000,000 sales produces a warranty expense/liability of:
questions.explain: 2% × $5,000,000 = $100,000 accrued at the time of sale.

questions.q: A short-term obligation may be classified as noncurrent only if the entity:
choices: Intends and has the ability to refinance long-term
questions.explain: Both intent and demonstrated ability (e.g., a noncancelable refinancing agreement) are required.

questions.q: An asset retirement obligation is initially measured at:
choices: The present value (fair value) of the future retirement cost
questions.explain: An ARO is recognized at fair value (present value) when incurred, with later accretion to the settlement amount.

weeks.title: FAR U5·W3 — Fair Value, Nonmonetary Exchanges & Accounting Changes
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — measurement and corrections

Three cross-cutting topics finish the measurement toolkit: how fair value is defined and ranked under ASC 820, how nonmonetary exchanges are recorded when one asset is swapped for another, and how accounting changes and errors are reported under ASC 250. Each appears across the statements — a Level 3 fair value, an equipment trade-in, a switch in inventory method — and each has a precise rule about what to record now and what to restate.

Fair value defined

Fair value (ASC 820) is an exit price — the price to sell an asset or transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. It is market-based, not entity-specific, and is measured in the principal market (or, absent one, the most advantageous market). Three valuation approaches may be used: the market approach (comparable prices), the income approach (discounted future cash flows), and the cost approach (current replacement cost). Fair value assumes the asset's highest and best use.

The fair-value hierarchy

ASC 820 ranks the inputs to a fair-value measurement, maximizing observable data. Level 1 inputs are quoted prices in active markets for identical assets (the most reliable). Level 2 inputs are observable but not Level 1 — quoted prices for similar assets, or observable rates and yields. Level 3 inputs are unobservable, reflecting the entity's own assumptions in a model (the least reliable, requiring the most disclosure). The level of the measurement is set by the lowest-level significant input, and the classification drives the audit scrutiny from AUD Unit 3.

Nonmonetary exchanges — the general rule

When a company swaps one nonmonetary asset for another (ASC 845), the general rule is to record the asset received at fair value and recognize the full gain or loss — the difference between the fair value and the book value of the asset given up. MBG trading a used loader plus cash for a different machine would normally recognize gain or loss immediately. The key question that can override this rule is whether the exchange has commercial substance.

Commercial substance and its exception

An exchange has commercial substance if the entity's future cash flows are expected to change significantly as a result (different amounts, timing, or risk). If it does, record at fair value and recognize the full gain or loss. If the exchange lacks commercial substance (e.g., trading similar assets), gains are generally deferred — the asset received is recorded at the book value (carryover basis) of the asset given up, so no gain is recognized (a loss is still recognized). The exception exists because a swap of essentially equivalent assets has not culminated an earnings process.

Boot in a no-commercial-substance exchange

A wrinkle arises when boot (cash) changes hands in an exchange lacking commercial substance. The party paying boot recognizes no gain. The party receiving boot recognizes a proportionate gain if the boot is less than 25% of the total consideration — the recognized gain equals total gain × (boot received ÷ total consideration received). If boot is 25% or more, the entire transaction is treated as monetary and both parties recognize the full gain. The 25% threshold is the dividing line tested on the exam.

Accounting changes — principle versus estimate

ASC 250 sorts changes into types with different treatments. A change in accounting principle (e.g., FIFO to weighted-average) is applied retrospectively — prior-period statements are restated and the cumulative effect adjusts the opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented. A change in accounting estimate (revised useful life, bad-debt rate) is applied prospectively — only the current and future periods are affected, with no restatement. When a change in principle is inseparable from a change in estimate (such as a change in depreciation method), it is treated as a change in estimate — prospective.

Reporting-entity changes and error corrections

Two more categories complete the framework. A change in reporting entity (e.g., presenting consolidated rather than separate statements) is applied retrospectively for all periods presented. An error correction — a mistake in a previously issued statement (a math error, a misapplied principle, fraud) — is not an accounting change; it is corrected by restating the prior-period statements, with a prior-period adjustment to the beginning balance of retained earnings. Distinguishing an error (restate) from an estimate change (prospective) is a frequent exam trap, because both can involve a revised number.

Disclosures and the fair value of liabilities

ASC 820 also governs measuring a liability at fair value — the price to transfer it to a market participant, incorporating the entity's own nonperformance risk (including its credit standing). Extensive disclosures accompany fair-value measurement: the level of each measurement, the valuation techniques and inputs, and for recurring Level 3 items a reconciliation of beginning-to-ending balances and the sensitivity of the measurement to the unobservable inputs. The disclosure burden rises as the inputs become less observable, precisely because Level 3 estimates are the least verifiable.

Retrospective application and its limits

Applying a change in principle retrospectively means restating each prior period presented as if the new principle had always been used, then adjusting the opening balance of retained earnings for the cumulative effect on periods before the earliest one shown. When it is impracticable to determine the period-specific or cumulative effects, the entity applies the new principle prospectively from the earliest date practicable. The goal of retrospective treatment is comparability — readers can compare years on a consistent basis — which is exactly why an error, which also distorts comparability, is likewise corrected by restatement rather than buried in current income.

Disclosing an accounting change

An accounting change carries its own disclosure requirements. For a change in principle, the entity discloses the nature and justification (why the new method is preferable), the method of applying it, and the effect on income, earnings per share, and the affected line items for each period presented. A material change in estimate is disclosed with its effect on current income. The disclosures let users understand why the comparatives moved — distinguishing a genuine economic change from a mere change in how the same events are reported.

CMA bridge

When MBG remeasures an asset to fair value, trades equipment, or switches an accounting method, FAR dictates the mechanics; the CMA program then explains the effect on the metrics. A retrospective principle change restates the comparatives the CFO presents to lenders, while an estimate change flows only forward — a distinction that matters when explaining a swing in reported results.

Practice and recap

  1. Define fair value as an exit price in the principal market; rank inputs Level 1 (quoted/identical) > Level 2 (observable) > Level 3 (unobservable), using the lowest significant input.
  2. Record nonmonetary exchanges at fair value with full gain/loss when there is commercial substance; defer gain (carryover basis) when there is none.
  3. Apply the boot rule for no-commercial-substance exchanges: payer recognizes no gain; receiver recognizes proportionate gain if boot < 25%, full gain if ≥ 25%.
  4. Classify ASC 250 changes: principle = retrospective; estimate = prospective; depreciation-method/inseparable = prospective (estimate); reporting entity = retrospective; error = restate (prior-period adjustment).

Recap: fair value is an exit price measured in the principal market, with inputs ranked Level 1 (quoted/identical) to Level 3 (unobservable) and the measurement set by the lowest significant input; nonmonetary exchanges record at fair value with full gain when they have commercial substance but defer gain at carryover basis when they do not (with a 25% boot threshold splitting proportionate from full gain recognition); and ASC 250 applies principle changes retrospectively, estimate changes (including depreciation-method changes) prospectively, reporting-entity changes retrospectively, and error corrections by restatement through a prior-period adjustment.

flashcards.back: Exit price to sell an asset / transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants, in the principal (or most advantageous) market. Market-based, not entity-specific.
Level 1: quoted prices, identical assets, active markets. Level 2: observable (similar assets, rates). Level 3: unobservable (model/own assumptions). Classified by the lowest significant input.
Record asset received at fair value; recognize full gain/loss (FV − book value of asset given up).
Future cash flows change significantly → fair value, full gain/loss. Lacks commercial substance → carryover (book) basis, defer gain (loss still recognized).
Payer of boot: no gain. Receiver: proportionate gain if boot < 25% [gain × boot/total]; full gain if boot ≥ 25% (treated as monetary, both recognize full gain).
Principle (e.g., FIFO→avg): retrospective, adjust opening retained earnings. Estimate (useful life, bad-debt %): prospective, no restatement.
A change in principle inseparable from a change in estimate → treated as a change in ESTIMATE → prospective.
Error in a prior issued statement → restate prior periods with a prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings (not an accounting change). Estimate change → prospective.

questions.q: Under ASC 820, fair value is:
choices: An exit price in the principal market
The entity's intended sale price to a related party
questions.explain: Fair value is the exit price to sell/transfer in an orderly transaction in the principal market.

questions.q: A fair-value measurement using a quoted price for a similar (not identical) asset is:
questions.explain: Quoted prices for similar assets are observable Level 2 inputs; identical-asset quotes are Level 1.

questions.q: A nonmonetary exchange that LACKS commercial substance is generally recorded at:
choices: The carryover (book) basis of the asset given up, deferring gain
questions.explain: Without commercial substance, gains are deferred — the asset received is recorded at carryover basis.

questions.q: In an exchange lacking commercial substance, the party PAYING boot recognizes:
questions.explain: The payer of boot recognizes no gain; the receiver may recognize a proportionate gain if boot < 25%.

questions.q: A change from FIFO to weighted-average inventory is applied:
questions.explain: A change in accounting principle is applied retrospectively.

questions.q: A change in the estimated useful life of equipment is applied:
questions.explain: A change in estimate is prospective, affecting only current and future periods.

questions.q: Correcting an error in a previously issued financial statement requires:
choices: Restating prior periods with a prior-period adjustment to retained earnings
questions.explain: Errors are corrected by restating prior periods, with a prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings.

weeks.title: FAR U5·W4 — Consolidated Financial Statements: Eliminations & Noncontrolling Interest
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — one economic entity

When a parent controls a subsidiary, GAAP requires consolidated financial statements that present the two as a single economic entity. BAR Unit 1 covered the acquisition-date accounting (ASC 805 — fair values, goodwill, measuring noncontrolling interest); this week covers the ongoing consolidation procedures — combining the books, eliminating intercompany transactions, and reporting the noncontrolling interest. For a multi-entity group like MBG and its affiliates, this is how the separate ledgers become one set of statements.

When to consolidate

Consolidation is required when one entity has a controlling financial interest in another — generally more than 50% of the voting interest, or being the primary beneficiary of a variable interest entity (VIE) (the party with power over the activities that most affect performance and exposure to its losses/returns). Control, not mere ownership percentage, is the trigger. Below control, the investment is reported under the equity method (significant influence) or as a financial asset, as covered in FAR Unit 2 — consolidation applies only when control exists.

The consolidation process

Consolidation combines 100% of the subsidiary's assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses with the parent's — even when the parent owns less than 100% — and then removes the double-counting through elimination entries made only on the consolidation worksheet (never on the separate books). The first elimination removes the parent's investment account against the subsidiary's equity at acquisition, establishing any goodwill and the noncontrolling interest. The remaining eliminations remove the effects of transactions between the affiliated companies, because a single economic entity cannot transact with itself.

Noncontrolling interest

The noncontrolling interest (NCI) is the portion of a subsidiary's equity not owned by the parent. Under current GAAP it is reported within consolidated equity — separately from the parent's equity — not as a liability or mezzanine item. Each period, consolidated net income is split between the amount attributable to the parent and the amount attributable to the NCI (the NCI's ownership percentage of the subsidiary's net income, adjusted for any fair-value depreciation and downstream/upstream profit). Total consolidated net income includes both shares; only the parent's portion flows to the parent's retained earnings.

Eliminating intercompany balances

The simplest eliminations remove intercompany balances and transactions that net to zero for the combined entity. Intercompany receivables and payables (a loan between parent and subsidiary) are eliminated against each other. Intercompany sales and the related cost of goods sold are eliminated so consolidated revenue reflects only sales to outside parties. Intercompany dividends paid by the subsidiary to the parent are eliminated. None of these affect consolidated net income on their own — they simply prevent inflating both sides of the statements with internal activity.

Unrealized intercompany inventory profit

The harder eliminations involve unrealized profit still inside the group. When one affiliate sells inventory to another at a markup and the buyer has not yet resold it to an outside party, the profit is unrealized and must be deferred — eliminated from consolidated income and from ending inventory. Worked example: the parent sells inventory costing $60,000 to the subsidiary for $100,000; if the subsidiary still holds it at year-end, the $40,000 intercompany profit is eliminated, reducing consolidated inventory to its original $60,000 cost. The profit is recognized only when the goods are sold outside the group.

Intercompany fixed assets and bonds

Two other unrealized items recur. On an intercompany sale of a depreciable fixed asset, the gain is eliminated at the date of sale and then realized gradually as the buyer depreciates the asset (an adjustment each year over its remaining life). On intercompany bonds — when one affiliate buys the other's debt from the market — the bonds are treated as retired in the consolidated statements, and any difference between the purchase price and carrying amount is a gain or loss on constructive retirement. Both ensure the consolidated entity reports only transactions with the outside world.

Upstream versus downstream

The direction of an intercompany sale matters for the NCI. A downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) generates profit on the parent's books, so deferred profit reduces only the parent's share of income. An upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) generates profit on the subsidiary's books, so the deferred unrealized profit is allocated between the parent and the NCI in proportion to ownership. Getting the direction right is what makes the split of consolidated net income between parent and NCI correct — a frequently tested nuance.

The consolidation worksheet

In practice, consolidation is performed on a worksheet that lists the parent and subsidiary trial balances in adjacent columns, adds elimination columns (debits and credits), and extends to a consolidated column. The eliminations are not posted to either company's books — they exist only on the worksheet and are re-created each period because the separate ledgers still contain the intercompany amounts. A common beginning-of-year elimination reverses the prior period's deferred profit so it is realized in the year the inventory is finally sold outside, keeping the cumulative consolidated income correct across periods.

Combined statements and push-down accounting

Two related presentations round out consolidation. Combined financial statements present entities under common control (e.g., affiliated companies owned by the same individual) without a parent-subsidiary relationship — using the same intercompany eliminations but no investment-elimination entry. Push-down accounting lets an acquired subsidiary restate its own books to the acquisition-date fair values, so its separate statements already reflect the new basis. Both are tools for presenting related entities faithfully, and both rest on the same elimination discipline that prevents a group from counting internal activity as real results.

Mid-year acquisitions and preacquisition earnings

When a subsidiary is acquired during the year, the consolidated income statement includes the subsidiary's revenues and expenses only from the acquisition date forward — the subsidiary's preacquisition earnings are excluded from consolidated net income. The balance sheet, however, consolidates the subsidiary in full at year-end, and the noncontrolling interest's share of income is likewise measured only on post-acquisition results. This timing convention ensures the group reports only the results it actually controlled, and it is a common exam wrinkle layered on top of the elimination mechanics.

CMA bridge

MBG's intercompany loans, equipment transfers, and material sales among affiliated entities are exactly the transactions these eliminations remove. The CMA program tracks the separate-entity results; FAR consolidation shows the group's true position to outside lenders by stripping out everything the affiliates did with each other — the same reciprocal-account discipline used in intercompany reconciliations.

Practice and recap

  1. Consolidate when control exists (>50% voting or VIE primary beneficiary); combine 100% of the subsidiary even if less than wholly owned.
  2. Eliminate the investment against subsidiary equity (establishing goodwill and NCI); report NCI within consolidated equity and split net income between parent and NCI.
  3. Eliminate intercompany receivables/payables, sales/COGS, and dividends; defer unrealized intercompany inventory profit until resold outside.
  4. Eliminate intercompany fixed-asset gains (realize over depreciation) and treat intercompany bonds as constructively retired; allocate upstream (not downstream) deferred profit between parent and NCI.

Recap: consolidation applies when a parent controls a subsidiary (>50% voting or VIE primary beneficiary), combining 100% of the subsidiary while eliminating the investment against its equity to establish goodwill and the noncontrolling interest, which sits within consolidated equity; intercompany receivables/payables, sales/COGS, and dividends are eliminated, and unrealized intercompany profit in inventory (a $40,000 markup still on hand) and fixed-asset gains are deferred until realized outside the group, with upstream deferrals — unlike downstream — shared between the parent and the NCI.

flashcards.back: A controlling financial interest: >50% of voting interest, OR being the primary beneficiary of a VIE (power + exposure to losses/returns). Control, not just ownership %, is the trigger.

flashcards.front: Consolidation combines how much of the sub?
flashcards.back: 100% of the subsidiary's assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses — even if the parent owns less than 100% — then eliminate intercompany items on the worksheet only.
The portion of the subsidiary's equity not owned by the parent; reported WITHIN consolidated equity (not a liability). Consolidated net income is split between parent and NCI.
Intercompany receivables/payables, intercompany sales/COGS, and intercompany dividends — so consolidated statements show only transactions with outside parties.
Defer profit on intercompany inventory still held at year-end. Parent sells $60k-cost goods for $100k; sub still holds → eliminate $40k profit, restate inventory to $60k. Recognize when sold outside.
Eliminate the gain at the sale date; realize it gradually as the buyer depreciates the asset over its remaining life.
When one affiliate buys the other's bonds, treat them as constructively retired; difference between price and carrying value = gain/loss on constructive retirement.
Downstream (parent→sub): deferred profit reduces only the parent's income. Upstream (sub→parent): deferred profit is shared between parent and NCI by ownership %.

questions.q: Consolidated financial statements are required when the parent has:
choices: A controlling financial interest (>50% voting or VIE primary beneficiary)
questions.explain: Control — generally >50% of voting interest or being a VIE's primary beneficiary — triggers consolidation.

questions.q: When a parent owns 80% of a subsidiary, consolidation combines:
choices: 100% of the subsidiary, with a 20% noncontrolling interest
questions.explain: Consolidation combines 100% of the subsidiary; the 20% not owned is the noncontrolling interest.

questions.q: The noncontrolling interest is reported:
choices: Within consolidated equity, separate from the parent's equity

units.title: AUD Unit 1 — Engagements & Ethics, the Audit Risk Model & Internal Control

weeks.title: AUD U1·W1 — Engagements, Ethics & Independence (CPA Core · from CMA m5/m12)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — who can audit MBG, and how independent must they be?

Auditing begins before any testing: the right engagement type, the auditor's ethics, and — above all — independence. CMA month 12 covered the IMA ethics standards from the preparer's side; AUD covers the AICPA Code from the auditor's side. The recurring exam theme is that an auditor's value comes entirely from being, and appearing, independent.

Levels of assurance and engagement types

  • Audit — the highest level, reasonable assurance, expressed as a positive opinion that the statements are fairly presented in accordance with the framework.
  • Review — limited (negative) assurance: "we are not aware of any material modifications needed." Based mainly on inquiry and analytical procedures.
  • Compilation — no assurance; the accountant assembles statements from management's data.
  • Examination / agreed-upon procedures — attestation engagements at varying assurance.

Reasonable assurance is high but not absolute — an audit is designed to detect material misstatement, not every error, because of sampling, judgment, and the nature of evidence.

The AICPA Code of Professional Conduct

Core principles: integrity, objectivity, independence, due care, and professional skepticism. The conceptual framework approach asks the CPA to identify threats to compliance (self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, undue influence) and apply safeguards that reduce them to an acceptable level. Professional skepticism — a questioning mind and critical assessment of evidence — runs through the entire audit.

Independence in fact and in appearance

Independence has two dimensions: in fact (an actual unbiased mindset) and in appearance (a reasonable, informed third party would conclude the auditor is unbiased). Both are required. A covered member generally may not have a direct financial interest, or a material indirect interest, in an attest client; may not have certain loans or business relationships; and may not perform management functions for the client. Performing the client's bookkeeping and then auditing it is a self-review threat that typically impairs independence for an issuer.

For MBG's auditor, independence would be impaired by owning an interest in MBG, by a partner's spouse working in MBG's finance function, or by the firm having set up MBG's books and now opining on them. Note independence is required for attest engagements (audit, review, examination) but not for a pure compilation or for non-attest tax/consulting work — though objectivity and integrity always apply.

Engagement acceptance and the preconditions for an audit

Before accepting, the auditor confirms the preconditions: management uses an acceptable financial-reporting framework and acknowledges its responsibility for the statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access to evidence. The terms are set in an engagement letter — the contract documenting the objective and scope, each party’s responsibilities, the inherent limitations, and the framework. For a first-year engagement the successor auditor must, with client permission, communicate with the predecessor auditor about disagreements, fraud or illegal acts, and the reason for the change; the client’s refusal to permit that contact is itself a red flag weighing against acceptance.

Independence frameworks beyond the AICPA

Three rule sets can apply at once. The AICPA Code governs private-company attest work through the threats-and-safeguards framework. For issuers, the stricter SEC and PCAOB rules add: a prohibition on most non-audit services (bookkeeping, financial-system design, internal-audit outsourcing, valuation, and management functions for the same audit client), mandatory audit-partner rotation (lead and concurring partners rotate off after five years), audit-committee pre-approval of all services, and a one-year cooling-off period before an audit-team member can take a key financial-reporting role at the client. Government audits add the GAO’s Yellow Book, whose conceptual framework parallels the AICPA but treats preparing the financial statements as a significant self-review threat requiring safeguards.

Financial interests, family, and employment

The detail of who and what impairs independence is heavily tested. A direct financial interest in an attest client impairs independence regardless of amount; an indirect interest (through a mutual fund, say) impairs only if material. Immediate family (spouse, dependents) are generally subject to the same restrictions as the covered member, so a spouse’s direct investment in the client impairs independence, and a spouse’s employment with the client impairs it if the spouse holds a key position. Close relatives (parents, siblings, nondependent children) impair independence in narrower circumstances — a key-position role or a material financial interest the covered member knows of. Most loans to or from a client impair independence, with narrow exceptions (a car loan or a fully collateralized mortgage from a financial-institution client on normal terms).

Fees, confidentiality, and acts discreditable

Several rules protect objectivity beyond independence. Contingent fees and commissions are prohibited for attest clients, because tying the fee to a result corrupts judgment; they are permitted for some non-attest clients with disclosure. The confidential client information rule bars disclosing client data without consent, subject to exceptions (a valid subpoena, a peer review, an authorized regulatory body). Acts discreditable — retaining client records to coerce payment, discrimination, or signing a materially false return — violate the Code regardless of independence. A CPA must also exercise due professional care, working with the competence and diligence of a reasonably prudent practitioner.

Quality management at the firm level

Independence is reinforced by firm-wide quality management. Under the AICPA’s quality-management standards (and PCAOB standards for issuers), a firm designs a system addressing leadership and the tone at the top, relevant ethical requirements including independence, acceptance and continuance of clients, engagement performance, resources, and monitoring and remediation. An engagement quality review — an objective partner not on the engagement reviewing significant judgments and the report before issuance — is required for issuer audits and certain others. The thread tying the week together: the auditor’s opinion is worth nothing unless the firm and the individual are competent, objective, and independent in both fact and appearance — everything in the rest of the audit assumes it.

The period of independence and network firms

Independence must be maintained throughout both the period of the professional engagement and the period covered by the financial statements, so a financial interest held even before the engagement letter is signed can impair independence for the year under audit. The rules also reach beyond the individual firm: in an alliance or network of firms, other network firms must be independent of an audit client where it is reasonable to expect the network is associated with the engagement. When an independence problem is discovered, the firm evaluates its significance, applies safeguards or removes the affected individuals, and documents the resolution. Independence is ultimately judged from the perspective of a reasonable and informed third party weighing all the facts — not from the auditor’s own belief that they remain objective.

CMA bridge

CMA month 12's IMA standards (integrity, credibility) parallel the AICPA principles; the difference is the auditor's independence requirement, which has no exact CMA counterpart because the management accountant is internal. Both, though, demand objectivity and a refusal to misrepresent.

Practice and recap

  1. Match engagement type to assurance level: audit (reasonable/positive), review (limited/negative), compilation (none).
  2. Apply the AICPA principles and the threats-and-safeguards framework; maintain professional skepticism.
  3. Require independence in fact and in appearance for attest engagements.
  4. Identify relationships that impair independence (financial interest, self-review, management functions).

Recap: an audit gives reasonable (not absolute) assurance via a positive opinion; the AICPA Code centers on integrity, objectivity, due care, skepticism, and — uniquely — independence in fact and appearance, which bookkeeping-then-auditing or a financial interest in the client would impair.

Limited (negative) assurance, based on inquiry and analytical procedures.
None — the accountant assembles statements without assurance.
No — reasonable but not absolute, due to sampling, judgment, and the nature of evidence.
Independence in fact (actual unbiased mindset) and in appearance (a reasonable third party's view).

flashcards.front: Five threats in the AICPA conceptual framework
flashcards.back: Self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, and undue influence.
A questioning mind and critical assessment of audit evidence throughout the engagement.
No (lack of independence is disclosed); attest engagements—audit, review, examination—require it.

questions.explain: A review gives limited assurance — 'no material modifications needed' — based on inquiry and analytics.

weeks.title: AUD U1·W2 — The Audit Risk Model & Materiality (CPA Core · from CMA m10)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — how much testing is enough?

The audit risk model is the engine that answers "how much evidence do we need?" It links the risk of material misstatement to the amount of substantive testing the auditor must perform. CMA month 10 assessed business risk; AUD turns risk assessment into a testing plan through this model and the materiality thresholds that frame it.

The audit risk model

Audit risk = Inherent risk × Control risk × Detection risk.

  • Audit risk (AR) — the risk the auditor gives an unmodified opinion on materially misstated statements. The auditor sets it low (commonly ~5%).
  • Inherent risk (IR) — susceptibility to misstatement before controls (estimates, complex transactions). The auditor assesses but cannot change it.
  • Control risk (CR) — risk that internal control fails to prevent/detect a misstatement. Assessed, not controlled by the auditor.
  • Detection risk (DR) — risk the auditor's procedures fail to catch a misstatement. This is the only component the auditor controls, by changing the nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures.

Solving for detection risk

Rearranging: DR = AR ÷ (IR × CR). The product IR × CR is the risk of material misstatement (RMM). Illustrative: target AR 5%, IR 80%, CR 50%. RMM = 0.80 × 0.50 = 40%. DR = 0.05 ÷ 0.40 = 0.125 (12.5%).

The key relationship is inverse: the higher the RMM, the lower the acceptable detection risk, which means the auditor must do more and better substantive testing — larger samples, more reliable evidence, and procedures performed at year-end rather than interim. When controls are strong (low CR), the auditor can accept higher DR and test less substantively (after testing those controls).

Materiality

Misstatements matter only if they could influence users' decisions. The auditor sets:

  • Overall (planning) materiality — usually a percentage of a benchmark (pre-tax income, revenue, or total assets) appropriate to the entity.
  • Performance materiality — set below overall materiality to reduce the chance that the aggregate of undetected and uncorrected misstatements exceeds overall materiality.
  • Clearly trivial threshold — amounts below which misstatements need not be accumulated.

Materiality has a quantitative and a qualitative side: a small misstatement can be material if it changes a loss to a profit, hides a trend, or affects debt covenants — exactly the kind of bank-covenant sensitivity MBG's surety and lenders watch.

Risk assessment procedures

The auditor does not guess at inherent and control risk — they are grounded in required risk assessment procedures: obtaining an understanding of the entity and its environment (industry, regulation, business model), its internal control, and the applicable framework. The procedures are inquiry of management and others, analytical procedures, observation, and inspection of documents. Risk assessment procedures alone do not provide sufficient audit evidence for an opinion — they direct where the substantive work goes. A required part of this phase is the engagement team discussion (the brainstorming session) about where the statements are susceptible to material misstatement, including from fraud.

Assertions — the unit of audit risk

Risk and materiality ultimately attach to management assertions embedded in the statements, and procedures are designed assertion by assertion. For account balances: existence, completeness, rights and obligations, and valuation/allocation. For transactions: occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cutoff, and classification. For presentation and disclosure: occurrence and rights, completeness, accuracy/valuation, and understandability. The auditor maps each significant risk to the specific assertion at stake — for a contractor, the existence of recorded receivables and the cutoff and accuracy of percentage-of-completion revenue are typically the assertions most at risk.

Significant risks and the revenue presumption

Some risks demand special audit consideration. A significant risk — one with higher inherent risk due to complexity, subjectivity, or fraud potential — requires substantive procedures specifically responsive to it and prohibits relying on prior-period control testing without re-testing the controls. Auditing standards presume revenue recognition is a fraud risk unless that presumption is rebutted, because revenue is the account most often manipulated; for a contractor that means heightened scrutiny of estimated costs to complete and the timing of recognized revenue. Significant risks frequently involve accounting estimates with measurement uncertainty, where the auditor evaluates the data, assumptions, and method management used.

From risk to response — nature, timing, extent

The assessed risk drives the further audit procedures along three dimensions. Nature: more reliable evidence for higher risk — external confirmations and inspection over inquiry, and tests of detail over analytics. Timing: testing at year-end rather than interim when risk is high, since interim testing leaves a roll-forward gap. Extent: larger sample sizes as the desired detection risk falls. Procedures are either tests of controls (do the controls operate?) or substantive procedures (tests of detail and substantive analytics); a dual-purpose test does both at once. The auditor responds to financial-statement-level risk with overall responses (more experienced staff, heightened skepticism) and to assertion-level risk with specific procedures.

Analytical procedures and revisiting materiality

Analytical procedures — evaluating financial data through plausible relationships — are required in the risk-assessment (planning) phase and again in the final review near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion; they are optional as a substantive procedure during fieldwork. Materiality is not static: if the auditor learns the benchmark was wrong (actual income differs sharply from the estimate used), materiality is revised and the planned procedures reconsidered. At the end, the auditor accumulates identified misstatements, compares them to materiality, and asks management to correct them — uncorrected misstatements above the clearly-trivial threshold are evaluated, individually and in aggregate, against overall materiality to decide whether the opinion must be modified. Risk and materiality thus bracket the entire audit: they size the work at the start and judge the result at the finish.

Sufficient appropriate evidence and sampling

The output of the risk model is a plan to gather sufficient appropriate audit evidence — sufficiency is the quantity (more is needed as risk rises) and appropriateness is the quality, comprising relevance (does it address the assertion?) and reliability (higher when from independent external sources, under effective controls, in documentary form, or obtained directly by the auditor). Evidence from a knowledgeable source outside the entity, such as a bank confirmation, outweighs the same fact asserted only by management. Because testing every item is rarely economical, the auditor often uses audit sampling, accepting a measured sampling risk that the sample is not representative; lowering the tolerable detection risk drives larger samples. The model, the assertions, materiality, and the evidence standard thus form one chain: risk sets how much and how good the evidence must be, and sampling delivers it efficiently.

CMA bridge

CMA month 10 quantified business risk (likelihood × impact, VaR); AUD's risk model is the audit analogue — assess inherent and control risk, then set detection risk to hold audit risk low. The mindset is identical: more risk demands more rigor.

Practice and recap

  1. Know AR = IR × CR × DR and that DR is the only component the auditor controls.
  2. Compute DR = AR ÷ (IR × CR); RMM = IR × CR.
  3. Apply the inverse relationship: higher RMM → lower DR → more substantive testing.
  4. Set overall and (lower) performance materiality; weigh qualitative materiality.

Recap: with AR 5%, IR 80%, and CR 50%, the risk of material misstatement is 40% and detection risk must be 12.5% — a low DR that forces extensive substantive testing. Performance materiality sits below overall materiality, and small misstatements can still be qualitatively material.

DR = AR ÷ (IR × CR).
Inherent risk × control risk (IR × CR).
Inverse: higher RMM → lower acceptable DR → more substantive testing.
Performance materiality is set below overall materiality to buffer aggregation risk.
A small misstatement that turns a loss into a profit or breaches a covenant is material.
