weeks.title: AUD U2·W2 — Audit Sampling (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — testing a slice of the whole

The auditor cannot examine every one of MBG's thousands of transactions, so it tests a sample and projects the result to the population. Audit sampling is applying a procedure to less than 100% of a population such that every item could be selected, to draw a conclusion about the whole. The discipline is managing the risk that the sample misleads — the subject of this heavily tested week.

Sampling risk versus nonsampling risk

Two risks attend a sample. Sampling risk is the risk that the sample is not representative, so a conclusion drawn from it differs from the conclusion the auditor would reach by testing the whole population — it is inherent to sampling and is controlled by sample size. Nonsampling risk is the risk of a wrong conclusion for any other reason — using an inappropriate procedure, misinterpreting evidence, or failing to recognize a misstatement — and is controlled by training, supervision, and review, not sample size.

Attribute sampling for tests of controls

Attribute sampling tests a rate of occurrence — how often a control fails (a deviation) — to decide whether to rely on the control. Sample size grows with the expected deviation rate and the desired confidence, and shrinks as the tolerable deviation rate (the maximum failure rate the auditor will accept and still rely) rises. Note that population size has little effect on sample size for a large population — a counterintuitive but tested point.

Evaluating a controls sample

After testing, the auditor computes the sample deviation rate (deviations ÷ sample size) and adds an allowance for sampling risk to get the upper deviation rate. If the upper deviation rate is at or below the tolerable rate, the auditor may rely on the control as planned; if it exceeds tolerable, the auditor cannot rely and must increase substantive testing. Worked example: with a tolerable deviation rate of 7%, a sample of 60 yields 2 deviations — a 3.3% sample rate; if the resulting upper deviation rate (say 6.5%) stays at or below 7%, reliance is supported.

Sampling risks in tests of controls

Two sampling risks have opposite consequences. The risk of assessing control risk too low (overreliance) is the danger that the sample suggests a control works when it does not — this relates to effectiveness and is the more serious risk, because it leads the auditor to do too little substantive work. The risk of assessing control risk too high (underreliance) suggests a good control is bad — a problem of efficiency, leading to unnecessary testing. Auditors guard most carefully against the effectiveness risk.

Substantive sampling and monetary-unit sampling

For substantive tests the auditor samples dollar amounts, not occurrence rates. Monetary-unit sampling (MUS), also called probability-proportional-to-size, treats each dollar as a sampling unit, so larger balances are automatically more likely to be selected — efficient when the auditor expects few misstatements and is testing for overstatement (it is the standard tool for receivables). MUS projects a most likely misstatement plus an allowance to an upper misstatement limit, compared against tolerable misstatement. A weakness: MUS handles understatement and zero/negative balances poorly.

Classical variables sampling

Classical variables sampling uses statistical estimation of an amount rather than a rate, with methods like mean-per-unit, ratio, and difference estimation. It is better suited than MUS when the auditor expects a larger number of misstatements or is concerned with understatement (testing completeness, such as searching for unrecorded liabilities). The trade-off is that it requires an estimate of the population's standard deviation and is more complex, but it gives a two-sided estimate MUS cannot.

Sampling risks in substantive tests

Substantive sampling has its own paired risks. The risk of incorrect acceptance is concluding a materially misstated balance is fairly stated — an effectiveness risk that, like overreliance, undermines the audit and is guarded against most. The risk of incorrect rejection is concluding a fairly stated balance is misstated — an efficiency problem that causes wasted work (extended testing that eventually clears the balance). Sample size rises as the auditor seeks to lower incorrect acceptance, as tolerable misstatement falls, and as expected misstatement rises.

Selecting the sample

How items are chosen affects whether a sample is representative. Random selection gives every item an equal chance; systematic selection takes every nth item after a random start (efficient, but risky if the population follows a pattern); monetary-unit selection picks dollars (favoring large balances); and haphazard selection is a non-statistical attempt at randomness without conscious bias. Block selection — choosing contiguous items — is generally inappropriate, because a block is unlikely to represent the population. Statistical sampling lets the auditor measure sampling risk; nonstatistical sampling relies on judgment; both are permitted if properly designed.

Factors that drive sample size

The exam rewards knowing how each factor moves sample size. For tests of controls, sample size increases with higher desired confidence and a higher expected deviation rate, and decreases as the tolerable deviation rate rises. For substantive tests, sample size increases as the assessed risk of material misstatement rises, as the desired assurance grows (a lower acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance), and as expected misstatement increases, and it decreases as tolerable misstatement rises. A dual-purpose test uses one sample to both test a control and substantiate the related transactions, sized as the larger of the two requirements. Population size, again, has a negligible effect once the population is large.

Projecting and concluding

Whatever the method, the auditor projects the sample result to the population and compares it to the relevant limit. In attribute sampling the projected (upper) deviation rate is compared to the tolerable deviation rate; in substantive sampling the projected misstatement plus an allowance for sampling risk is compared to tolerable misstatement. If the projection exceeds the limit, the auditor responds — expanding the sample, performing alternative procedures, or proposing an adjustment — and never simply accepts a result that breaches tolerance. The discipline is the same across methods: estimate, add a margin for sampling risk, and conclude against a pre-set threshold.

CMA bridge

Sampling is the statistical backbone behind the substantive procedures and tests of controls from AUD Unit 1. The risk-of-incorrect-acceptance and overreliance risks are the sampling expression of the audit-risk model — both are about wrongly concluding things are fine when they are not, the core danger the whole audit is built to avoid.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish sampling risk (controlled by sample size) from nonsampling risk (controlled by supervision and review).
  2. Use attribute sampling for controls: compare the upper deviation rate to the tolerable deviation rate; population size barely affects sample size.
  3. Use MUS for overstatement with few expected misstatements; use classical variables when more misstatements or understatement is the concern.
  4. Guard most against the effectiveness risks — assessing control risk too low (overreliance) and incorrect acceptance — over the efficiency risks.

Recap: sampling risk is the chance an unrepresentative sample misleads, managed by sample size, while nonsampling risk is managed by review; attribute sampling relies on a control only when the upper deviation rate stays at or below tolerable; MUS targets overstatement of larger balances while classical variables sampling handles understatement and more misstatements; and the auditor most fears the effectiveness errors — overreliance and incorrect acceptance — that make a flawed balance look fine.

flashcards.back: Sampling risk = the sample is unrepresentative (controlled by sample size); nonsampling risk = wrong conclusion for any other reason (controlled by training/supervision/review).
Tests a rate of occurrence (control deviation rate) to decide whether to rely on a control.

flashcards.front: Tolerable deviation rate effect on sample size
flashcards.back: A higher tolerable deviation rate lowers required sample size; population size has little effect for large populations.

flashcards.front: Relying on a control from a sample
flashcards.back: Rely if the upper deviation rate (sample rate + allowance for sampling risk) is at or below the tolerable deviation rate.

flashcards.front: Risk of assessing control risk too LOW
flashcards.back: Overreliance — concluding a control works when it doesn't; an EFFECTIVENESS risk (most serious), leading to too little substantive testing.
Each dollar is a sampling unit (PPS); efficient for overstatement with few expected misstatements (e.g., receivables); weak for understatement and zero/negative balances.
Estimates an amount (mean-per-unit/ratio/difference); better when more misstatements or understatement (completeness) is the concern.

flashcards.front: Risk of incorrect acceptance vs rejection
flashcards.back: Incorrect acceptance = a misstated balance looks fair (effectiveness, most serious); incorrect rejection = a fair balance looks misstated (efficiency, wasted work).

questions.q: Sampling risk is controlled primarily by:
questions.explain: Sampling risk (an unrepresentative sample) is managed by sample size; nonsampling risk is managed by supervision/review.

questions.q: Attribute sampling is used to test:
choices: The rate of deviation in a control
The dollar amount of a balance
questions.explain: Attribute sampling tests a rate of occurrence — typically control deviations.

questions.q: An auditor may rely on a control when the:
choices: Upper deviation rate is at or below the tolerable deviation rate
Sample deviation rate is zero only
questions.explain: Reliance is supported when the upper deviation rate does not exceed the tolerable rate.

questions.q: The risk of assessing control risk too LOW (overreliance) primarily affects audit:
questions.explain: Overreliance leads to too little substantive testing — an effectiveness (and the more serious) risk.

questions.q: Monetary-unit sampling is MOST efficient when the auditor:
choices: Expects few misstatements and tests for overstatement
questions.explain: MUS suits few-expected-misstatement, overstatement testing (e.g., receivables); it is weak for understatement and zero balances.

questions.q: Classical variables sampling is preferable to MUS when:
choices: A larger number of misstatements or understatement is expected
questions.explain: Classical variables sampling handles more misstatements and understatement (completeness) better than MUS.

questions.q: The risk of incorrect acceptance is the risk that:
choices: A materially misstated balance is concluded to be fairly stated
A fairly stated balance is rejected
questions.explain: Incorrect acceptance — a misstated balance looks fair — is the effectiveness risk the auditor guards against most.

weeks.title: AUD U2·W3 — Substantive Procedures for Specific Accounts (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the right procedure for the right assertion

With evidence and sampling settled, the auditor designs substantive procedures account by account, each aimed at the assertion most at risk. For assets the dominant worry is usually existence and valuation (overstatement); for liabilities it is completeness (understatement). This week walks MBG's major accounts and the signature procedures the exam tests for each.

Cash

Cash is small in balance but high in risk because it is liquid. The auditor sends a standard bank confirmation directly to the bank, obtains the year-end bank reconciliation and tests its reconciling items, and reviews the cutoff bank statement to verify reconciling items cleared. To detect kiting — overstating cash by exploiting the float on interbank transfers around year-end — the auditor prepares an interbank transfer schedule to confirm each transfer was recorded in the same period in both the disbursing and receiving accounts.

Accounts receivable

The signature procedure for receivables is confirmation with customers (existence and rights). Positive confirmations are used for large or risky accounts; non-responses are followed with alternative procedures — examining subsequent cash receipts and the underlying shipping documents and invoices. The auditor separately evaluates the allowance for doubtful accounts (valuation) by reviewing aging, collection history, and subsequent collections, and tests sales cutoff to ensure revenue and receivables fall in the correct period.

Inventory

For inventory the auditor must observe the physical count (a required procedure when inventory is material) to test existence, performing independent test counts and noting the condition of goods. Valuation is tested with price testing (vendor invoices for cost) and the lower-of-cost-or-net-realizable-value rule for obsolete or slow-moving stock. Cutoff is tested by examining receiving and shipping documents around year-end, and consigned or off-site inventory is confirmed. For a contractor, materials inventory is smaller than work in progress, which is audited as part of the construction-revenue work below.

Property, plant, and equipment

PP&E favors vouching additions to invoices and authorizations (existence and rights), examining title documents, and recomputing depreciation. Because PP&E accumulates over years, the auditor focuses on the current-period activity — additions, disposals, and the gain/loss on disposal — rather than re-auditing the whole balance each year, and watches for repairs improperly capitalized or capital items expensed. For MBG, the heavy-equipment fleet and the depreciation that drives the tax shield are the focus.

Accounts payable and the search for unrecorded liabilities

Liabilities flip the risk: the worry is understatement, so the key assertion is completeness and the signature procedure is the search for unrecorded liabilities. The auditor examines cash disbursements after year-end, unmatched receiving reports and vendor invoices, and unpaid bills, looking for obligations that belong in the period but were not recorded. Payables may be confirmed (especially with major vendors and any with small or zero balances, where understatement hides), and accrued liabilities — payroll, warranty, interest — are recomputed.

Revenue

Auditing standards presume revenue recognition is a fraud risk, so revenue gets heightened attention. The core procedures test occurrence (vouching recorded sales to shipping documents and customer orders) and cutoff (examining transactions around year-end to ensure sales are recorded in the right period), supported by substantive analytics comparing margins and trends. For a construction company, revenue is recognized over time under percentage-of-completion, so the auditor focuses on the measure of progress and the cost-to-complete estimate rather than shipping documents.

Long-term debt, equity, investments, and the construction WIP

For long-term debt the auditor confirms balances and terms with lenders and tests interest expense and covenant compliance; for equity, it confirms shares with the transfer agent (or examines the stock ledger) and reviews board minutes for dividends and issuances; for investments, it confirms or inspects securities and tests fair value. The contractor's defining audit area is work in progress: the auditor tests accumulated job costs, re-estimates cost to complete, recomputes percentage complete, and verifies the resulting over- and under-billings — the construction-specific application of the revenue and estimate rules.

The transaction cycles and directional testing

Auditors organize work by transaction cycle — revenue/receipts, purchases/disbursements, payroll, inventory/production, and financing/investing — because controls and risks cluster there. Within a cycle, direction of testing targets the assertion: to test existence/occurrence the auditor vouches from the recorded entry back to source documents (is this recorded sale real?); to test completeness the auditor traces from source documents forward into the records (was every shipment billed?). For an overstatement concern, vouch; for an understatement concern, trace. Misapplying the direction is a classic error — confirming receivables tests existence, not completeness, so it would never catch unrecorded sales.

Litigation, contingencies, and related parties

Three judgment areas demand specific procedures. For litigation, claims, and assessments, the auditor obtains a legal letter (attorney's letter of inquiry) from the client's lawyers — the primary evidence about pending or threatened litigation and the related loss contingencies under ASC 450; a lawyer's refusal to respond is a scope limitation. Related-party transactions are tested for proper authorization and disclosure — they are not eliminated like intercompany transactions, but their existence and terms must be transparent, because related parties are a common vehicle for fraud. And the fair-value and estimate procedures from last week reappear in every cycle: the auditor evaluates the method, the assumptions, and management's potential bias, corroborating with market data or an independent estimate where possible.

Cutoff and analytical review at the close

A theme across every account is cutoff — recording transactions in the correct period. The auditor examines sales, purchases, and cash transactions in the days around year-end against shipping and receiving documents, because a misstated cutoff shifts revenue, expense, and the related asset or liability between periods. Construction cutoff is especially sensitive, because a job's costs and the revenue recognized on them must land in the same period for percentage-of-completion to be faithful. Near the end of fieldwork the auditor performs a final analytical review, standing back to ask whether the statements as a whole make sense — do the ratios from the BAR analysis move as the year's events would predict, and is any unexpected relationship explained? This overall review, with the accumulation of misstatements against materiality, is the last check before the team concludes on each account and on the statements taken as a whole.

CMA bridge

Every procedure here targets a balance MBG's accounting produces. The search for unrecorded liabilities tests the completeness of the payables the CMA cost system records, and the WIP procedures audit the percentage-of-completion estimate at the heart of construction accounting — the auditor independently re-performing the cost-to-complete judgment the controller makes.

Practice and recap

  1. Audit assets mainly for existence/valuation (overstatement); audit liabilities mainly for completeness (understatement).
  2. Cash: bank confirmation, reconciliation, cutoff statement, interbank transfer schedule for kiting.
  3. Receivables: confirm and use subsequent receipts for non-responses; evaluate the allowance and test cutoff. Inventory: observe the count, price-test, apply lower of cost or NRV.
  4. Payables: search for unrecorded liabilities (subsequent disbursements). Revenue: presumed fraud risk — test occurrence and cutoff; for a contractor, audit WIP and cost-to-complete.

Recap: procedures follow the at-risk assertion — existence/valuation for assets, completeness for liabilities; cash uses confirmations and an interbank transfer schedule, receivables use confirmation plus subsequent receipts, inventory requires observing the count, payables require the search for unrecorded liabilities, and revenue (a presumed fraud risk) is tested for occurrence and cutoff — with the construction WIP and cost-to-complete estimate getting the closest scrutiny.

flashcards.back: Assets — existence/valuation (overstatement risk); liabilities — completeness (understatement risk).
Prepare an interbank transfer schedule to confirm each transfer is recorded in the same period in both accounts (no float overstatement).
Alternative procedures: examine subsequent cash receipts and underlying shipping documents/invoices.
Observe the physical count (required when material) and perform independent test counts; price-test for valuation; apply lower of cost or NRV.
The key completeness test for payables: examine post-year-end cash disbursements, unmatched receiving reports, and unpaid invoices.
Presumed fraud risk — test occurrence (vouch to shipping/orders) and cutoff; use analytics on margins.
Emphasize major vendors and small/zero-balance accounts, where understatement is most likely to hide.
Test accumulated job costs, re-estimate cost to complete, recompute percentage complete, and verify over/under-billings.

questions.q: The primary assertion of concern for LIABILITIES is:
questions.explain: Liabilities are most at risk of understatement, so completeness is the key assertion.

questions.q: To detect kiting, the auditor prepares a(n):
questions.explain: An interbank transfer schedule verifies transfers are recorded in the same period in both accounts.

questions.q: For receivable confirmations that receive no response, the auditor performs:
choices: Alternative procedures such as examining subsequent cash receipts
questions.explain: Non-responses to positive confirmations are followed with alternative procedures like subsequent receipts and shipping documents.

questions.q: Observing the client's physical inventory count primarily tests:
questions.explain: Observing the count tests inventory existence (with test counts); price testing addresses valuation.

questions.q: The search for unrecorded liabilities primarily addresses which assertion?
questions.explain: It targets completeness — finding obligations that belong in the period but were not recorded.

questions.q: Auditing standards presume which account carries a fraud risk?
questions.explain: Improper revenue recognition is a presumed fraud risk, so revenue gets heightened occurrence and cutoff testing.

questions.q: For a construction contractor, the most judgment-intensive audit area is:
choices: Work in progress and the cost-to-complete estimate
questions.explain: WIP and the percentage-of-completion cost-to-complete estimate are the contractor's most judgmental, closely audited numbers.

weeks.title: AUD U2·W4 — Audit Reports & Communications (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the report is the product

Every procedure exists to support one deliverable: the auditor's report. The opinion expressed there is what users rely on, so the rules for which opinion to issue, and what to add to or change in the report, are the payoff of the whole audit. This week covers the standard report, the modified opinions, the extra paragraphs, and the communications that surround the report.

The unmodified opinion and report structure

When the statements are fairly presented in accordance with the framework, the auditor issues an unmodified (nonissuer) or unqualified (issuer) opinion. The report has a defined structure: a title referencing independence, the addressee, an Opinion section (now placed first), a Basis for Opinion section (stating independence and that sufficient appropriate evidence was obtained), the responsibilities of management (including going-concern evaluation), the auditor's responsibilities (reasonable assurance, materiality, professional skepticism), and the firm's signature, city, and date. The report date is no earlier than the date the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate evidence.

When to modify the opinion

Two problems force a modification, and their severity sets the type. A GAAP departure (a misstatement) or a scope limitation (unable to obtain sufficient evidence) leads to a qualified opinion when the matter is material but not pervasive. When the matter is material AND pervasive, a GAAP departure yields an adverse opinion (the statements are not fairly presented) and a scope limitation yields a disclaimer (the auditor expresses no opinion). The two-by-two — issue type by pervasiveness — is the single most tested reporting concept.

Emphasis-of-matter and other-matter paragraphs

Sometimes the opinion is unmodified but the auditor adds a paragraph. An emphasis-of-matter (EOM) paragraph highlights something properly presented in the statements that is fundamental to users' understanding — a major catastrophe, a significant related-party transaction, or a justified change in accounting principle. An other-matter (OM) paragraph addresses something not in the statements but relevant to the audit or report — for example, prior-period statements audited by a predecessor. Neither changes the opinion; they direct the reader's attention.

Going concern

Management must evaluate whether there is substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period (generally one year). If substantial doubt exists but is adequately disclosed, the auditor typically issues an unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section (an emphasis-of-matter). If the disclosure is inadequate, it becomes a GAAP departure (qualified or adverse). A severe, multiple-uncertainty situation can support a disclaimer. The auditor evaluates management's plans to mitigate the doubt before concluding.

Critical and key audit matters

For a PCAOB issuer audit, the report communicates critical audit matters (CAMs) — the matters arising from the audit that involved especially challenging, subjective, or complex auditor judgment and that relate to material accounts or disclosures. The AU-C/IAASB analogue, key audit matters (KAMs), applies to nonissuer and international reporting and is communicated when the auditor is engaged or required to do so. Neither CAMs nor KAMs modify the opinion; both simply give users insight into where the audit focused, increasing the report's informational value without changing the bottom-line conclusion.

Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts

Events after the balance-sheet date but before the report is issued get two treatments (from FAR): a Type I (recognized) event provides evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date and adjusts the statements; a Type II (nonrecognized) event reflects new conditions and is disclosed. If the auditor learns of facts after the report is issued that, had they been known, would have changed the report, the auditor investigates and, if the statements are affected and people are relying on them, ensures the issue is addressed (revised statements or notification). The management representation letter, dated as of the report date, documents management's assertions and is required audit evidence.

Other engagements and communications

Not every engagement is an audit. A review (SSARS for nonissuers) gives limited assurance via inquiry and analytics; a compilation gives no assurance. Statements may be prepared under a special-purpose framework (cash, tax, or regulatory basis), which the report describes and which uses an emphasis-of-matter paragraph. In a group audit, the group auditor decides whether to reference a component auditor (dividing responsibility) or to take full responsibility. Throughout, the auditor must communicate with those charged with governance — significant findings, significant deficiencies and material weaknesses (in writing), disagreements with management, and the auditor's responsibilities — closing the loop the audit opened.

Comparative statements, consistency, and other information

Reports rarely cover a single year. With comparative statements, the auditor's opinion covers all periods presented; if a predecessor audited a prior year, either the predecessor reissues its report or the successor adds an other-matter paragraph describing the prior audit. A change in accounting principle that is properly applied and disclosed warrants an emphasis-of-matter paragraph on consistency — the opinion stays unmodified. The auditor also reads the other information in an annual report (management's discussion, the chair's letter) for material inconsistencies with the audited statements; a refusal by management to correct a material inconsistency can require the auditor to describe it or take further action.

Reporting on internal control and the integrated audit

For an issuer, the auditor of an accelerated or large accelerated filer also reports on the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting in an integrated audit (the §404(b) attestation from AUD Unit 1), and a material weakness there produces an adverse opinion on ICFR even when the financial-statement opinion is unmodified. For nonissuers, an examination of internal control is a separate attestation engagement. The thread tying the unit together is that the report is a calibrated statement: the opinion, the added paragraphs, the ICFR conclusion, and the communications each carry a precise meaning, and the auditor's craft is choosing exactly the right combination for what the evidence showed.

CMA bridge

AUD Unit 1's control deficiencies and Unit 2's evidence all converge here, in the opinion. The going-concern and subsequent-event rules tie back to FAR; the report is where the auditor translates everything learned about MBG's statements into the single conclusion users act on — fairly presented, qualified, adverse, or no opinion at all.

Practice and recap

  1. Know the unmodified report structure (Opinion first, then Basis, responsibilities, signature/date).
  2. Choose the modification by issue and pervasiveness: qualified (material, not pervasive); adverse (GAAP departure, pervasive); disclaimer (scope limitation, pervasive).
  3. Add an EOM (something properly in the statements) or OM (something outside them); report going concern as an EOM when disclosure is adequate; communicate CAMs in PCAOB issuer reports (KAMs only when engaged/required under nonissuer/international standards).
  4. Apply Type I (adjust) vs Type II (disclose) subsequent events; obtain the management representation letter; communicate with those charged with governance.

Recap: the unmodified report leads with the opinion; a material-but-not-pervasive problem yields a qualified opinion, a pervasive GAAP departure an adverse opinion, and a pervasive scope limitation a disclaimer; emphasis-of-matter and going-concern paragraphs flag matters without changing the opinion; critical audit matters (CAMs) inform PCAOB issuer readers (KAMs under nonissuer/international standards when required); and subsequent-event, representation-letter, and governance-communication rules surround the report the audit produces. Comparative statements carry the opinion across all periods presented, a properly disclosed change in principle draws a consistency emphasis-of-matter, and for an issuer the integrated audit adds an ICFR opinion that turns adverse on a material weakness — each element a precisely calibrated signal to the user.

flashcards.back: Title (independence), addressee, Opinion section FIRST, Basis for Opinion, management's responsibilities, auditor's responsibilities, signature/city/date.
A GAAP departure or scope limitation that is material but NOT pervasive.
Adverse = pervasive GAAP departure (statements not fairly presented); disclaimer = pervasive scope limitation (no opinion expressed).
EOM = something properly presented IN the statements that is fundamental; OM = something relevant but NOT in the statements. Neither changes the opinion.
Unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section (emphasis-of-matter); inadequate disclosure → GAAP departure (qualified/adverse).

PCAOB issuer reports communicate CRITICAL audit matters (CAMs); KEY audit matters (KAMs) are the AU-C/IAASB nonissuer/international concept, communicated when engaged/required. Neither modifies the opinion.

flashcards.front: Type I vs Type II subsequent events
flashcards.back: Type I (conditions existing at year-end) → adjust; Type II (new conditions after year-end) → disclose.
Audit = reasonable assurance (opinion); review = limited (negative) assurance; compilation = no assurance.

questions.q: A GAAP departure that is material but NOT pervasive results in a(n):
questions.explain: Material-but-not-pervasive issues (departure or scope limitation) yield a qualified opinion.

questions.q: A scope limitation that is material AND pervasive results in a(n):
questions.explain: A pervasive scope limitation → disclaimer; a pervasive GAAP departure → adverse.

questions.q: A pervasive GAAP departure (statements not fairly presented) results in a(n):
questions.explain: A material and pervasive GAAP departure yields an adverse opinion.

questions.q: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph is used to highlight:
choices: A matter properly presented in the statements that is fundamental to users
questions.explain: EOM highlights something correctly presented in the statements; it does not change the opinion.

questions.q: When substantial going-concern doubt exists but is adequately disclosed, the auditor usually issues:
choices: An unmodified opinion with a going-concern (emphasis-of-matter) section
questions.explain: Adequate disclosure → unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section; inadequate disclosure → qualified/adverse.

questions.q: A subsequent event providing evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date is:
choices: A Type I event — adjust the statements
A Type II event — disclose only
questions.explain: Type I (recognized) events adjust the statements; Type II (nonrecognized) events are disclosed.

questions.q: A review engagement provides:
questions.explain: A review gives limited assurance via inquiry and analytics; an audit gives reasonable assurance; a compilation none.

units.title: AUD Unit 3 — IT Auditing, Cycles & Estimates, Group Audits & Other Engagements

weeks.title: AUD U3·W1 — Auditing in an IT Environment: ITGCs, Application Controls & Data Analytics
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the ledger lives in a system

MBG's general ledger, payroll, and job-cost records live in software, so the auditor cannot evaluate controls without evaluating the information technology that runs them. This week covers the two layers of IT control — general and application — the techniques for testing controls inside a system, the rise of audit data analytics, and the SOC reports that let an auditor rely on a service organization. It extends the internal-control foundation from AUD Unit 1 into the systems where the data actually lives.

General IT controls

IT general controls (ITGCs) are the pervasive controls over the IT environment that make application controls trustworthy. They fall into four areas: access security (logical access, passwords, segregation of incompatible duties in the system), program change management (authorizing, testing, and approving changes to software), program development (controls over acquiring and implementing new systems), and computer operations (job scheduling, backup, recovery). Weak ITGCs undermine every application control they support — if a programmer can change code without approval, no automated control can be relied upon.

Application controls

Application controls operate within a specific process to ensure transactions are complete, accurate, and authorized. They are classified by stage: input controls (validation and edit checks, such as a field that rejects a non-numeric invoice amount, or a check digit), processing controls (batch totals, run-to-run reconciliations, limit and reasonableness tests), and output controls (distribution restrictions, output reconciliation). An automated application control can be tested once for design and a single operation, provided the supporting ITGCs establish that the program did not change during the period — the efficiency payoff of a strong IT environment.

Testing controls inside the system

To test automated controls, the auditor uses computer-assisted techniques. The test-data approach runs the auditor's fictitious transactions — including deliberately invalid ones — through the client's program to see whether controls catch them. An integrated test facility embeds a dummy entity in the live system, and parallel simulation reprocesses real data through the auditor's own program and compares results. Generalized audit software (GAS) reads client data files to recompute, summarize, and test — extracting exceptions the auditor then investigates. These CAATs turn the system from an obstacle into a testing tool.

The reliance decision

The IT evaluation feeds the same audit-risk logic as Unit 1. If ITGCs and application controls are designed and operating effectively, the auditor can assess control risk below maximum and reduce substantive testing. If ITGCs are weak, the auditor cannot rely on automated controls and must shift to a substantive strategy — testing the outputs directly with more extensive procedures. In a highly automated environment, a purely substantive approach may even be impossible (no paper trail), forcing reliance on controls and making the IT evaluation mandatory rather than optional.

Audit data analytics

Audit data analytics (ADAs) apply analysis to entire populations rather than samples, surfacing relationships and anomalies. Uses span the audit: risk assessment (visualizing revenue by location to spot outliers), tests of details (matching every shipment to an invoice), and the required journal-entry testing for fraud (filtering for round-dollar, post-period, or unusual-user entries). ADAs do not replace professional judgment — every flagged item is a notable item to evaluate, not automatically a misstatement — but they let the auditor cover 100% of a population where sampling once covered a fraction.

Service organizations and SOC reports

When MBG outsources a process — payroll to a provider, hosting to a cloud vendor — the relevant controls sit at the service organization. Under AU-C 402, the user auditor obtains a SOC 1 report (controls relevant to user financial reporting) prepared by the service auditor. A Type 1 report opines on the design of controls at a point in time; a Type 2 report also tests operating effectiveness over a period — so only a Type 2 supports the user auditor's reliance on those controls. SOC 2 reports address security, availability, confidentiality, and privacy for broader stakeholders, and complementary user-entity controls remind the user that some controls remain its own responsibility.

Cybersecurity and data integrity

The auditor also considers how cybersecurity risk could affect the financial statements — a breach that corrupts data, triggers a contingent liability, or impairs going concern. While a financial-statement audit is not a cybersecurity audit, the auditor evaluates relevant controls over data integrity and remains alert to the financial-reporting consequences of an incident. The reliability of every number the audit touches ultimately rests on whether the systems that produced it were secure and controlled.

Segregation of duties in a computerized system

In a manual system, duties are separated among people; in an IT system, the same principle applies to access rights. The auditor verifies that no individual holds incompatible logical access — for example, the ability to both create a vendor and approve a payment, or to both write program code and move it into production. Privileged access (system and database administrators) is especially sensitive because it can override application controls, so it is restricted, logged, and reviewed. Where the entity is too small to separate duties, the auditor looks for compensating controls such as detailed management review of system logs and exception reports.

End-user computing and spreadsheets

Material figures often flow through spreadsheets built outside the formal IT environment — a depreciation schedule, a percentage-of-completion calculation, a consolidation worksheet. These end-user computing tools fall outside ITGCs, so they carry elevated risk of formula errors, broken links, and unauthorized changes. The auditor tests the spreadsheet's logic and integrity directly — re-performing key formulas, checking that ranges are complete, and confirming version control — because a single wrong cell reference can misstate a material balance just as surely as a coding error in the core system.

Continuous auditing and the audit trail

Automation also reshapes when the auditor works. Continuous auditing techniques — embedded audit modules and exception flags that capture transactions as they occur — let the auditor monitor controls throughout the period rather than only at year-end. The premise of all of it is a reliable audit trail: the system must log enough detail (who, what, when) to trace any balance back to its source transactions. Where the trail is electronic and short-lived, the auditor plans procedures to capture evidence before it is overwritten, because lost data cannot be re-created after the fact.

CMA bridge

CMA month 6 built the internal-control and systems perspective for MBG; AUD applies it from the auditor's chair — testing the ITGCs and application controls that management designed. The same job-cost system MBG uses to accumulate WIP is what the auditor must evaluate before relying on a single automated cost figure.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify ITGCs (access, change management, development, operations) and recognize that weak ITGCs undermine the application controls they support.
  2. Identify application controls by stage (input edit checks/check digits, processing batch totals, output controls).
  3. Apply CAATs — test data, integrated test facility, parallel simulation, generalized audit software — and use ADAs for full-population and journal-entry testing.
  4. Distinguish SOC 1 Type 1 (design) from Type 2 (operating effectiveness over a period); only Type 2 supports reliance.

Recap: auditing in an IT environment means evaluating ITGCs (access, change, development, operations) that make application controls (input/processing/output) reliable; testing them with CAATs like test data, parallel simulation, and generalized audit software; using audit data analytics for full-population and fraud journal-entry testing; and obtaining a SOC 1 Type 2 report — operating effectiveness over a period — before relying on a service organization's controls.

flashcards.back: Pervasive controls: access security, program change management, program development, and computer operations. Weak ITGCs undermine every application control they support.
Process-level controls by stage: input (edit checks, check digits), processing (batch totals, reconciliations), output (distribution/reconciliation).
Test data: run auditor's fictitious transactions through the client's program. Parallel simulation: reprocess real client data through the auditor's own program and compare.
Software that reads client data files to recompute, summarize, and extract exceptions for the auditor to investigate.
Analysis of entire populations (not samples) for risk assessment, tests of details, and fraud journal-entry testing; flagged items are 'notable items' to evaluate.
Type 1: design of controls at a point in time. Type 2: design AND operating effectiveness over a period. Only Type 2 supports the user auditor's reliance.
Controls the SOC report assumes the user organization itself performs; reliance on the service org's controls depends on them.
In a highly automated, paperless environment a purely substantive approach may be impossible, forcing reliance on (and testing of) controls.

questions.q: If IT general controls are weak, the auditor should:
choices: Not rely on automated application controls and increase substantive testing
Rely fully on application controls anyway
questions.explain: Weak ITGCs undermine the application controls they support, so the auditor cannot rely on them.

questions.q: A check digit on an account number is an example of a(n):
questions.explain: Check digits validate data at entry — an input application control.

questions.q: Reprocessing actual client data through the auditor's own program and comparing results is:
questions.explain: Parallel simulation reruns real data through the auditor's program; test data runs fictitious transactions through the client's program.

questions.q: Which SOC 1 report supports the user auditor's reliance on a service organization's controls?
choices: Type 1 (design at a point in time)
questions.explain: Only a Type 2 report tests operating effectiveness over a period, supporting reliance.

questions.q: Audit data analytics differ from sampling because they:
questions.explain: ADAs analyze whole populations; flagged 'notable items' still require auditor judgment.

questions.q: Required journal-entry testing for fraud commonly filters for:
questions.explain: Fraud journal-entry testing targets unusual characteristics like round amounts, post-period dates, and odd preparers.

questions.q: Complementary user-entity controls are:
choices: Controls the user organization itself must perform for the service org's controls to be effective
questions.explain: A SOC report assumes certain controls operate at the user entity; reliance depends on them.

weeks.title: AUD U3·W2 — Auditing Specific Cycles & Accounting Estimates
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — different cycles, different risks

The substantive procedures from AUD Unit 2 take their specific shape from the transaction cycle being audited. Revenue and payables carry opposite primary risks; inventory turns on a physical observation; estimates turn on management judgment the auditor must challenge. This week walks the major cycles, then tackles the hardest evidence of all — accounting estimates — and the use of specialists. It is where the evidence framework meets MBG's actual accounts.

The revenue cycle

Because management is generally motivated to overstate revenue and receivables, the auditor's primary concern is occurrence and existence. Core procedures: confirm receivables directly with customers (positive confirmations for large or disputed balances), perform sales cutoff testing around period-end to ensure revenue is recorded in the right period, vouch recorded sales to shipping documents (occurrence), and evaluate the allowance for doubtful accounts. Revenue recognition is a presumed fraud risk under the standards, so the auditor designs procedures specifically responsive to that risk.

The purchases and payables cycle

Payables carry the opposite risk: management may understate liabilities to improve the balance sheet, so the primary assertion is completeness. The signature procedure is the search for unrecorded liabilities — examining cash disbursements after period-end, unmatched receiving reports, and unpaid invoices to find obligations that belong in the prior period. The auditor also tests cutoff of purchases and traces from source documents (receiving reports) into the records — the direction that detects omissions, the mirror image of the revenue cycle's vouching.

Payroll and the inventory observation

Payroll testing addresses occurrence (no ghost employees), accuracy of rates and hours, and proper classification — often highly automated, so control reliance is efficient. Inventory demands a distinctive procedure: the auditor must observe the physical count (a required procedure when inventory is material), testing existence by vouching from the records to the floor (does a recorded item physically exist?) and completeness by tracing from the floor — the count tags — to the records (was every physical item recorded?), while noting condition for obsolescence. Inventory valuation then tests cost-flow accuracy and lower of cost and net realizable value, and cutoff ties the count to shipping/receiving at period-end.

Investments and other cycles

Investments are audited for existence (confirm with the custodian or inspect securities) and valuation (recompute fair value, evaluate the classification and impairment from FAR Unit 2). Financing accounts — debt and equity — are typically few but individually large, so the auditor confirms debt terms with lenders, recomputes interest, and reads agreements for covenants and restrictions. Across every cycle, the auditor links the procedure to the assertion most at risk, which is the analytical heart of designing an efficient audit program.

Auditing accounting estimates

Estimates — allowances, warranty reserves, fair values, the percentage-of-completion that drives MBG's revenue — are the riskiest evidence because they rest on management judgment. Under AU-C 540, the auditor chooses among three approaches: test management's process and assumptions, develop an independent estimate for comparison, or review subsequent events that reveal the actual outcome. The auditor specifically evaluates the risk of management bias — whether estimates cluster at the favorable end of a reasonable range — because a pattern of optimistic estimates can itself indicate a material misstatement or fraud.

Fair value and complexity

Fair-value estimates raise the difficulty further. The auditor evaluates the valuation model, the reasonableness of significant assumptions (discount rates, growth), and the reliability of the underlying data, with more scrutiny as inputs move from observable (Level 1) to unobservable (Level 3). The higher the estimation uncertainty, the more persuasive the evidence required and the greater the chance the estimate becomes a significant risk demanding a tailored response — a direct application of the risk model to the softest numbers in the statements.

Using the work of a specialist

When valuation, engineering, or legal matters exceed the auditor's expertise, AU-C 620 governs using an auditor's specialist (engaged by the auditor) — the auditor evaluates the specialist's competence, capabilities, and objectivity, agrees on the scope, and assesses whether the work supports the relevant assertions. A management's specialist (e.g., MBG's appraiser) is instead treated as audit evidence the auditor must evaluate. Either way, using a specialist does not divide responsibility — the auditor alone owns the opinion, just as with the report rules from AUD Unit 2.

Receivable confirmations in depth

Confirmation is the revenue cycle's signature procedure, and its design matters. A positive confirmation asks the customer to respond whether or not the balance agrees and is used for large or higher-risk accounts; a negative confirmation asks for a response only if the customer disagrees and is appropriate only when risk is low, many small balances exist, and a high response rate is expected. Nonresponses to positive confirmations require alternative procedures — examining subsequent cash receipts, shipping documents, and invoices. Confirming directly with the customer provides external, third-party evidence, which the reliability hierarchy from AUD Unit 2 ranks above internally generated documents.

Related-party transactions

Because related-party transactions are not at arm's length, they pose a heightened risk of misstatement and disguised fraud. The auditor performs procedures to identify related parties (reading minutes, prior filings, and confirmations), evaluates whether transactions were properly authorized and disclosed, and remains alert to transactions with no apparent business purpose — a classic red flag. The auditor does not simply accept management's assertion that a transaction occurred at market terms unless that assertion can be substantiated, applying the professional skepticism that runs through the entire evidence framework.

Analytical procedures across the cycles

Substantive analytical procedures complement tests of details in every cycle: comparing gross margin by job, payroll as a percentage of revenue, or receivable turnover against prior years and expectations. A relationship that does not behave as predicted — margin rising while a fixed-price job runs over budget — directs attention to a potential misstatement. The auditor develops an independent expectation, defines a threshold for investigation, and follows up unexpected differences with corroboration rather than simply accepting management's explanation, tying the cycle work back to the risk model. Analytics are generally more effective when the data is disaggregated — monthly and by job rather than as annual totals — because offsetting movements that hide inside an aggregate become visible at a finer grain.

CMA bridge

The cycle structure mirrors the operating cycles the CMA program managed for MBG — revenue, procurement, payroll, inventory. The auditor tests the same cycles management runs, but with assertion-driven skepticism. Auditing the percentage-of-completion estimate is exactly where AUD's estimate rules meet FAR's construction revenue and the CMA's job-cost discipline.

Practice and recap

  1. Match the primary risk to the cycle: revenue/receivables = occurrence/existence (overstatement); payables = completeness (understatement, search for unrecorded liabilities).
  2. Observe the physical inventory count; test existence (vouch records→floor) and completeness (trace floor→records); value at LCNRV.
  3. Audit estimates by testing management's process, developing an independent estimate, or reviewing subsequent events; evaluate management bias and estimation uncertainty.
  4. Use a specialist per AU-C 620 (evaluate competence and objectivity); the auditor retains sole responsibility for the opinion.

Recap: each cycle has a primary assertion — revenue/receivables risk overstatement (confirm, cutoff, occurrence), payables risk understatement (search for unrecorded liabilities, trace in), inventory requires observing the count (existence and completeness) and LCNRV valuation; accounting estimates are audited by testing the process, building an independent estimate, or reviewing subsequent events while watching for management bias; and a specialist's work is evaluated for competence and objectivity but never shifts the auditor's sole responsibility for the opinion.

flashcards.back: Overstatement → occurrence/existence. Confirm receivables, test sales cutoff, vouch to shipping docs. Revenue recognition is a presumed fraud risk.
Understatement → completeness. Signature procedure: search for unrecorded liabilities (examine post-period disbursements, unmatched receiving reports).
Vouch records→source = existence/occurrence (overstatement). Trace source→records = completeness (understatement/omissions).
Required when material. Existence: vouch records→floor. Completeness: trace floor (count tags)→records. Note condition (obsolescence); value at lower of cost and NRV.
(1) Test management's process/assumptions, (2) develop an independent estimate, (3) review subsequent events. Evaluate management bias and estimation uncertainty.
Estimates clustering at the favorable end of a reasonable range can signal misstatement or fraud.
Auditor's specialist (engaged by auditor): evaluate competence/objectivity, agree scope. Management's specialist: treat their work as audit evidence to evaluate.
Using a specialist does not divide audit responsibility — the auditor alone owns the opinion.

questions.q: The primary assertion concern for accounts payable is:
questions.explain: Management may understate liabilities, so completeness is the primary concern — hence the search for unrecorded liabilities.

questions.q: Confirming receivables and testing sales cutoff primarily address the risk of:
questions.explain: Revenue/receivables carry overstatement risk, addressed by confirmations and cutoff testing.

questions.q: To test inventory EXISTENCE during the observation, the auditor selects items:
choices: From the records and vouches to the floor
From the floor and traces to the records
questions.explain: Existence: start with the records and vouch to the floor (does the recorded item exist?). Completeness goes the other way — floor/count tags traced to the records.

questions.q: The search for unrecorded liabilities focuses on:
choices: Cash disbursements and invoices after period-end
questions.explain: Examining post-period disbursements and unmatched receiving reports detects liabilities omitted from the prior period.

questions.q: Under AU-C 540, one valid approach to auditing an estimate is to:
choices: Develop an independent estimate for comparison
questions.explain: The auditor may test management's process, develop an independent estimate, or review subsequent events.

questions.q: An auditor evaluating an auditor's specialist must assess the specialist's:
questions.explain: AU-C 620 requires evaluating the specialist's competence, capabilities, and objectivity.

questions.q: Estimates clustering at the favorable end of a reasonable range may indicate:
questions.explain: A pattern of favorable estimates can signal management bias and possible misstatement or fraud.

weeks.title: AUD U3·W3 — Group Audits, Using the Work of Others & Quality Management
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — when one auditor isn't enough

Large or multi-location engagements pull in other people's work — component auditors on a group audit, the client's internal audit function, outside specialists — and every firm operates under a system of quality management that governs how engagements are performed. This week covers how the auditor uses (and remains responsible for) others' work, how the engagement is documented, and the firm-level and engagement-level quality structures that stand behind the opinion.

Group audits

When financial statements include multiple components (subsidiaries, divisions, locations), AU-C 600 governs the group audit. The group engagement team sets group materiality and a lower component materiality, identifies significant components (individually material or carrying significant risks), and directs the work of component auditors. The group engagement partner is responsible for the group opinion. Under current standards the group auditor generally assumes responsibility for the components' work and does not reference the component auditor in the report — and if it cannot obtain sufficient evidence over a significant component, that is a scope limitation.

Communicating with component auditors

The group team's involvement is active: it communicates its requirements to component auditors (materiality, significant risks, timing), evaluates their competence and independence, and reviews their work in proportion to component risk. For a significant component, an audit of the full financial information is performed; for others, the group team may use specified procedures or analytical procedures at the group level. Throughout, the group team retains responsibility for the sufficiency of evidence supporting the group opinion — delegation of work is never delegation of responsibility.

Using internal auditors

A strong internal audit function can make the external audit more efficient under AU-C 610 in two ways: using their work (procedures internal audit already performed) and obtaining direct assistance (internal auditors working under the external auditor's direction). Both require evaluating internal audit's competence and objectivity — objectivity is higher when internal audit reports to the audit committee rather than to management. The external auditor must still perform enough work itself on significant judgments and high-risk areas; it cannot delegate those, preserving sole responsibility for the opinion.

Audit documentation

The audit file is the record of work performed. Under AU-C 230, documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no prior connection to the engagement to understand the nature, timing, and extent of procedures, the evidence obtained, and the conclusions reached — including who performed and reviewed the work and when. The auditor assembles the final file within a documentation completion period (60 days after the report date for AICPA engagements; 45 for PCAOB) and retains it (5 years AICPA; 7 years PCAOB). After the completion date, documentation may be added but not deleted, with the reason recorded.

Firm-level quality management

Behind every engagement sits the firm's system of quality management (SQM). The AICPA's quality-management standards (SQMS) require a firm to design a risk-based system across components including governance and leadership, the firm's risk-assessment process, relevant ethical requirements, acceptance and continuance of clients, engagement performance, resources, information and communication, and monitoring and remediation. The firm sets quality objectives, identifies quality risks, and designs responses — then evaluates the system at least annually. It is the structural assurance that the firm can consistently perform quality engagements.

Engagement quality reviews

Certain engagements require an engagement quality review (EQR) — an objective evaluation by a qualified reviewer who was not on the engagement team, completed before the report is released. The reviewer assesses the significant judgments and conclusions, particularly on risk and independence. At the engagement level, AU-C 220 makes the engagement partner responsible for overall quality, direction, supervision, and review — the bridge between the firm's system and the individual audit, ensuring quality is delivered where it matters: on the engagement itself.

Putting responsibility in one place

The thread tying this week together is that responsibility does not divide. Whether the auditor relies on a component auditor, internal audit, or a specialist, and however robust the firm's quality system, the engagement partner owns the opinion and must ensure sufficient appropriate evidence supports it. Quality management and documentation are the mechanisms that make that responsibility demonstrable — to a reviewer, a regulator, or a court — long after the report is signed.

Communication with those charged with governance

The auditor must communicate specified matters to those charged with governance (typically the audit committee): the auditor's responsibilities and the planned scope and timing, significant findings (qualitative aspects of accounting practices, significant difficulties encountered, uncorrected misstatements), and any significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in internal control — the latter in writing. The auditor also reports fraud involving senior management and identified illegal acts. These communications, required by AU-C 260 and 265, keep governance informed of matters that bear on its oversight of the financial-reporting process.

Acceptance and continuance

Quality begins before fieldwork, at client acceptance and continuance. The firm evaluates management integrity, its own competence and resources to perform the engagement, and compliance with independence and ethical requirements, and communicates with the predecessor auditor (with the client's permission) about disagreements and the reasons for the change. An engagement the firm should never have accepted is the root of many quality failures, which is why acceptance and continuance is an explicit component of the system of quality management — the gate that keeps unacceptable risk out of the firm.

Monitoring and remediation

A quality system is only as good as its monitoring. The firm performs ongoing and periodic monitoring — including inspection of completed engagements — to detect deficiencies, then evaluates their severity and remediates root causes. Findings from external peer review or PCAOB inspection feed the same loop. This continuous monitor-and-remediate cycle is what makes the system of quality management a living process rather than a binder on a shelf, closing the gap between how engagements are supposed to be performed and how they actually are.

CMA bridge

For a multi-entity construction group like MBG and its affiliates, the group-audit and component-materiality concepts are exactly how a consolidated audit would be scoped. The internal-control and consolidation work from the CMA and FAR units is what a component auditor would test — and what the group team would direct and take responsibility for.

Practice and recap

  1. Scope a group audit: group vs component materiality, significant components, the group partner's responsibility for the opinion (assume responsibility; don't reference component auditors).
  2. Use internal audit (their work + direct assistance) and specialists only after evaluating competence and objectivity; keep high-risk judgments in-house.
  3. Document so an experienced auditor can understand the work; assemble within 60 days (AICPA), retain 5 years (7 for PCAOB).
  4. Apply the firm's risk-based system of quality management (SQMS components) and engagement quality reviews completed before report release.

Recap: group audits set group and component materiality and the group partner owns the opinion (assuming responsibility for component work); internal auditors and specialists may be used after evaluating competence and objectivity, but high-risk judgments stay with the auditor; documentation must let an experienced auditor understand the work and is assembled within 60 days and retained 5–7 years; and a risk-based system of quality management plus engagement quality reviews stand behind every report — with responsibility always resting on the engagement partner.

flashcards.back: Group materiality for the consolidated statements; a lower component materiality for components. Significant components are individually material or carry significant risks.
The group engagement partner is responsible for the group opinion; under current standards the group auditor assumes responsibility and does NOT reference component auditors in the report.
Two modes: using their work and direct assistance. Both require evaluating competence and objectivity (higher when IA reports to the audit committee).
Enough for an experienced auditor with no prior connection to understand nature/timing/extent, evidence, conclusions, and who did/reviewed the work and when.
Assemble final file within 60 days (AICPA) / 45 (PCAOB); retain 5 years (AICPA) / 7 (PCAOB). After completion, add but don't delete (record reasons).
Risk-based firm system: governance/leadership, risk assessment, ethics, acceptance/continuance, engagement performance, resources, information/communication, monitoring/remediation.
Objective review by a qualified person NOT on the engagement, completed before the report is released; evaluates significant judgments and conclusions.
Responsible for overall engagement quality, direction, supervision, and review — the link between the firm's quality system and the individual audit.

questions.q: In a group audit, responsibility for the group audit opinion rests with:
questions.explain: The group engagement partner is responsible for the group opinion and the sufficiency of evidence.

questions.q: Before using the work of internal auditors, the external auditor must evaluate their:
questions.explain: AU-C 610 requires evaluating internal audit's competence and objectivity.

questions.q: Audit documentation should be sufficient for:
choices: An experienced auditor with no prior connection to understand the work
questions.explain: AU-C 230 sets the experienced-auditor understandability standard.

questions.q: For a non-issuer (AICPA) audit, the final documentation is assembled within:
questions.explain: AICPA documentation completion period is 60 days (PCAOB is 45).

questions.q: The AICPA's system of quality management is best described as:
choices: A risk-based system with quality objectives, risks, and responses
questions.explain: SQMS requires a risk-based system: set quality objectives, identify quality risks, design responses, and monitor.

questions.q: An engagement quality review must be completed:
choices: Only if the client requests it
questions.explain: The EQR by a non-team reviewer must be completed before releasing the report.

questions.q: Using a component auditor's work means the group auditor:
choices: Still retains responsibility for the sufficiency of evidence for the group opinion
Has no responsibility for that component
questions.explain: Delegating work is not delegating responsibility; the group team owns the sufficiency of evidence.

weeks.title: AUD U3·W4 — Other Engagements: SSARS, Attestation & Governmental Auditing
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — beyond the financial-statement audit

Not every CPA engagement is an audit. A practitioner may prepare, compile, or review statements; examine or perform agreed-upon procedures on other subject matter; or audit a government grant under GAGAS and the Single Audit. Each carries a different level of assurance, report, and independence rule. This final AUD week maps the engagement continuum — the knowledge that lets you pick the right service and the right report for MBG or any client.

The assurance continuum

Engagements differ chiefly in the assurance provided. An audit or examination gives reasonable (high) assurance and a positive opinion. A review gives limited (negative) assurance — "nothing came to our attention" — based mainly on inquiry and analytics. A compilation and a preparation give no assurance. Agreed-upon procedures give no assurance and no opinion — only findings the specified users evaluate themselves. The level of assurance drives the procedures, the report, and the fee.

SSARS engagements

The Statements on Standards for Accounting and Review Services (SSARS) govern non-audit work on a nonissuer's statements. A preparation engagement produces statements with no report and no assurance (a legend states no assurance is provided); independence is not required and need not be disclosed. A compilation adds a brief report but still no assurance and no procedures to verify; if the accountant is not independent, that fact is disclosed. A review provides limited assurance through inquiry and analytical procedures and requires independence; lack of independence precludes a review.

Attestation engagements

The Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements (SSAE) apply when a practitioner reports on subject matter other than historical financial statements — internal control, sustainability metrics, compliance with a contract, prospective financial information. The three forms mirror the assurance continuum: an examination (reasonable assurance, opinion), a review (limited assurance), and agreed-upon procedures (findings, no opinion). All attestation engagements require independence and a responsible party that takes responsibility for the subject matter — the framework for the wide range of assurance services CPAs increasingly provide.

Issuers versus nonissuers

The standard-setter depends on the entity. Issuers (public companies) are audited under PCAOB standards, with the integrated audit and critical audit matters (CAMs) from AUD Unit 2. Nonissuers are audited under the AICPA's Statements on Auditing Standards (SAS / AU-C), which permit key audit matters (KAMs) only when engaged to report them. Recognizing whether an engagement is for an issuer or a nonissuer determines the entire body of standards that applies — a frequent exam trigger.

Governmental auditing and GAGAS

Audits of government entities and recipients of government funds follow Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS) — the Yellow Book — which build on GAAS with added requirements: heightened independence (a conceptual-framework evaluation of nonaudit services), expanded reporting on internal control and compliance, and stricter continuing education. A GAGAS financial audit produces, in addition to the opinion, a report on internal control over financial reporting and on compliance with laws and regulations — reflecting the public-accountability purpose that distinguishes government auditing.

The Single Audit

An entity that expends $1,000,000 or more of federal awards in a year (the Uniform Guidance threshold effective for fiscal years beginning on or after October 1, 2024) must obtain a Single Audit — an organization-wide audit covering both the financial statements (under GAGAS) and compliance for major federal programs. Major programs are identified with a risk-based approach. The auditor reports an opinion on compliance for each major program and on internal control over compliance, and prepares a schedule of findings and questioned costs. Compliance audits generally follow AU-C 935.

Special-purpose and single-statement reports

Finally, the auditor may report on statements prepared under a special-purpose framework (AU-C 800) — cash basis, tax basis, regulatory basis, or contractual basis — which requires an emphasis-of-matter paragraph alerting users that the framework is not GAAP. The auditor may also report on a single financial statement or a specific element (AU-C 805). These tailored reports let a CPA serve users whose needs do not fit a full GAAP audit while still being transparent about the basis of presentation.

Prospective and pro forma information

CPAs also report on prospective financial information — forecasts (based on expected conditions) and projections (based on hypothetical "what-if" assumptions) — under the attestation standards. A forecast may be issued for general use, but a projection is restricted to specified users who understand its hypothetical basis. The practitioner can examine, perform agreed-upon procedures on, or (for internal use) compile the information, and every report emphasizes that prospective results may not be achieved. Pro forma information — showing the effect of a transaction as if it had occurred earlier — is examined or reviewed under a parallel framework.

Reporting on controls and the reach of attestation

The attestation framework reaches a growing range of subject matter. A practitioner may examine management's description of its internal control and the suitability of its design — the SOC 1/SOC 2 engagements from this unit's IT week, viewed from the service auditor's side. The same standards support assurance on sustainability and greenhouse-gas disclosures, compliance with contractual or regulatory requirements, and other emerging metrics. As stakeholders demand assurance beyond the financial statements, the SSAE framework gives the profession a consistent structure — subject matter, criteria, responsible party, and level of assurance — for whatever needs to be attested.

Restricted use and report tailoring

Many of these reports are restricted in use. Agreed-upon-procedures reports, projections, and reports on special-purpose frameworks intended for specific parties carry an alert paragraph limiting distribution to the users who understand the basis and the procedures. Matching the report to the engagement — its assurance level, its framework, and its intended users — is the final discipline of the AUD section: the same factual work can support very different reports. A report issued on the wrong basis, or distributed beyond its intended users, exposes the practitioner to liability even when the underlying work was sound.

CMA bridge

A privately held contractor like MBG more often needs a review or compilation for its lender than a full audit, and if it takes federal infrastructure money it could face a Single Audit. Knowing the assurance continuum lets the CFO commission the right engagement — and lets the auditor scope it correctly. This closes the AUD discipline that began with engagement acceptance in Unit 1.

Practice and recap

  1. Rank assurance: audit/examination (reasonable) > review (limited) > compilation/preparation (none); agreed-upon procedures report findings only.
  2. Apply SSARS (preparation: no report; compilation: report, no assurance; review: limited assurance, independence required) and SSAE attestation forms.
  3. Audit issuers under PCAOB (CAMs) and nonissuers under AICPA AU-C (KAMs only when engaged).
  4. Apply GAGAS (Yellow Book) added requirements and the Single Audit ($1,000,000 federal-award threshold; opinion on compliance for major programs).

Recap: engagements span an assurance continuum — audit/examination give reasonable assurance, review gives limited assurance, compilation/preparation give none, and agreed-upon procedures report only findings; SSARS governs preparation/compilation/review of nonissuer statements (review requires independence), SSAE governs attestation on other subject matter, issuers follow PCAOB and nonissuers follow AICPA standards, and government work adds GAGAS reporting on internal control and compliance plus a Single Audit when federal awards expended reach $1,000,000.
