weeks.title: REG U3·W2 — The Federal Gift Tax (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — taxing the transfer, not the income

The income tax reaches what you earn; the transfer taxes reach what you give. When Jordan Reed gifts shares of MBG to the children to move value out of a taxable estate, the gift tax applies — paid by the donor, not the recipient. The gift tax is unified with the estate tax (one lifetime exemption covers both), so this week's rules feed directly into next week's estate tax.

What is a taxable gift

A gift is a completed, gratuitous transfer in which the donor gives up dominion and control for less than full consideration. Both the giver's donative intent and delivery matter; an incomplete transfer (one the donor can revoke) is not yet a gift. The donor files Form 709 and, importantly, uses the lifetime exemption before any tax is actually due — most gifts reduce the exemption rather than generate a check.

The annual exclusion

Each donor may give up to the annual exclusion — $19,000 per donee for 2025 (indexed annually for inflation) — to any number of recipients every year, free of gift tax and without using any exemption. The catch: the exclusion applies only to a present interest — a gift the donee can enjoy immediately. A future interest (the right to receive property only later, as in many trusts) does not qualify for the annual exclusion.

Gift splitting and the unlimited deductions

A married couple may elect gift splitting, treating a gift by one spouse as made one-half by each — effectively doubling the annual exclusion to $38,000 per donee. Two transfers are entirely exempt: the unlimited marital deduction (gifts to a U.S.-citizen spouse) and the unlimited charitable deduction. Separately, direct payments of tuition or medical expenses — paid straight to the school or provider — are excluded without limit and do not even use the annual exclusion.

Computing taxable gifts and the unified exemption

Taxable gifts = total gifts − annual exclusions − marital and charitable deductions. Tax is computed on cumulative lifetime taxable gifts, but the unified credit shelters gifts up to the basic exclusion amount — about $15 million per individual for 2026, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21 and indexed thereafter. Worked example: in 2025 Reed gives $50,000 to each of three children. After the $19,000 annual exclusion, taxable gifts are ($50,000 − $19,000) × 3 = $93,000, which simply reduces the lifetime exemption — no tax is due until cumulative taxable gifts exceed the exemption. With gift splitting, the $38,000 combined exclusion drops the taxable gifts to $12,000 × 3 = $36,000.

Present versus future interests and Crummey powers

Because the annual exclusion needs a present interest, gifts into trust normally fail to qualify — the beneficiary cannot touch the property now. Estate planners solve this with a Crummey power: the trust gives the beneficiary a brief window to withdraw the contribution, which converts it into a present interest that does qualify for the annual exclusion, even though the beneficiary is expected not to withdraw. This is a heavily tested wrinkle linking the gift tax to trust planning.

Valuation and family-business discounts

Gifts are valued at fair market value on the date of the gift. When Reed gifts a minority block of MBG stock, the value may be reduced by a minority-interest discount (the block cannot control the company) and a lack-of-marketability discount (closely held shares are hard to sell) — legitimate reductions that move more value to the next generation per dollar of exemption used. Aggressive discounts invite IRS scrutiny and a qualified appraisal, but the technique is central to transferring a family construction business.

Carryover basis and the income-tax aftermath of a gift

A gift carries an income-tax consequence the donee inherits with the property: gifted property keeps the donor's carryover basis (the dual-basis rule from Unit 1 for losses), so the appreciation is not erased — it shifts to the donee, who pays income tax on the built-in gain when the property is later sold. This is the key contrast with property held until death, which receives a basis step-up. Gifting therefore trades a potential estate-tax saving (moving future appreciation out of the estate) against the loss of the step-up, and the planner must weigh the two: gift assets expected to appreciate (to remove future growth from the transfer-tax base) but consider holding highly appreciated assets until death (to capture the step-up). For a family construction business expected to grow, gifting minority interests early can move substantial future value out of the estate.

Indirect gifts and special situations

The gift tax reaches more than outright transfers. A below-market loan to a family member is treated as a gift of the forgone interest; forgiving a debt, paying another's expense (other than direct tuition or medical), or selling property for inadequate consideration are all gifts. A net gift — where the donee agrees to pay the gift tax — reduces the taxable gift by the tax assumed, and can even generate income to the donor to the extent that tax exceeds basis. A qualified disclaimer lets a beneficiary refuse a gift or bequest (in writing, within nine months, before accepting any benefit) so the property passes to the next taker as if the disclaimant had predeceased — a tool to redirect transfers and use exemptions efficiently. And a gift to a minor through a §2503(c) trust or a custodial account qualifies for the annual exclusion even though the child cannot yet manage the property.

Gift versus bequest — a worked comparison

The recurring planning question is whether to gift an asset now or let it pass at death. Consider MBG stock with a $100,000 basis and a $400,000 value. Gift it today: the donee takes the $100,000 carryover basis, the value (less the annual exclusion) uses lifetime exemption, and all future appreciation grows in the child's hands — but the child faces income tax on the $300,000 built-in gain whenever the stock is sold. Hold it until death: the stock is in the gross estate at its date-of-death value, yet the heir takes a stepped-up basis equal to that value, erasing the built-in gain for income-tax purposes. The answer turns on the spread between transfer-tax and income-tax rates, how much more the asset is expected to appreciate, and whether the estate will even be taxable given the large exemption. For most families under the roughly $15 million exemption the step-up often wins for highly appreciated assets, while gifting wins for assets expected to appreciate sharply that the family wants out of a potentially taxable estate.

CMA bridge

CMA valued MBG as a going concern; the gift tax values fractional interests in it, with minority and marketability discounts — the same enterprise, now measured for a generational transfer. The exemption Reed uses gifting shares this year is the same unified exemption that will shelter the estate next week.

Practice and recap

  1. Recognize a completed gift (donative intent + delivery + relinquished control); the donor pays and files Form 709.
  2. Apply the annual exclusion ($19,000 for 2025, indexed) to present-interest gifts to unlimited donees; future interests do not qualify.
  3. Use gift splitting ($38,000), the unlimited marital/charitable deductions, and the direct tuition/medical exclusion.
  4. Shelter cumulative taxable gifts with the ~$15 million (2026, PL 119-21) unified exemption; use Crummey powers and valuation discounts in planning.

Recap: the donor-paid gift tax allows a $19,000 (2025) annual exclusion per donee for present-interest gifts, unlimited marital and charitable deductions, and a direct tuition/medical exclusion; taxable gifts reduce a unified lifetime exemption of about $15 million per person for 2026 under Public Law 119-21; and Crummey powers plus minority/marketability discounts move a family business out of the estate efficiently.

About $15 million per individual, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21 (indexed); shared by gift and estate tax.
A short withdrawal right that converts a gift in trust into a present interest qualifying for the annual exclusion.
Minority-interest and lack-of-marketability discounts reduce the value of gifted closely held business interests.

weeks.title: REG U3·W3 — The Federal Estate & Generation-Skipping Tax (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the second half of the unified system

Last week's gift tax taxed lifetime transfers; the estate tax taxes the transfer at death, using the same unified exemption. When Jordan Reed dies, the executor files Form 706, totals everything Reed owned or controlled, subtracts deductions, and applies the unified credit. Because the exemption is so large, most estates owe nothing — but the computation, the inclusion surprises, and portability are squarely tested.

The gross estate

The gross estate is everything the decedent owned or controlled at death, valued at fair market value on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date six months later, if electing it lowers both the estate and the tax). It includes probate property, cash and securities (the MBG shares), real estate, and business interests — but the inclusion rules reach further than probate.

Inclusion rules that surprise

Several items pulled into the gross estate trip up candidates. Life insurance is included if the decedent owned the policy or held any incidents of ownership, or if proceeds are payable to the estate. Retained interests are caught: property the decedent transferred but kept a life estate (§2036) or the power to alter or revoke (§2038) is fully included. Gifts made within three years of death are generally not pulled back — except the gift tax paid on them (the gross-up rule) and transfers of life insurance. Jointly held property, general powers of appointment, and certain annuities are also included.

Deductions from the gross estate

From the gross estate the executor subtracts: funeral and administration expenses, the decedent's debts and unpaid taxes, casualty losses during administration, the unlimited marital deduction (property passing to a surviving U.S.-citizen spouse), the unlimited charitable deduction, and state death taxes. The marital deduction is the great deferral device — it pushes tax on the first spouse's estate to the death of the second.

From taxable estate to tax

The taxable estate is the gross estate minus deductions. To it the computation adds back post-1976 adjusted taxable gifts (so the brackets account for lifetime giving), produces a tentative tax at rates topping out near 40%, then subtracts gift taxes already paid and the unified credit. The credit shelters the basic exclusion amount — about $15 million per individual for 2026, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21 and indexed thereafter. Only estates above that exemption (net of lifetime gifts) actually owe tax.

Portability of the exemption

A spouse who dies without using the full exemption can pass the unused amount — the deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) — to the surviving spouse, who adds it to their own. Portability is not automatic: the executor must elect it on a timely filed Form 706, even for an estate too small to owe tax. With portability a married couple can shelter roughly twice the individual exemption without complex trust planning.

The generation-skipping transfer tax and the basis step-up

The generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax is a separate, flat tax at the top rate layered on transfers that skip a generation — for example, a gift or bequest straight to a grandchild — to stop families from avoiding a layer of transfer tax. It has its own exemption (tracking the unified amount). Finally, the estate tax pairs with an income-tax benefit: property included in the gross estate gets a basis step-up to date-of-death fair market value, so heirs who later sell recognize gain only on post-death appreciation — the reason holding appreciated MBG stock until death can beat gifting it during life.

Putting it together on the family estate

Suppose Reed dies in 2026 with a $10 million gross estate, $1 million of debts and expenses, and $2 million passing to a spouse. The taxable estate is $10M − $1M − $2M (marital) = $7 million. Because that is well under the roughly $15 million exemption, the unified credit eliminates the tax entirely — and the executor may still file Form 706 to elect portability of the unused exemption to the surviving spouse, and the heirs take the assets with a stepped-up basis. The estate-and-gift system has taxed the transfer once, at a generous threshold, with the income tax forgiving the built-in gain.

Marital-deduction planning and estate liquidity

The unlimited marital deduction defers tax but does not erase it, so planning shapes how property passes to a spouse. A QTIP (qualified terminable interest property) trust lets the first spouse to die give the survivor a lifetime income interest while controlling who ultimately receives the property — and the estate elects to treat it as qualifying for the marital deduction, deferring tax to the survivor's death. A credit-shelter (bypass) trust instead uses the first spouse's exemption at the first death, keeping that amount and its future growth out of the survivor's estate; with portability now permanent many couples rely on the DSUE election, though a bypass trust still shelters post-death appreciation that portability does not.

Large estates also face a liquidity problem: estate tax is generally due nine months after death, yet much of a construction family's wealth may be illiquid business interests and real estate. §6166 lets an estate in which a closely held business exceeds 35% of the adjusted gross estate pay the tax in installments over up to fourteen years at a reduced interest rate — relief built precisely for a family business like MBG, so heirs need not fire-sale the company to pay the tax. The executor weighs this against the alternate valuation date and the deductions to settle the estate without dismantling it.

Filing, payment, and the alternate valuation election

The estate-tax return, Form 706, is generally due nine months after death (a six-month extension is available) and must be filed when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the exemption — or, for smaller estates, to elect portability. The executor may elect the alternate valuation date (six months after death) only if doing so decreases both the gross estate and the estate tax, which stops taxpayers from cherry-picking a higher basis without a tax cost; property sold or distributed during the six months is valued at that transaction date. These mechanics, with §6166 installments and the portability election, give the executor a toolkit to settle even an illiquid estate on time without dismantling the family business to raise cash.

CMA bridge

The gift tax (last week) and the estate tax (this week) draw on one unified exemption; together they decide how much of MBG's value Reed can move to the next generation tax-free. The date-of-death basis step-up ties back to FAR/REG property rules — the heir's basis in the inherited MBG stock is its FMV at death, not Reed's original cost.

Practice and recap

  1. Build the gross estate at date-of-death FMV (or alternate valuation); include life insurance with incidents of ownership, retained-interest transfers, and the gift tax on within-3-years gifts.
  2. Subtract debts/expenses and the unlimited marital and charitable deductions to reach the taxable estate.
  3. Add back adjusted taxable gifts, apply the ~40% rates, and shelter with the ~$15 million (2026, PL 119-21) unified credit.
  4. Elect portability of the DSUE on a timely Form 706; know the separate GST tax and the date-of-death basis step-up.

Recap: the estate tax totals everything the decedent owned or controlled (including life insurance with incidents of ownership and retained-interest transfers), subtracts the unlimited marital and charitable deductions, and shelters about $15 million per person for 2026 under Public Law 119-21; portability passes a spouse's unused exemption via a timely Form 706; the GST tax adds a flat top-rate layer on generation-skipping transfers; and inherited property takes a date-of-death basis step-up.

A surviving spouse may use the deceased spouse's unused exemption, but only if elected on a timely filed Form 706.
A separate flat tax at the top rate on transfers that skip a generation; has its own exemption.

weeks.title: REG U3·W4 — Tax-Exempt Organizations (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — when an entity pays no income tax

If Jordan Reed endows a family foundation or MBG supports a local charity, a different creature appears: a tax-exempt organization that pays no federal income tax on income furthering its exempt purpose. Exemption is a privilege with strings — strict organizational rules, prohibited activities, special taxes on private foundations, and a tax on business income unrelated to the mission. This closes REG Unit 3.

Qualifying under §501(c)(3)

The best-known exemption, §501(c)(3), covers organizations organized and operated exclusively for charitable, religious, educational, scientific, or literary purposes. Two tests must both be met: the organizational test (the governing documents limit the entity to exempt purposes and dedicate assets to charity on dissolution) and the operational test (it actually operates that way). A §501(c)(3) is uniquely valuable because contributions to it are tax-deductible to donors.

The prohibited activities

Exemption is lost or penalized for three things. Private inurement — letting the organization's earnings benefit insiders (excess compensation, sweetheart deals) — is strictly forbidden, and excess benefit transactions trigger intermediate-sanction excise taxes on the insiders. Lobbying must be insubstantial (or within a measured election). And political campaign activity — supporting or opposing a candidate — is an absolute prohibition for a §501(c)(3); even a single endorsement can cost the exemption.

Applying for recognition

An organization seeks recognition of exemption by filing Form 1023 (a streamlined 1023-EZ exists for small organizations). The IRS issues a determination letter. While churches and very small organizations have relief from applying, recognition is what assures donors their gifts are deductible and the entity is exempt — so most file. Recognition is prospective discipline, not a one-time pass: the entity must keep meeting the operational test.

Public charity versus private foundation

Every §501(c)(3) is presumed a private foundation unless it qualifies as a public charity — typically by passing a public support test (drawing a broad base of public donations) or by being an inherently public institution like a church, school, or hospital. The distinction matters greatly: private foundations (such as Reed's family foundation, funded by one family) face a battery of excise taxes and tighter rules that public charities escape.

Private foundation excise taxes

Private foundations bear special excise taxes designed to force charitable use and prevent abuse: a tax on net investment income; a penalty for failing to make the required minimum distributions (roughly 5% of investment assets) for charitable purposes each year; prohibitions on self-dealing between the foundation and its insiders; limits on excess business holdings (owning too much of a business); and taxes on jeopardizing investments and improper taxable expenditures (such as lobbying). These rules are why a family foundation is more tightly regulated than a community public charity.

Unrelated business income tax (UBIT)

Even an exempt organization pays regular corporate tax — UBIT, reported on Form 990-T — on income from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and not substantially related to its exempt purpose. The classic example: a charity that runs a commercial business unrelated to its mission. Debt-financed income is also taxed. But key exceptions remove income produced by substantially all volunteer labor, the sale of donated goods, or activities run for the convenience of members (a hospital cafeteria) — and passive dividends, interest, and rents are generally excluded. UBIT keeps tax-exempt entities from competing untaxed with ordinary businesses.

Annual compliance and other exempt types

Most exempt organizations file an annual information return — Form 990 (with 990-EZ and the postcard 990-N for smaller groups; private foundations file 990-PF). Failing to file for three consecutive years automatically revokes exemption. Beyond §501(c)(3), other categories exist — §501(c)(4) social-welfare organizations (which may lobby and do limited political work, but gifts are not deductible) and §501(c)(6) trade associations and chambers of commerce, the kind a construction industry group would use. Each is exempt, but only the §501(c)(3) offers donors a deduction.

Intermediate sanctions and donor substantiation

Two compliance points round out §501(c)(3) practice. Rather than revoking exemption for every insider abuse, the IRS can impose intermediate sanctions — excise taxes on a disqualified person who receives an excess benefit (and on managers who knowingly approve it) — a more proportionate remedy than killing the charity. And to claim a deduction, donors must meet substantiation rules: a contemporaneous written acknowledgment for any gift of $250 or more, additional appraisal requirements for larger noncash gifts, and disclosure on the receipt of the value of any goods or services the donor received in return (the quid pro quo rule). A charity that fails to provide these disclosures can itself be penalized — tying the exempt entity's compliance directly to its donors' deductions.

Choosing among the exempt categories

Not every mission fits §501(c)(3). A §501(c)(4) social-welfare organization may engage in substantial lobbying and some political activity that a charity cannot, but contributions to it are not deductible — a trade-off advocacy groups accept. A §501(c)(6) business league, trade association, or chamber of commerce serves a common business interest (a construction-contractors association, say); member dues may be deductible as a business expense, though the portion used for lobbying is not. §501(c)(7) social clubs round out the common list. The throughline of REG Unit 3 is that the tax law follows the purpose of a transfer or an entity — income earned, value transferred at gift or death, or income devoted to charity — taxing each once under its own regime, leaving the planner to route value through the regime that serves the family and the mission at the least tax.

State registration and the compliance calendar

Exempt status is federal, but an organization must also register and report under state charity and solicitation laws and maintain the governance records the §990 makes public — board minutes, a conflict-of-interest policy, and documented compensation approvals. The §990 has itself become a transparency document: it discloses program-versus-overhead spending, the highest-paid people, and related-party transactions, so the form a charity files is in practice its public accountability statement. For a family foundation like Reed's the calendar is unforgiving — the annual 990-PF, the excise-tax computation on net investment income, and the yearly 5% minimum distribution must all be met, and a lapse converts the privilege of exemption into penalties. Exemption, in short, is earned every year, not granted once.

CMA bridge

CMA's ethics and governance themes reappear here as the law of the nonprofit sector: the private-inurement bar and self-dealing rules are the legal backbone of the tone-at-the-top controls a foundation's board must keep — and the §990 information return is the public's window into how an exempt organization actually spends its money.

Practice and recap

  1. Qualify under §501(c)(3) by meeting the organizational and operational tests; contributions are deductible only to (c)(3) organizations.
  2. Avoid private inurement, keep lobbying insubstantial, and never engage in political campaign activity.
  3. Distinguish public charities (public support test) from private foundations, which bear net-investment-income, minimum-distribution, self-dealing, and excess-business-holdings excise taxes.
  4. Pay UBIT (Form 990-T) on regularly carried-on unrelated business income and debt-financed income; file the annual Form 990 (three missed years revokes exemption).

Recap: a §501(c)(3) must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes, avoid private inurement and political activity, and offers donors a deduction; private foundations face extra excise taxes (net investment income, 5% minimum distribution, self-dealing, excess business holdings) that public charities escape; UBIT taxes unrelated, regularly carried-on business income; and the annual Form 990 is the compliance backbone — three missed filings revoke the exemption.

flashcards.back: Organized AND operated exclusively for charitable/religious/educational/scientific purposes; meets the organizational and operational tests. Contributions are tax-deductible.
Private inurement (insider benefit), more-than-insubstantial lobbying, and ANY political campaign activity (absolute bar).
File Form 1023 (or 1023-EZ for small orgs); the IRS issues a determination letter.
Every (c)(3) is a private foundation unless it passes a public support test or is an inherently public institution (church/school/hospital).
Net investment income tax, ~5% minimum-distribution requirement, self-dealing, excess business holdings, jeopardizing investments, and taxable expenditures.
Regular tax (Form 990-T) on a trade/business regularly carried on and not substantially related to the exempt purpose; debt-financed income too.
Volunteer labor, sale of donated goods, member-convenience activities, and passive dividends/interest/rents are generally excluded.
Form 990 series (990/990-EZ/990-N; 990-PF for foundations); failing to file for 3 consecutive years revokes exemption.

units.title: REG Unit 4 — Property Transactions, Nontaxable Exchanges, Contracts/UCC & Debtor-Creditor Law

weeks.title: REG U4·W1 — Property Transactions: Basis, Character & Depreciation Recapture (2026)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — what happens when MBG sells an asset

When Meridian Building Group sells a used excavator or a parcel of land, three questions decide the tax: how much gain or loss is realized, how much is recognized, and what character (ordinary or capital) it carries. REG Unit 1 introduced property transactions; this week works the mechanics at exam depth — basis determination, the capital-gain netting process, the special §1231 rules for business property, and depreciation recapture. All figures use the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline.

Realized versus recognized gain

Gain or loss realized equals the amount realized (cash plus the fair value of property received plus liabilities assumed by the buyer) minus the adjusted basis of the asset given up. Gain recognized is the portion actually taxed — usually equal to realized gain, except where a nonrecognition rule (like the §1031 exchange covered next week) defers it. The first discipline of every property problem is to separate the two: compute the realized amount mechanically, then ask whether any provision limits recognition.

Cost and adjusted basis

Basis begins at cost — what was paid, including debt incurred. It is then increased by capital improvements and decreased by depreciation, depletion, and amortization allowed (or allowable). For MBG's equipment, the adjusted basis is original cost minus accumulated depreciation; for land, basis is cost plus improvements with no depreciation. Getting adjusted basis right is essential because it is the figure subtracted from the amount realized — an overstated basis understates the gain.

Basis of gifted and inherited property

Two transfers receive special basis rules. Gifted property takes a carryover (transferred) basis for computing gain, but for computing a loss the basis is the lower of carryover basis or fair value at the gift date — the dual-basis rule, which can produce no gain or loss if the sale price falls between the two. The donee's holding period tacks (includes the donor's). Inherited property instead takes a stepped-up (or down) basis equal to fair value at the date of death, and its holding period is automatically long-term regardless of how long it is actually held — a powerful planning feature that erases the decedent's unrealized appreciation.

Character: capital versus ordinary

The character of gain drives the rate. A capital asset is defined by exclusion under §1221 — everything except inventory, accounts receivable, and depreciable property or real property used in a trade or business (and a few others). So MBG's inventory of spec homes produces ordinary income, while a personal investment in stock produces capital gain. Long-term treatment requires a holding period of more than one year; one year or less is short-term, taxed at ordinary rates.

Capital gain and loss netting

Capital gains and losses run through a netting process: short-term items net against each other, long-term items net against each other, and the two results are then combined. A net long-term capital gain enjoys preferential rates — 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income — with special rates for unrecaptured §1250 gain (25%) and collectibles (28%), plus the 3.8% net investment income tax for higher earners. A net capital loss for an individual offsets ordinary income only up to $3,000 per year, with the excess carried forward indefinitely (corporations carry capital losses back 3 and forward 5, usable only against capital gains).

Section 1231 property

Depreciable property and real property used in a business and held more than one year are §1231 assets — and they get the best of both worlds. At year-end the taxpayer nets all §1231 gains and losses: a net §1231 gain is treated as long-term capital gain (preferential rate), while a net §1231 loss is treated as ordinary (fully deductible). A five-year lookback prevents abuse: a current net §1231 gain is recharacterized as ordinary to the extent of net §1231 losses deducted in the prior five years. This is the classification MBG's equipment and buildings fall into.

Depreciation recapture

Before §1231 capital treatment applies, depreciation recapture claws back the benefit of past deductions as ordinary income. §1245 (personal property — equipment, machinery) recaptures all prior depreciation as ordinary income, up to the amount of gain. Worked example: MBG buys an excavator for $100,000, takes $60,000 of depreciation (adjusted basis $40,000), and sells it for $90,000. The $50,000 gain is entirely ordinary because the recapture potential ($60,000) exceeds the gain. §1250 (real property) recaptures only depreciation taken in excess of straight-line — usually zero today since real property uses straight-line — but the prior depreciation becomes unrecaptured §1250 gain taxed at a maximum 25%.

A capital-gain netting walkthrough

The netting process rewards careful ordering. Suppose an investor has a $10,000 long-term capital gain, a $4,000 long-term capital loss, a $3,000 short-term capital gain, and a $9,000 short-term capital loss. First net within each group: long-term nets to a $6,000 net long-term gain; short-term nets to a $6,000 net short-term loss. Combining the two leaves $0 — the net short-term loss fully offsets the net long-term gain, and the preferential rate never comes into play. Had the long-term gain been larger, the excess would keep its preferential character; had the short-term loss been larger, up to $3,000 would offset ordinary income with the rest carried forward. Sequencing the buckets correctly is what makes these problems mechanical rather than guesswork.

Personal-use property and casualty losses

Not every asset behaves like an investment. A gain on personal-use property (a personal vehicle, a residence beyond the §121 exclusion) is taxable as a capital gain, but a loss on purely personal-use property is generally nondeductible. Under the 2026 Public Law 119-21 rules, an individual's personal casualty loss remains deductible only when attributable to a federally declared disaster (with state-declared disasters now also recognized under the updated rules), subject to the per-event and AGI floors. This asymmetry — tax the gain, deny the loss — is a recurring trap on personal assets that MBG's owner must remember for his own return.

CMA bridge

The CMA program tracked MBG's equipment basis and depreciation for book purposes; REG shows the tax consequences when that equipment is sold — §1245 recapture turning a seemingly capital gain into ordinary income. The book-versus-tax basis difference is exactly the kind of schedule the CFO must maintain to forecast the tax on an asset sale.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute realized gain (amount realized − adjusted basis); separate realized from recognized.
  2. Apply basis rules: cost (adjusted for improvements/depreciation), gift (carryover for gain, dual-basis for loss, tacked holding period), inheritance (FMV at death, automatically long-term).
  3. Determine character (capital asset by §1221 exclusion; LT requires >1 year), then net capital gains/losses ($3,000 ordinary offset, carryforward).
  4. Apply §1231 (net gain = LTCG, net loss = ordinary, 5-year lookback) after §1245 (full) and §1250 (excess-over-SL; 25% unrecaptured) recapture.

Recap: realized gain is amount realized minus adjusted basis; basis is cost adjusted for improvements and depreciation, carryover-with-dual-basis for gifts, and stepped to FMV (automatically long-term) for inheritances; character turns on the §1221 capital-asset definition and the >1-year holding period, with long-term gains taxed at 0/15/20% (25% unrecaptured §1250, 28% collectibles) and a $3,000 net capital loss offset; and business property is §1231 (net gain = capital, net loss = ordinary, 5-year lookback) only after §1245 recaptures all depreciation as ordinary and §1250 captures excess-over-straight-line — illustrated by MBG's excavator generating $50,000 of fully ordinary recapture income.

flashcards.back: Realized = amount realized (cash + FMV property + liabilities assumed) − adjusted basis. Recognized = the portion taxed (usually = realized unless a nonrecognition rule defers it).
Gain: carryover (donor's) basis. Loss: lower of carryover basis or FMV at gift date. Sale price between the two → no gain or loss. Holding period tacks.
FMV at date of death (stepped up or down); holding period is automatically long-term regardless of actual holding time.
Defined by exclusion: everything EXCEPT inventory, A/R, and depreciable/real property used in a business. Business inventory = ordinary; investments = capital.
0/15/20% by income; unrecaptured §1250 gain 25%; collectibles 28%; plus 3.8% NIIT. Net capital loss offsets ordinary income up to $3,000/yr (carryforward).
Net §1231 gain → long-term capital gain (preferential). Net §1231 loss → ordinary (fully deductible). 5-year lookback recharacterizes current gain as ordinary to the extent of prior §1231 losses.
Personal property (equipment): recaptures ALL prior depreciation as ordinary income, up to the gain. Excess gain above original cost is §1231.
Real property: recaptures only depreciation above straight-line (usually $0). Prior SL depreciation becomes unrecaptured §1250 gain, taxed at a max 25%.

questions.q: Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to:
choices: Fair value at the date of death
The lower of cost or FMV
questions.explain: Inherited property is stepped to FMV at death and is automatically long-term.

questions.q: For gifted property sold at a LOSS, the basis is:
choices: The lower of carryover basis or FMV at the gift date
questions.explain: The dual-basis rule uses the lower of carryover basis or gift-date FMV for losses.

questions.q: MBG's inventory of spec homes, when sold, produces:
questions.explain: Inventory is excluded from the §1221 capital-asset definition, so it is ordinary.

questions.q: Equipment cost $100,000, depreciation $60,000 (basis $40,000), sold for $90,000. The $50,000 gain is:
questions.explain: §1245 recaptures depreciation ($60,000 potential) as ordinary; since gain ($50,000) is less, all of it is ordinary.

questions.q: A net §1231 gain for the year is treated as:
choices: Long-term capital gain (subject to the 5-year lookback)
questions.explain: Net §1231 gain is long-term capital gain; net §1231 loss is ordinary. A 5-year lookback can recharacterize gain as ordinary.

questions.q: An individual's net capital loss offsets ordinary income up to:
choices: $3,000 per year, with the excess carried forward
questions.explain: Individuals deduct up to $3,000 of net capital loss against ordinary income, carrying forward the rest.

questions.q: Unrecaptured §1250 gain (prior straight-line depreciation on real property) is taxed at a maximum rate of:
questions.explain: Unrecaptured §1250 gain is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.

weeks.title: REG U4·W2 — Nontaxable Exchanges & Special Dispositions (2026)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — deferring the tax on a disposition

Not every gain is taxed when realized. The Code lets taxpayers defer gain on certain exchanges and dispositions — the §1031 like-kind exchange MBG uses to roll one parcel into another, the §1033 deferral when property is condemned, the §121 exclusion on a home sale, and the §453 installment method that spreads gain over time. This week works each nonrecognition rule plus the loss-limitation traps (related parties, wash sales) and the special small-business stock benefits, all on the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline.

Section 1031 like-kind exchanges

A §1031 exchange defers gain when real property held for business or investment is exchanged for like-kind real property. Since the 2017 Act, §1031 applies to real property only — equipment and other personal property no longer qualify. Gain is deferred, not eliminated: it is preserved in a carryover basis in the replacement property. If the taxpayer receives boot (cash or non-like-kind property, including net debt relief), gain is recognized to the extent of the lesser of realized gain or boot received. Losses are never recognized in a like-kind exchange. Strict 45-day identification and 180-day completion deadlines apply to deferred exchanges.

Boot and basis mechanics

Worked example: MBG exchanges land (adjusted basis $200,000, fair value $300,000) for like-kind land worth $260,000 plus $40,000 cash. Realized gain is $100,000; recognized gain is the lesser of $100,000 or $40,000 boot = $40,000. The basis of the replacement land is the carryover basis $200,000 + $40,000 gain recognized − $40,000 boot received = $200,000, preserving the $60,000 of deferred gain. The basis formula — old basis plus gain recognized minus boot received plus boot paid — is the heart of every exchange problem.

Section 1033 involuntary conversions

When property is destroyed, stolen, or condemned and the taxpayer receives insurance or a condemnation award, §1033 allows gain deferral if the proceeds are reinvested in qualifying replacement property within the replacement period — generally two years after the year of gain (three years for condemned real property used in a business or held for investment). Gain is recognized only to the extent proceeds are not reinvested. Unlike §1031, §1033 is generally elective and the replacement need only be similar or related in service or use.

Section 121 home-sale exclusion

An individual may exclude up to $250,000 ($500,000 for married filing jointly) of gain on the sale of a principal residence, provided the ownership and use tests are met — owned and used as the principal residence for at least two of the five years before sale. The full exclusion is generally available once every two years; a partial exclusion is allowed for a sale forced by a change in employment, health, or unforeseen circumstances. Gain above the exclusion is capital gain, and any depreciation taken (for a home office) is recaptured as unrecaptured §1250 gain.

Installment sales

The installment method (§453) spreads gain over the years payments are received: each payment recognizes gain equal to the payment times the gross-profit percentage (gross profit ÷ contract price). It applies automatically to gains from a sale with at least one payment after the year of sale, but it is not available for inventory/dealer dispositions, for losses, or for the recapture portion (§1245/§1250 recapture is recognized in full in the year of sale regardless of payments). MBG financing a buyer's purchase of surplus land over several years would use this method to defer recognizing the gain.

Loss-limitation traps

Several rules disallow losses. Under §267, a loss on a sale to a related party (family, or a >50% owned entity) is disallowed — though the related buyer may later use the disallowed loss to offset gain on a subsequent sale. The wash-sale rule (§1091) disallows a loss on stock or securities if substantially identical securities are purchased within 30 days before or after the sale; the disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement securities. These provisions stop taxpayers from harvesting a loss while keeping the economic position.

Small-business stock benefits

Two provisions reward investing in small corporations. §1244 lets an individual treat a loss on qualifying small-business stock as an ordinary loss (up to $50,000, or $100,000 on a joint return) rather than a capital loss. §1202 excludes gain on qualified small business stock (QSBS) held long enough; under the 2026 Public Law 119-21 rules, QSBS issued after enactment qualifies for a tiered exclusion — 50% at a 3-year hold, 75% at 4 years, and 100% at 5 years — with the per-issuer cap raised to $15 million and the corporate gross-asset ceiling raised to $75 million. Together they soften the downside and reward the upside of funding a new business.

Exchange timing and related-party limits

Deferred ("Starker") exchanges run on a strict clock: the replacement property must be identified within 45 days and received within 180 days of transferring the relinquished property — missing either deadline makes the whole transaction taxable. A qualified intermediary holds the proceeds so the taxpayer never has constructive receipt of cash. Special related-party rules also apply: if a §1031 exchange is made with a related party, both must hold the exchanged properties for two years, or the deferral is retroactively lost. These mechanical guardrails are tested precisely because they are where real exchanges most often fail.

What "like-kind" really means

For real property, like-kind is interpreted broadly — improved land can be exchanged for unimproved land, an office building for a warehouse, a fee interest for a long-term leasehold — as long as both are U.S. real property held for business or investment. It is the nature of the interest, not its grade or quality, that matters. Property held for personal use or as inventory (MBG's spec homes) never qualifies, which is why the held-for-investment requirement is the first thing to test in any exchange problem.

CMA bridge

When MBG rolls one investment parcel into another or finances a land sale to a buyer, the §1031 and §453 rules decide how much gain is taxed now versus deferred — a cash-flow decision the CFO models directly. The tax deferral is real working capital, which is why the entity-structuring work from REG Unit 2 and the property rules here feed the same planning.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply §1031 (real property only; defer gain; recognize lesser of gain or boot; no loss; carryover basis + gain − boot).
  2. Apply §1033 (reinvest within 2 years / 3 for condemned realty) and §121 ($250k/$500k; 2-of-5-year ownership/use).
  3. Use the installment method (gross-profit % × payment), excluding dealer/inventory, losses, and recapture (recognized fully in year of sale).
  4. Disallow §267 related-party losses and §1091 wash-sale losses (add to replacement basis); apply §1244 ordinary loss and §1202 QSBS tiered exclusion.

Recap: §1031 defers real-property exchange gain (recognized only to the lesser of gain or boot, never a loss, with carryover basis); §1033 defers involuntary-conversion gain on timely reinvestment; §121 excludes $250k/$500k of home gain after a 2-of-5-year ownership/use test; the installment method spreads gain by the gross-profit percentage but not for dealers, losses, or recapture; and the §267 related-party and §1091 wash-sale rules disallow losses while §1244 (ordinary loss) and the 2026 §1202 QSBS tiered 50/75/100% exclusion reward small-business investment.

flashcards.back: REAL property held for business/investment only. Defer gain (carryover basis); recognize the LESSER of realized gain or boot received; losses never recognized. 45-day ID / 180-day completion.
Replacement basis = old adjusted basis + gain recognized + boot paid − boot received. Preserves the deferred gain.
Basis $200k land for $260k land + $40k cash: realized gain $100k, recognized = lesser of $100k or $40k boot = $40k; new basis $200k.
Defer gain if proceeds reinvested in similar property within 2 years (3 for condemned business/investment realty). Elective; gain recognized to extent not reinvested.
Exclude $250k single / $500k MFJ of gain; owned + used as principal residence 2 of last 5 years; generally once every 2 years (partial for hardship).
Gain per payment = payment × gross-profit % (gross profit ÷ contract price). NOT for dealer/inventory, losses, or recapture (recapture recognized fully in year of sale).

§267: related-party loss disallowed (buyer may offset later gain). §1091 wash sale: loss disallowed if substantially identical securities bought within 30 days before/after; add disallowed loss to replacement basis.

§1244: ordinary loss up to $50k ($100k MFJ) on qualifying small-business stock. §1202 QSBS (post-OBBBA): 50%/75%/100% gain exclusion at 3/4/5-year holds; $15M per-issuer cap; $75M gross-asset ceiling.

questions.q: After the 2017 Act, §1031 like-kind exchange treatment applies only to:
choices: Real property held for business or investment
questions.explain: §1031 is now limited to real property held for business or investment; personal property no longer qualifies.

questions.q: Land (basis $200,000) is exchanged for like-kind land worth $260,000 plus $40,000 cash; realized gain is $100,000. Recognized gain is:
questions.explain: Recognized gain is the lesser of realized gain ($100,000) or boot received ($40,000) = $40,000.

questions.q: The §121 exclusion on a principal residence for married filing jointly is up to:
questions.explain: MFJ may exclude up to $500,000 ($250,000 single) after the 2-of-5-year ownership/use test.

questions.q: The installment method may NOT be used for:
choices: Dealer/inventory sales, losses, or the recapture portion
questions.explain: Installment reporting is unavailable for dealer/inventory dispositions, losses, and depreciation recapture (recognized fully in the year of sale).

questions.q: A loss on a sale of stock is disallowed under the wash-sale rule if substantially identical securities are bought:
choices: Within 30 days before or after the sale
questions.explain: §1091 disallows the loss if substantially identical securities are purchased within 30 days before or after; the loss is added to the replacement basis.

questions.q: Under §1244, a loss on qualifying small-business stock for a joint return is treated as ordinary up to:
questions.explain: §1244 allows ordinary-loss treatment up to $50,000 ($100,000 MFJ); the rest is capital loss.

questions.q: Under the 2026 §1202 rules, QSBS held at least five years receives a gain exclusion of:
questions.explain: Post-OBBBA QSBS uses a tiered exclusion: 50% at 3 years, 75% at 4 years, and 100% at 5 years.

weeks.title: REG U4·W3 — Business Law I: Contracts, UCC Sales & Agency
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the legal backbone of a construction deal

Every MBG project rests on contracts — with the owner, the subcontractors, and the material suppliers — and on the agents who sign them. REG tests business law alongside tax, and this week covers the law of contracts (common law), the UCC Article 2 rules that govern the sale of goods, and the agency doctrines that decide who is bound when an employee or officer acts. These are the rules that make a handshake — or a purchase order — enforceable.

Contract formation

A valid contract requires an offer, an acceptance, and consideration (a bargained-for exchange of legal value), plus capacity and a legal purpose. An offer shows present intent and definite terms; it can be revoked any time before acceptance unless an exception holds it open. Acceptance must generally mirror the offer under common law (the mirror-image rule), and under the mailbox rule an acceptance is effective when dispatched. Consideration must be new — past consideration and a pre-existing duty do not count.

Defenses to formation and enforcement

Even a formed contract may be void or voidable. Defenses include lack of capacity (a minor's contract is voidable by the minor), duress, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, mutual mistake, and illegality. The Statute of Frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged: contracts for an interest in land, those that cannot be performed within one year, a suretyship (promise to pay another's debt), and — under the UCC — sales of goods of $500 or more. The parol evidence rule then bars prior or contemporaneous oral terms that contradict a final written contract.

Performance, breach, and remedies

Common-law contracts require substantial performance; a material breach excuses the non-breaching party and triggers remedies. The usual remedy is compensatory damages (the benefit of the bargain), plus consequential damages that were foreseeable. Specific performance is available only for unique subject matter (real estate, rare goods) — not personal services. Liquidated-damages clauses are enforceable if the amount was a reasonable estimate and not a penalty, and the non-breaching party must mitigate its losses. These remedies aim to put the injured party where performance would have.

UCC Article 2 — sale of goods

The UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods (movable, tangible things) and relaxes several common-law rules, with extra duties for merchants. A merchant's signed firm offer stays open without consideration for the stated time (up to three months). Article 2 also abandons the mirror-image rule: under the battle of the forms (§2-207), an acceptance with additional terms can still form a contract, and between merchants those terms may become part of the deal unless they materially alter it, are objected to, or the offer limited acceptance. A contract can form even with open terms if the parties intended to contract.

Risk of loss and warranties

Article 2 allocates risk of loss. In a shipment contract (FOB seller's location) risk passes to the buyer when the seller delivers to the carrier; in a destination contract (FOB buyer's location) risk passes on tender at the destination. Goods carry warranties: an express warranty from an affirmation or sample; the implied warranty of merchantability (goods are fit for ordinary use — given automatically by a merchant seller); and the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose when the seller knows the buyer is relying on the seller to select suitable goods. The perfect-tender rule lets a buyer reject goods that fail to conform in any respect, subject to the seller's right to cure.

Agency — authority

An agency is a relationship in which an agent acts on behalf of a principal. An agent can bind the principal through actual authority — express (stated) or implied (reasonably necessary to carry out the express authority) — or through apparent authority, created by the principal's conduct toward the third party that reasonably leads the third party to believe the agent is authorized. Ratification can bind a principal to an unauthorized act done on its behalf if the principal later approves it with knowledge of the facts. Apparent authority is why MBG must be careful about what its job superintendents appear empowered to sign.

Agency — liability and duties

Whether the principal and agent are liable on a contract depends on disclosure. For a disclosed principal (the third party knows who it is), the principal is liable and the agent generally is not. For a partially disclosed (identity unknown) or undisclosed principal, both the agent and the principal can be held liable. The agent owes the principal fiduciary duties — loyalty, obedience, care, and accounting — and the principal owes the agent compensation and reimbursement. In tort, a principal is liable under respondeat superior for an employee's torts committed within the scope of employment.

Discharge, assignment, and third-party rights

Contract obligations can end other than by performance. A contract is discharged by accord and satisfaction (agreeing to and rendering a substitute performance), by novation (substituting a new party with everyone's consent), by impossibility or impracticability, or by mutual rescission. Rights can be assigned and duties delegated — though duties involving personal skill or that materially change the obligee's risk cannot be delegated. A third-party beneficiary who was intended to benefit (not merely an incidental beneficiary) can enforce the contract. A party who learns of an anticipatory repudiation — the other side's clear statement that it will not perform — may treat the contract as breached immediately and sue without waiting for the performance date. These doctrines decide who, beyond the original two parties, can sue or be released on a deal.

CMA bridge

MBG's purchase orders for lumber and steel are UCC Article 2 contracts; its agreements with the owner and subcontractors are common-law construction contracts; and the authority of its project managers to bind the company is pure agency law. The CFO who understands which body of law governs a document — and who is authorized to sign it — manages real legal and cash-flow risk.

Practice and recap

  1. Form a contract (offer + acceptance + consideration); apply the mirror-image and mailbox rules under common law.
  2. Spot defenses and the Statute of Frauds writing requirements (land, >1 year, suretyship, goods ≥$500); apply the parol evidence rule.
  3. Apply UCC Article 2 for goods: merchant firm offer, battle of the forms (§2-207), risk of loss (shipment vs destination), warranties, perfect tender.
  4. Analyze agency: actual (express/implied) vs apparent authority, ratification, disclosed/undisclosed principal liability, fiduciary duties, respondeat superior.

Recap: a contract needs offer, acceptance, and consideration, with common law using the mirror-image and mailbox rules and the Statute of Frauds requiring writings for land, >1-year, suretyship, and ≥$500 goods contracts; UCC Article 2 governs goods with merchant firm offers, the §2-207 battle of the forms, shipment-vs-destination risk of loss, merchantability/fitness warranties, and perfect tender; and agency binds a principal through actual or apparent authority, with disclosed principals liable (agent not) and undisclosed principals leaving both exposed, all under the agent's fiduciary duties.

flashcards.back: Offer + acceptance + consideration (bargained-for legal value), plus capacity and legality. Past consideration and pre-existing duty are not valid consideration.
Mailbox: acceptance effective when dispatched. Mirror-image (common law): acceptance must match the offer exactly. UCC relaxes mirror-image via §2-207.
Land interests, contracts not performable within 1 year, suretyship (promise to pay another's debt), and UCC sales of goods ≥ $500.
A merchant's signed written offer stays open without consideration for the time stated, up to 3 months.
An acceptance with additional terms can still form a contract; between merchants, additional terms join unless they materially alter, are objected to, or the offer limited acceptance.
Shipment contract (FOB seller): risk passes when goods given to the carrier. Destination contract (FOB buyer): risk passes on tender at destination.
Merchantability (fit for ordinary use — automatic from a merchant seller); fitness for a particular purpose (seller knows buyer relies on seller to select goods).

Actual = express or implied authority the principal gives the agent. Apparent = principal's conduct toward a third party makes the agent appear authorized. Disclosed principal liable; undisclosed → both liable.

questions.q: Under the Statute of Frauds, which contract must be in writing?
choices: A sale of goods for $500 or more
An oral agreement to lend a tool
questions.explain: UCC requires a writing for sales of goods of $500 or more; land, >1-year, and suretyship contracts also require writings.

questions.q: A merchant's signed written firm offer stays open without consideration for up to:
questions.explain: A UCC firm offer is irrevocable for the stated time, up to 3 months, without consideration.

questions.q: In a shipment contract (FOB seller's location), risk of loss passes to the buyer when:
choices: The seller delivers the goods to the carrier
questions.explain: In a shipment contract risk passes when conforming goods are delivered to the carrier.

questions.q: The implied warranty of merchantability is given automatically by:
choices: A merchant seller of goods of that kind
questions.explain: Merchantability is implied whenever the seller is a merchant who deals in goods of that kind.

questions.q: Apparent authority is created by:
choices: The principal's conduct toward the third party
questions.explain: Apparent authority arises from the principal's manifestations to the third party, not the agent's own statements.

questions.q: When a principal is UNDISCLOSED, liability on the contract falls on:
choices: Both the agent and the principal
questions.explain: With an undisclosed (or partially disclosed) principal, both the agent and the principal can be liable.

questions.q: Specific performance is generally available for:
choices: Unique subject matter such as real estate
questions.explain: Specific performance applies to unique goods or real estate; courts will not order personal services.

weeks.title: REG U4·W4 — Business Law II: Debtor-Creditor, Secured Transactions, Bankruptcy & Securities
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — what happens when debts go bad

A contractor lives on credit — supplier accounts, equipment loans, surety bonds — so the law of debtor and creditor matters as much as tax. This final REG week covers suretyship, the UCC Article 9 rules that govern secured transactions, the bankruptcy process when a debtor cannot pay, and the federal securities laws that regulate raising capital. These are the rules that decide who gets paid, in what order, when money runs short.

Suretyship

A surety promises a creditor to answer for the debt of another (the principal debtor) — the construction performance and payment bonds a contractor posts are suretyship arrangements. A surety is primarily liable (the creditor can pursue it directly), whereas a guarantor is typically secondarily liable. A surety who pays gains powerful rights: subrogation (stepping into the creditor's position), reimbursement from the debtor, and contribution from co-sureties. Key surety defenses include fraud on the surety and a material modification of the underlying contract without consent — though the debtor's personal defenses (like incapacity) generally do not protect the surety.

Secured transactions — attachment

UCC Article 9 governs a security interest in personal property and fixtures. The interest first attaches — becoming enforceable against the debtor — when three things exist: (1) value is given by the creditor, (2) the debtor has rights in the collateral, and (3) there is a security agreement (authenticated/signed describing the collateral) or the creditor takes possession or control. Attachment is what makes the lender a secured party as between it and the borrower — but not yet against the rest of the world.

Secured transactions — perfection and priority

Perfection makes the security interest effective against third parties, usually by filing a financing statement (debtor name, secured party, collateral) in the public records, or by possession, by control (for deposit accounts/investment property), or automatically for a purchase-money security interest in consumer goods. Priority rules then rank competing claims: a perfected interest beats an unperfected one; between two perfected interests, the first to file or perfect wins; and a purchase-money security interest (PMSI) in inventory or equipment can take superpriority if its special timing and notice requirements are met. On default, the secured party may repossess and dispose of the collateral in a commercially reasonable manner.

Bankruptcy — the basics and the chapters

Federal bankruptcy gives an honest debtor a fresh start and an orderly creditor payout. Chapter 7 is liquidation — a trustee sells nonexempt assets and distributes the proceeds. Chapter 11 is business reorganization under a court-approved plan. Chapter 13 is an individual's adjustment of debts from future income. Filing triggers the automatic stay, which immediately halts collection efforts, lawsuits, and foreclosures — giving the estate breathing room and protecting the orderly process.

Bankruptcy — the estate, preferences, and priority

The trustee can avoid certain pre-bankruptcy transfers. A voidable preference is a payment to a creditor on an antecedent debt made while insolvent within 90 days before filing (or one year for an insider) that lets that creditor receive more than it would in liquidation — the trustee claws it back for equal treatment. Fraudulent transfers can be unwound too. Distribution follows a strict order: secured creditors are paid from their collateral first, then priority unsecured claims (administrative expenses, certain employee wages up to a cap, and certain taxes), then general unsecured creditors pro rata. The debtor receives a discharge of most remaining debts — but some debts (recent taxes, most student loans, alimony/child support, debts from fraud) are nondischargeable.

Federal securities — the 1933 Act

The Securities Act of 1933 regulates the initial issuance of securities: a public offering must be registered with the SEC and accompanied by a prospectus full disclosure, unless an exemption applies. Common exemptions include Regulation D private placements (notably Rule 506, allowing unlimited capital from accredited investors), intrastate offerings, and small offerings. Liability under the 1933 Act attaches for material misstatements or omissions in the registration statement — a near-strict-liability standard for the issuer, with a due-diligence defense available to others.

Federal securities — the 1934 Act

The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 governs ongoing trading and reporting (the 10-K/10-Q/8-K filings from BAR Unit 2). Its antifraud core, §10(b) and Rule 10b-5, prohibits fraud or material misstatements in connection with the purchase or sale of any security — the basis for most insider-trading cases, which require scienter (intent). §16(b) forces insiders (officers, directors, >10% owners) to disgorge short-swing profits on purchases and sales within six months. Together the two Acts protect investors at issuance and in the secondary market, completing the legal framework REG tests.

Other creditor remedies and consumer protections

Beyond Article 9, creditors have remedies and limits. An unsecured creditor who obtains a judgment can enforce it through a writ of execution against property, a garnishment of wages (capped by federal law to protect a portion of earnings), or a judgment lien on real estate. Construction creditors have a special tool — the mechanic's lien — securing payment for labor and materials supplied to improve real property, and a fixture filing lets a secured party claim goods that become attached to real estate. On the protective side, federal consumer statutes — the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the Truth in Lending Act, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act — regulate how debts are collected, disclosed, and reported, and certain debtor property (a homestead, tools of the trade, basic personal items) is exempt from creditors. A creditor's choice among these remedies turns on what the debtor owns and which liens have already attached, so the secured, judgment, and statutory tools are weighed together. These rules shape the practical contest between a creditor trying to collect and a debtor trying to survive.

CMA bridge

MBG's equipment lenders file Article 9 financing statements to perfect their liens; its surety backs the performance bonds on public jobs; and if a major customer files bankruptcy, the preference and priority rules decide whether MBG keeps payments it already received. The CFO who tracks lien positions and bond obligations is applying exactly this body of law to protect the company's cash.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish a surety (primarily liable) from a guarantor; identify subrogation, reimbursement, and contribution rights and surety defenses.
  2. Apply Article 9: attachment (value + debtor rights + security agreement/possession), perfection (file/possess/control/automatic PMSI), priority (perfected > unperfected; first to file/perfect; PMSI superpriority).
  3. Compare bankruptcy Chapters 7/11/13, the automatic stay, voidable preferences (90 days / 1 year insiders), the priority waterfall, and nondischargeable debts.
  4. Apply the 1933 Act (registration + Reg D/Rule 506 exemptions) and the 1934 Act (§10(b)/Rule 10b-5 fraud, §16(b) short-swing profits).

Recap: a surety is primarily liable with rights of subrogation, reimbursement, and contribution; an Article 9 security interest attaches with value, debtor rights, and a security agreement, then perfects by filing/possession/control (or automatically for a consumer-goods PMSI), with priority to the first to file or perfect and superpriority for a PMSI; bankruptcy halts collection via the automatic stay, lets the trustee avoid preferences (90 days, or 1 year for insiders), and pays secured then priority then general unsecured creditors before discharging dischargeable debts; and the 1933 Act governs registration of new offerings (with Reg D exemptions) while the 1934 Act polices trading through Rule 10b-5 and §16(b).

flashcards.back: Surety: primarily liable (creditor can pursue directly). Guarantor: usually secondarily liable. A paying surety gets subrogation, reimbursement, and contribution from co-sureties.
Security interest becomes enforceable against the debtor when: (1) value given, (2) debtor has rights in collateral, (3) security agreement (authenticated) OR creditor possession/control.
Effective against third parties by filing a financing statement, possession, control, or automatically for a PMSI in consumer goods.
Perfected beats unperfected; between perfected, first to file or perfect wins; a PMSI can take superpriority with proper timing/notice.
Ch 7 = liquidation (trustee sells nonexempt assets). Ch 11 = business reorganization. Ch 13 = individual debt adjustment from future income. Filing triggers the automatic stay.
Payment on an antecedent debt while insolvent within 90 days of filing (1 year for insiders) giving more than liquidation would; trustee claws it back.

Secured creditors (from collateral) → priority unsecured (admin expenses, certain wages up to cap, certain taxes) → general unsecured pro rata. Some debts nondischargeable (recent taxes, support, fraud, most student loans).

1933: registration of new offerings + prospectus (Reg D/Rule 506 exemptions for accredited investors). 1934: ongoing reporting, §10(b)/Rule 10b-5 antifraud (scienter), §16(b) short-swing profit recovery.

questions.q: A security interest attaches when value is given, the debtor has rights in the collateral, and:
choices: There is a security agreement (or the creditor has possession/control)
questions.explain: Attachment requires value, debtor rights, and a security agreement (or possession/control). Filing is for perfection, not attachment.

questions.q: Between two perfected security interests in the same collateral, priority goes to:
choices: The first to file or perfect
questions.explain: Among perfected interests, the first to file or perfect has priority (with PMSI superpriority exceptions).

questions.q: A payment to an ordinary creditor on an old debt, made while insolvent 60 days before filing, may be:
choices: A voidable preference clawed back by the trustee
questions.explain: Preferential transfers within 90 days (1 year for insiders) can be avoided by the trustee.

questions.q: Which bankruptcy chapter is a business reorganization?
questions.explain: Chapter 11 is reorganization; Chapter 7 is liquidation; Chapter 13 is individual debt adjustment.

questions.q: Rule 506 of Regulation D allows an issuer to raise capital primarily from:
questions.explain: Rule 506 permits unlimited capital from accredited investors (with limits on non-accredited investors).

questions.q: Section 16(b) of the 1934 Act requires insiders to disgorge:
choices: Short-swing profits on trades within six months
questions.explain: §16(b) recovers short-swing profits from purchases and sales within a six-month period by insiders.

questions.q: A surety who pays the creditor is entitled to:
choices: Subrogation and reimbursement from the debtor
questions.explain: A paying surety steps into the creditor's rights (subrogation) and may seek reimbursement from the debtor and contribution from co-sureties.

units.title: BAR Unit 1 — Financial Analysis, Forecasting, Business Combinations & Financial Instruments

weeks.title: BAR U1·W1 — Ratio & Financial-Statement Analysis (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — reading the company through its ratios

The CPA BAR discipline (Business Analysis & Reporting) is where the analysis skills from the CMA program become an exam section. It reuses the most construction content of any discipline — WIP, working capital, and ratios — so MBG is the perfect lens. This week turns the financial statements into ratios that reveal liquidity, efficiency, solvency, and profitability, and decomposes return with the DuPont model.

Liquidity ratios

Liquidity measures the ability to pay short-term obligations. The current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities (a contractor wants comfortably above 1.0, often 1.2–1.5 for bonding). The quick (acid-test) ratio = (current assets − inventory − prepaids) ÷ current liabilities, a sterner test that strips slow assets. The cash ratio uses only cash and equivalents. Working capital (current assets − current liabilities) is the absolute-dollar cushion sureties scrutinize before bonding a job.

Activity ratios and the cash cycle

Activity ratios gauge how efficiently assets are used. Receivables turnover = net credit sales ÷ average receivables, converted to days sales outstanding (DSO) = 365 ÷ turnover. Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory, converted to days inventory. Payables turnover gives days payable. Combine them into the operating cycle (DSO + days inventory) and the cash conversion cycle (operating cycle − days payable) — the number of days cash is tied up before a job's costs are recovered, a central liquidity driver for a builder financing work in progress.

Solvency and leverage

Solvency measures long-run ability to meet obligations. Debt-to-equity = total liabilities ÷ total equity and debt-to-assets = total liabilities ÷ total assets gauge leverage. Times interest earned = EBIT ÷ interest expense shows how comfortably operating earnings cover interest, and the debt-service-coverage ratio extends that to principal-plus-interest. Sureties and lenders cap a contractor's leverage because a thinly capitalized builder cannot absorb a problem job.

Profitability

Profitability ratios scale earnings to sales or capital. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue, operating margin = operating income ÷ revenue, and net margin = net income ÷ revenue. Return on assets (ROA) = net income ÷ average assets, return on equity (ROE) = net income ÷ average equity, and return on invested capital (ROIC) measures after-tax operating return on debt-plus-equity capital. For a contractor, gross margin by job type is the most actionable — it isolates estimating and field execution.

The DuPont decomposition

The DuPont model breaks ROE into three levers: ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier (profitability × efficiency × leverage). Worked example: if MBG earns a 5% net margin, turns assets 2.0 times, and carries an equity multiplier (assets ÷ equity) of 2.5, then ROE = 5% × 2.0 × 2.5 = 25%. The power of the decomposition is diagnostic: a high ROE driven by leverage rather than margin is riskier, and DuPont tells you which lever is doing the work.

Construction-specific analysis

A contractor's statements carry accounts general analysis ignores. Costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings (underbillings) is an asset signaling work performed but not yet billed; billings in excess of costs (overbillings) is a liability signaling the job is billed ahead of cost — generally the healthier financing position. The backlog (signed but unperformed work) predicts future revenue, and the ratio of working capital and equity to backlog is exactly what a surety tests to set bonding capacity. Underbillings that grow faster than revenue can warn of estimating problems or unapproved change orders — a red flag the analyst learns to chase.

Horizontal, vertical, and common-size analysis

Ratios gain meaning in context. Horizontal (trend) analysis compares line items across periods to spot direction; vertical analysis expresses each line as a percentage of a base (sales for the income statement, total assets for the balance sheet); and common-size statements let you compare MBG to a larger competitor despite different scale. The analyst always asks for a benchmark — prior periods, industry medians, or covenant thresholds — because a ratio alone is just a number until it is compared. The standard caveats apply: ratios rely on historical cost, can be distorted by accounting choices, and must be read together, never in isolation.

Market and valuation ratios

Investors layer market ratios on top of the operating ratios. Earnings per share (EPS) drives the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio (market price ÷ EPS), the headline valuation multiple. The dividend yield (dividend per share ÷ price) and the dividend payout ratio (dividends ÷ net income) describe distribution policy, while the retention ratio (1 − payout) feeds sustainable growth. Book value per share and the price-to-book ratio compare market and accounting value, and enterprise-value multiples such as EV/EBITDA value the whole capital structure rather than just equity. A privately held contractor has no market price, so analysts apply these multiples from comparable public companies (with discounts) to estimate value — the same comparable-company logic used to value MBG for a sale or an owner buy-in.

Quality of earnings and the limits of ratios

Ratios are only as good as the earnings beneath them, so the analyst probes quality of earnings. Net income built on aggressive accruals — recognizing revenue early, under-reserving, capitalizing costs that should be expensed — diverges from cash flow, so a persistent gap between net income and operating cash flow is a warning sign. One-time gains, changes in accounting estimates, and off-balance-sheet arrangements can flatter a ratio without improving the business. The disciplined analyst reconciles earnings to cash, strips out nonrecurring items, reads the notes and segment data, and benchmarks against peers — because a single ratio, divorced from cash quality and context, can mislead as easily as inform. For a contractor, the classic distortion is an optimistic estimated cost to complete that inflates percentage-of-completion profit; the analyst tests it against physical progress and change-order history.

Cash-flow-based metrics

Because earnings can be managed, analysts lean on cash. Free cash flow (operating cash flow − capital expenditures) measures the cash a business actually generates after sustaining itself, and operating-cash-flow ratios (operating cash flow ÷ current liabilities, or ÷ total debt) test solvency without accrual noise. The cash-flow-to-net-income ratio gauges earnings quality directly. For a contractor whose reported profit depends on percentage-of-completion estimates, these cash-based measures are an essential cross-check on the accrual story.

CMA bridge

CMA month 7 introduced these same ratios and the DuPont model for internal performance; BAR tests them at exam depth and adds the construction-specific WIP and bonding analysis. The under/overbilling accounts trace straight back to the CMA cost-management and FAR revenue-recognition units — here they become analytical signals.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute liquidity (current, quick, cash, working capital) and read them against bonding thresholds.
  2. Build the operating and cash conversion cycles from DSO, days inventory, and days payable.
  3. Assess leverage (debt-to-equity, times interest earned) and profitability (margins, ROA, ROE, ROIC).
  4. Decompose ROE with DuPont (margin × turnover × leverage) and layer in construction WIP/backlog analysis.

Recap: ratios convert the statements into signals — liquidity and the cash conversion cycle for short-term health, leverage and coverage for solvency, margins and returns for profitability — and DuPont splits a 25% ROE into margin (5%), turnover (2.0), and leverage (2.5) so you can see which lever drives it; for a contractor, underbillings, overbillings, and backlog add the bonding lens a general analysis would miss, while cash-based measures like free cash flow guard against earnings flattered by optimistic percentage-of-completion estimates.

flashcards.back: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio strips inventory and prepaids (a sterner liquidity test).
Operating cycle (DSO + days inventory) − days payable; days cash is tied up before costs are recovered.
EBIT ÷ interest expense; how comfortably operating earnings cover interest.
ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier (profitability × efficiency × leverage).
5% margin × 2.0 turnover × 2.5 equity multiplier = 25% ROE.
Underbillings (costs/earnings in excess of billings) = asset (work done, not billed); overbillings (billings in excess of costs) = liability (billed ahead of cost).
Backlog = signed but unperformed work; sureties test working capital and equity against backlog to set bonding capacity.
Vertical = each line as a % of a base (sales or total assets); horizontal = trend across periods; common-size enables cross-company comparison.

questions.q: The quick (acid-test) ratio differs from the current ratio by:
choices: Excluding inventory and prepaids from current assets
questions.explain: The quick ratio removes inventory and prepaids — the least liquid current assets.
