weeks.title: BAR U3·W2 — Capital Budgeting & Investment Decisions (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — should MBG buy the crane?

When Meridian Building Group weighs a $400,000 tower crane against years of rental, it is making a capital-budgeting decision — committing cash now for returns spread over years. BAR tests the techniques that rank such investments: net present value, internal rate of return, payback, and the profitability index, all resting on the time value of money and the cost of capital (WACC) from BAR Unit 2. This week builds the toolkit for deciding which long-term investments create value.

Relevant cash flows

Capital budgeting analyzes incremental, after-tax cash flows, not accounting income. Only future cash flows that differ between accepting and rejecting matter: the initial outlay, the operating cash inflows, the depreciation tax shield (depreciation is non-cash but reduces taxes), changes in working capital, and any salvage value. Sunk costs (already spent) and allocated overhead that will not change are excluded. Getting the cash flows right — incremental and after tax — is the foundation; the discounting techniques are only as good as the flows fed into them.

Net present value

Net present value (NPV) discounts all expected cash flows to the present at the firm's required rate of return (typically WACC) and subtracts the initial investment. The rule: accept if NPV is positive (the project earns more than the cost of capital and creates value); reject if negative. Worked example: a project costs $100,000 and returns $30,000 per year for five years; at a 10% discount rate the annuity factor is about 3.7908, so the inflows are worth $113,724 and NPV = $13,724 — positive, so accept. NPV is the theoretically preferred method because it measures value created in dollars and uses a realistic reinvestment assumption.

Internal rate of return

The internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero — the project's own expected return. The rule: accept if IRR exceeds the hurdle rate (the cost of capital). IRR is intuitive because it is expressed as a percentage, but it has drawbacks: it assumes cash flows are reinvested at the IRR (often unrealistic), can produce multiple IRRs with unconventional cash flows, and can conflict with NPV when ranking mutually exclusive projects of different size or timing. When NPV and IRR disagree on mutually exclusive projects, NPV governs.

Payback and discounted payback

The payback period is the time required to recover the initial investment from cash inflows — a $100,000 project returning $25,000 a year pays back in four years. It is simple and emphasizes liquidity and risk, but it ignores the time value of money and any cash flows after payback. The discounted payback period fixes the first flaw by using discounted cash flows, but still ignores post-payback flows. Payback is best as a screening or risk filter, not the primary accept/reject criterion.

Profitability index and accounting rate of return

The profitability index (PI) divides the present value of inflows by the initial investment; a PI greater than 1 means a positive NPV, so accept. PI is useful for ranking projects when capital is rationed, because it measures value created per dollar invested. The accounting rate of return (ARR) divides average accounting income by the investment — but because it uses accrual income and ignores the time value of money, it is the weakest method and is tested mainly as a contrast to the discounted techniques.

Comparing the methods

Each method answers a slightly different question. NPV gives value created in dollars (the best single measure); IRR gives a return percentage (intuitive but flawed for ranking); PI gives value per dollar (best under capital rationing); payback gives a liquidity/risk read. The discount rate matters enormously — a higher required return lowers every present value and can flip a positive NPV negative — which is why the WACC estimate from BAR Unit 2 is so consequential. For independent projects NPV and IRR agree; the conflicts arise only among mutually exclusive ones.

Risk and sensitivity

Because the inputs are forecasts, the analysis must test uncertainty. Sensitivity analysis changes one variable at a time (the discount rate, the cash-flow estimate) to see how the decision shifts; scenario analysis models coherent best/base/worst cases; and a higher risk-adjusted discount rate can be applied to riskier projects. For MBG, recognizing that a crane's value hinges on assumed utilization — and stress-testing that assumption — is as important as the point-estimate NPV. A single number hides the risk that sensitivity analysis reveals.

The time value of money toolkit

Every discounting technique rests on the time value of money: a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later because it can be invested. The building blocks are the present value of $1 (discount a single future amount), the present value of an annuity (discount a stream of equal payments — the factor used in the NPV example), and their future-value counterparts. The discount rate reflects the required return, and compounding frequency matters — more frequent compounding raises the effective rate. Mastering which factor applies to which cash-flow pattern is the mechanical core of every capital-budgeting and valuation computation across BAR.

Capital rationing and mutually exclusive projects

Real firms face limited capital, so they must rank projects, not just accept every positive-NPV one. Under capital rationing, the profitability index helps select the combination of projects that maximizes total NPV per dollar of the constrained budget. Mutually exclusive projects (only one can be chosen — buy the crane or the larger one) are ranked by NPV, accepting the highest. Unequal lives are compared with techniques such as the equivalent annual annuity. The recurring lesson is that the accept/reject rule for an independent project differs from the ranking needed when resources or choices are constrained.

Real options in capital budgeting

Static NPV can understate a project's value by ignoring managerial flexibility. Real options — the option to expand a successful project, abandon a failing one, or defer investment until uncertainty resolves — carry value that traditional NPV misses. Recognizing that MBG could scale up crane use if its project pipeline grows, or sell the asset if work dries up, adds option value to the base analysis. The concept reminds analysts that a single discounted number is a starting point, not the whole decision.

CMA bridge

CMA months 8 and 11 built MBG's capital-budgeting and cost-of-capital models; BAR tests them at exam depth and ties them to the WACC and valuation work from BAR Unit 2. The equipment-versus-rent decision the CFO models every season is exactly the NPV/IRR analysis that decides whether a long-term investment creates value.

Practice and recap

  1. Use incremental, after-tax cash flows (include depreciation tax shield and working capital; exclude sunk costs).
  2. Apply NPV (accept if > 0; discount at WACC) and IRR (accept if > hurdle rate); when they conflict on mutually exclusive projects, NPV governs.
  3. Compute payback (ignores TVM and post-payback flows), discounted payback, and the profitability index (PI > 1 accept; ranks under capital rationing).
  4. Test risk with sensitivity and scenario analysis and a risk-adjusted discount rate.

Recap: capital budgeting discounts incremental after-tax cash flows; NPV (accept if positive — a $100,000 project returning $30,000 for five years at 10% has a $13,724 NPV) is the preferred measure of dollar value created, IRR (accept if above the hurdle) is an intuitive percentage that can conflict with NPV on mutually exclusive projects (where NPV governs), payback and discounted payback gauge liquidity but ignore later flows, and the profitability index (>1) ranks projects per dollar under capital rationing — all stress-tested with sensitivity and scenario analysis.

flashcards.back: Incremental, after-tax cash flows: initial outlay, operating inflows, depreciation tax shield, working-capital changes, salvage. Exclude sunk costs and unchanged allocated overhead.

$100,000 cost; $30,000/yr × 5 yrs at 10% (annuity factor 3.7908) = $113,724 PV; NPV = $13,724 > 0 → accept.

Discount rate where NPV = 0 (the project's return). Accept if IRR > hurdle rate. Flaws: reinvestment-at-IRR assumption, possible multiple IRRs, conflicts with NPV on mutually exclusive projects (NPV governs).

PV of inflows ÷ initial investment. PI > 1 → positive NPV → accept. Best for ranking projects under capital rationing (value per dollar invested).
Average accounting income ÷ investment. Weakest method — uses accrual income and ignores the time value of money.
For independent projects they agree. For mutually exclusive projects differing in scale/timing they can conflict — NPV governs.

weeks.title: BAR U3·W3 — Technical Reporting: Lessor Leases, R&D & Software Costs (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the harder accounting BAR owns

BAR's technical-reporting area takes selected topics deeper than the FAR core. This week covers the lessor side of leasing (FAR Unit 1 built the lessee side), the research and development rules that expense innovation, and the nuanced software-cost capitalization rules that split internal-use from for-sale software. These are the judgment-heavy areas — when to capitalize, when to expense — that a discipline-level CPA must apply, and where MBG's investment in a custom job-cost system gets its accounting.

Lessor lease classification

Under ASC 842, a lessor classifies each lease as sales-type, direct financing, or operating. A lease is a sales-type lease if it meets any of the same criteria that make a lessee's lease a finance lease — transfer of ownership, a reasonably certain purchase option, a lease term for the major part of the asset's life, the present value of payments equals substantially all of fair value, or a specialized asset with no alternative use. If none are met but the lessor still recovers its investment plus a return through payments and a third-party residual guarantee, it is direct financing; otherwise it is an operating lease.

Sales-type and direct-financing leases

In a sales-type lease, the lessor effectively sells the asset: at commencement it derecognizes the asset, records a net investment in the lease (the present value of payments plus any residual), and recognizes selling profit immediately (the difference between the fair value and carrying amount) — plus interest income over the term. A direct-financing lease defers any selling profit into the net investment and recognizes it as interest income over time. Both put a receivable, not the asset, on the lessor's books — the financing view of the arrangement.

Operating leases (lessor) and the symmetry

In an operating lease, the lessor keeps the asset on its books, continues to depreciate it, and recognizes lease income on a straight-line basis over the term. There is an important asymmetry to remember: lessor and lessee classifications are tested separately and need not match in label, though they use related criteria. For a contractor that both leases equipment to others and leases its own, understanding both sides prevents the common error of assuming the two parties mirror each other's accounting.

Research and development costs

Research and development (ASC 730) costs are expensed as incurred — both the research (planned search for new knowledge) and the development (translating findings into a plan or design) phases. The rationale is the high uncertainty that R&D will produce future benefit. The key exception: materials, equipment, or facilities with an alternative future use are capitalized and depreciated (the depreciation on R&D equipment is itself an R&D expense). Costs incurred for others under a contract are not the company's R&D expense — they are costs of providing a service.

Internal-use software

Software developed for the company's own use (ASC 350-40) follows a three-stage model. Costs in the preliminary project stage (conceptual evaluation, alternatives) are expensed. Costs in the application development stage (coding, configuration, testing) are capitalized. Costs in the post-implementation/operation stage (training, maintenance) are expensed. The capitalized asset is then amortized over its useful life. So MBG's spending to build a custom job-cost system is expensed during planning, capitalized during build, and expensed again once it goes live — the stage, not the type of cost, drives the treatment.

Software to be sold or marketed

Software developed to be sold, leased, or marketed (ASC 985-20) turns on technological feasibility. Costs incurred before technological feasibility (the detailed program design or a working model) are expensed as R&D. Costs incurred after technological feasibility, until the product is available for general release, are capitalized. Capitalized software costs are then amortized at the greater of the straight-line amount or the ratio of current revenue to total expected revenue. The technological-feasibility threshold is the dividing line the exam tests.

Putting the capitalization rules together

The unifying theme is when future benefit becomes probable enough to capitalize. Pure R&D is too uncertain — expense it. Internal-use software crosses the line at the application-development stage; for-sale software crosses it at technological feasibility. Misapplying these triggers either overstates assets (capitalizing too early) or understates them (expensing capitalizable costs), distorting both the balance sheet and the expense pattern. Recognizing which framework applies — and where its trigger falls — is the core skill this week builds.

Lease remeasurement and other lessor topics

Several refinements complete lessor accounting. A lessor remeasures the net investment when a lease is modified in a way that is not a separate contract, and tests the net investment (and any unguaranteed residual) for impairment using the credit-loss model. Initial direct costs are deferred and recognized over the lease term for direct-financing and operating leases, but expensed at commencement for a sales-type lease that recognizes selling profit. Sale-leaseback transactions require determining whether a real sale occurred under ASC 606 before applying lease accounting. These nuances show that the lessor model, like the lessee model, is built on the same control and revenue concepts running through GAAP.

Cloud computing and other intangibles

The software rules extend to modern arrangements. Costs to implement a cloud-computing (hosting) arrangement that is a service are capitalized using the same model as internal-use software (capitalize the application-development-stage implementation costs) and amortized over the term of the service contract. Start-up and organization costs, by contrast, are expensed as incurred, and most internally generated intangibles (brands and customer lists developed internally) are not capitalized at all. Knowing which costs attach to an asset and which are period expenses is the same capitalize-versus-expense judgment that governs R&D and software.

Disclosure and the leveraged lease

Lease accounting carries robust disclosure requirements: lessors disclose the components of the net investment, lease income by type, and a maturity analysis of lease receivables. A leveraged lease grandfathered under prior guidance continues its specialized accounting until it ends. The disclosures give users insight into the timing and risk of the lessor's lease cash flows — the same transparency objective that runs through every reporting standard in this unit.

The lessee side, in depth

Although this week centers on the lessor, the lessee accounting from FAR Unit 1 is worth reinforcing because the two interlock. A lessee classifies a lease as finance or operating using the same five criteria, but in both cases records a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability at the present value of the lease payments. The difference is the expense pattern: a finance lease produces front-loaded expense (separate interest on the liability plus straight-line amortization of the ROU asset), while an operating lease produces a single straight-line lease expense. Short-term leases of twelve months or less may be exempted from capitalization. Understanding that the lessee almost always capitalizes — while the lessor may show a receivable, a retained asset, or operating income — prevents the common error of assuming the two sides mirror one another.

A worked sales-type lease

Numbers make the lessor entries concrete. Suppose MBG, acting as a dealer-lessor, leases equipment with a carrying amount of $80,000 and a fair value of $100,000 under a lease whose payments have a present value of $100,000, meeting a sales-type criterion. At commencement the lessor derecognizes the $80,000 asset, records a net investment in the lease of $100,000, and recognizes selling profit of $20,000 (the $100,000 fair value minus the $80,000 cost) — exactly as it would on an outright sale. Over the term, each payment is split between interest income (the implicit rate applied to the declining net investment) and a reduction of the net investment. This lease is sales-type precisely because the present value of the payments equals the asset's fair value — one of the classification criteria. A direct-financing lease is different by construction: no sales-type criterion is met (the substantially-all-fair-value threshold is reached only by counting a third-party residual guarantee), and any dealer profit is deferred into the net investment and released as interest income rather than recognized at commencement.

Amortizing and testing capitalized software

Capitalizing software is only the start; the asset must then be amortized and tested. Internal-use software is amortized on a straight-line basis over its estimated useful life, beginning when the software is ready for its intended use. For-sale software uses the greater of the straight-line amount or the revenue-based ratio, and its unamortized cost is compared each period to net realizable value, writing the asset down if NRV is lower. Both kinds of capitalized software are also subject to impairment testing when events suggest the carrying amount may not be recoverable — the same long-lived-asset discipline from FAR Unit 4. So the capitalize-versus-expense decision does not end the analysis; the capitalized asset carries an ongoing amortization and impairment obligation that keeps it from lingering on the balance sheet beyond its real value.

CMA bridge

When MBG invests in equipment leasing or builds its own software, BAR decides the accounting the CMA program then reports. The lessor rules determine whether a leased asset becomes a receivable; the software rules determine how much of a system build sits on the balance sheet — both directly affecting the asset base and the margins the CFO analyzes.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify lessor leases: sales-type (finance criteria met → derecognize asset, net investment, immediate selling profit) vs direct financing (defer profit into interest income) vs operating (keep/depreciate asset, straight-line income).
  2. Expense R&D as incurred (ASC 730); capitalize only materials/equipment with alternative future use.
  3. Internal-use software (350-40): expense preliminary + post-implementation; capitalize application-development stage.
  4. For-sale software (985-20): expense before technological feasibility, capitalize after until release; amortize at the greater of straight-line or revenue ratio.

Recap: a lessor records a sales-type lease as a sale (derecognize the asset, book a net investment, recognize selling profit and interest), a direct-financing lease by deferring profit into interest income, and an operating lease by keeping and depreciating the asset with straight-line income; R&D is expensed as incurred except for assets with alternative future use; internal-use software capitalizes only the application-development stage; and for-sale software capitalizes costs after technological feasibility until release, amortized at the greater of straight-line or the revenue ratio.

flashcards.back: Sales-type (any finance-lease criterion met), direct financing (recovers investment + return via payments and third-party residual guarantee), or operating (neither).
Derecognize the asset; record net investment in the lease (PV of payments + residual); recognize selling profit immediately + interest income over the term.
Defer any selling profit into the net investment and recognize it as interest income over time. Receivable on the books, not the asset.
Keep and depreciate the asset; recognize lease income straight-line. Lessor and lessee classifications are tested separately and need not match.
Expense both research and development as incurred. Exception: materials/equipment/facilities with alternative future use are capitalized and depreciated.
Preliminary project stage: expense. Application development stage: capitalize. Post-implementation/operation: expense. Then amortize the capitalized cost.
Expense costs before technological feasibility (as R&D); capitalize after feasibility until available for release; amortize at the GREATER of straight-line or revenue ratio.
Capitalize when future benefit is probable enough: internal-use at the application-development stage; for-sale at technological feasibility; pure R&D never (too uncertain).

choices: Derecognizes the asset and recognizes selling profit
Keeps the asset and depreciates it
questions.explain: A sales-type lease is treated as a sale: derecognize the asset, record a net investment, and recognize selling profit plus interest income.

questions.q: A lessor's operating lease income is recognized:
questions.explain: In an operating lease the lessor keeps the asset and recognizes lease income on a straight-line basis.

questions.q: Research and development costs under ASC 730 are generally:
questions.explain: R&D is expensed as incurred; only materials/equipment with alternative future use are capitalized.

questions.q: For internal-use software, costs in the application development stage are:
questions.explain: ASC 350-40 capitalizes application-development-stage costs; preliminary and post-implementation costs are expensed.

questions.q: For software to be sold, capitalization begins when:
questions.explain: ASC 985-20 expenses costs until technological feasibility, then capitalizes until the product is available for release.

questions.explain: Assets with alternative future use are capitalized; their depreciation is charged as R&D expense.

choices: The greater of straight-line or the revenue ratio
questions.explain: Amortization is the greater of the straight-line amount or the current-to-total expected revenue ratio.

weeks.title: BAR U3·W4 — Non-Financial Measures, Sustainability Reporting & Employee Benefit Plans (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — beyond the financial statements

Financial results are lagging indicators — they report what already happened. To manage and report performance fully, BAR tests non-financial measures, the balanced scorecard that frames them, the fast-growing field of sustainability (ESG) reporting, and the specialized accounting for employee benefit plans. For Meridian Building Group, leading indicators like safety incidents and schedule adherence predict the financial results long before they appear — and lenders increasingly ask about sustainability too.

Non-financial performance measures

Non-financial measures capture drivers that financial statements miss: customer satisfaction, on-time delivery, defect rates, employee turnover, safety records. They are valuable because they are often leading indicators — a rising defect rate today forecasts warranty cost and lost customers tomorrow. Good key performance indicators (KPIs) are specific, measurable, and tied to strategy. The limitation is that non-financial data can be harder to verify and easier to manipulate, so it complements rather than replaces financial measurement.

The balanced scorecard

The balanced scorecard organizes performance across four perspectives, linking strategy to measures: financial (how do we look to shareholders — profit, ROI), customer (how do customers see us — satisfaction, retention), internal business process (what must we excel at — cycle time, quality, safety), and learning and growth (how can we keep improving — training, employee skills, innovation). The power of the scorecard is the cause-and-effect linkage: investing in learning improves processes, which improves customer outcomes, which ultimately drives financial results — making strategy measurable and balanced across leading and lagging indicators.

Sustainability and ESG reporting

Sustainability (ESG) reporting communicates an entity's environmental, social, and governance performance to investors and stakeholders. Demand has driven formal frameworks: the GRI standards (broad stakeholder impact), the investor-focused standards now consolidated under the ISSB (IFRS S1 general and S2 climate disclosures, incorporating the former SASB and TCFD work), and various jurisdictional rules. A central concept is materiality — disclosing the ESG matters that affect the business or that the business affects. Reporting is moving from voluntary narrative toward standardized, comparable disclosure.

Assurance on sustainability information

As ESG disclosures gain weight, users want assurance on them. CPAs provide this under the attestation standards from AUD Unit 3 — an examination (reasonable assurance) or, more commonly today, a review (limited assurance) over greenhouse-gas metrics or other sustainability data against suitable criteria (a chosen framework). The challenges mirror auditing estimates: data systems for non-financial metrics are less mature, and the criteria are still evolving. This is a major growth area for the profession, and BAR tests the accountant's role in it.

Employee benefit plans — the reporting entity

An employee benefit plan is itself a reporting entity with its own financial statements (distinct from the sponsoring employer's pension accounting in FAR Unit 4). A defined benefit pension plan (ASC 960) reports a statement of net assets available for benefits, a statement of changes in those net assets, and — critically — the actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits and the changes in it. Plan investments are reported at fair value. These statements show whether the plan's assets are sufficient to meet its promised benefits.

Defined contribution and health/welfare plans

Other plan types follow parallel models. A defined contribution plan (ASC 962) — such as a 401(k) — reports net assets available for benefits and the changes, with each participant's account reflecting contributions plus investment results; there is no actuarial benefit obligation because the benefit is simply the account balance. A health and welfare plan (ASC 965) reports net assets and, for defined-benefit-type promises, the benefit obligations. Across all three, the plan's financial statements are audited under the employee-benefit-plan audit rules — a specialized engagement many firms perform.

Tying performance reporting together

The thread of this week is that reporting extends beyond GAAP financials. Non-financial KPIs and the balanced scorecard give a forward-looking, strategy-linked view; sustainability reporting communicates ESG performance to a widening audience with growing assurance demand; and benefit-plan statements report on entities whose stakeholders are employees. A discipline-level CPA must move fluidly among these reporting frameworks — knowing which measures matter, which standards apply, and what level of assurance attaches — because stakeholders now judge an entity on far more than its net income.

Designing and using KPIs

Effective performance measurement requires well-designed KPIs. A good measure is aligned with a strategic objective, is within the manager's control (the controllability principle), balances short and long term, and resists gaming — a single metric pushed in isolation (cut costs) can harm others (quality, safety). Benchmarking against internal history, competitors, or industry standards turns a raw number into a judgment. The balanced scorecard guards against the classic trap of over-weighting financial measures by forcing attention to the customer, process, and learning drivers that produce them — a portfolio of measures rather than a single score.

Sustainability assurance and the CPA's evolving role

As ESG disclosure standardizes, the accountant's role widens from preparation to controls and assurance. Entities must build data systems and internal controls over non-financial metrics — emissions, workforce data — to the same reliability standard as financial data, an area where many lack maturity. Regulators increasingly mandate disclosure (jurisdictional climate rules), moving ESG from voluntary to required and raising the stakes on accuracy. For the CPA, this is the convergence of the reporting frameworks in this unit with the attestation skills from AUD — positioning the profession to assure the non-financial information that now sits alongside the financial statements in stakeholders' decisions.

Integrated reporting

A further step is integrated reporting, which combines financial and non-financial information into a single narrative of how an organization creates value over time across multiple capitals — financial, human, intellectual, social, and natural. Rather than treating sustainability as a separate report, integrated reporting connects strategy, governance, performance, and prospects in one coherent picture. It reflects the broader shift this unit traces: stakeholders want to understand the whole business, not just its net income, and the accountant increasingly assembles and assures that fuller story.

CMA bridge

The CMA program built MBG's KPI dashboards and balanced scorecard; BAR adds the external-reporting frameworks — ESG disclosure and benefit-plan statements — that surround them. As lenders and owners ask about safety records and sustainability alongside margins, the CFO who can report and obtain assurance on non-financial measures meets a real and growing demand.

Practice and recap

  1. Use non-financial KPIs as leading indicators tied to strategy; recognize they complement (not replace) financial measures.
  2. Apply the balanced scorecard's four perspectives — financial, customer, internal process, learning & growth — linked by cause and effect.
  3. Identify ESG frameworks (GRI; ISSB IFRS S1/S2 incorporating SASB/TCFD) and the materiality concept; provide assurance via SSAE examination or review.
  4. Report employee benefit plans: defined benefit (ASC 960 — net assets + actuarial PV of accumulated benefits), defined contribution (962 — account balances), health/welfare (965).

Recap: non-financial measures are leading, strategy-linked indicators framed by the balanced scorecard's four perspectives (financial, customer, internal process, learning & growth) connected through cause and effect; sustainability reporting communicates ESG performance under frameworks such as GRI and the ISSB's IFRS S1/S2 (absorbing SASB and TCFD), with CPAs providing examination or review assurance; and employee benefit plans are separate reporting entities — defined benefit plans (ASC 960) report net assets available for benefits and the actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits, defined contribution plans (962) report account balances, and health/welfare plans follow ASC 965.

flashcards.back: Leading indicators (customer satisfaction, defect rate, on-time delivery, safety, turnover) tied to strategy; complement—not replace—financial measures; harder to verify.
Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, and Learning & Growth — linked by cause and effect (learning → process → customer → financial).
GRI (broad stakeholder impact); ISSB IFRS S1 (general) and S2 (climate), incorporating the former SASB and TCFD. Driven by materiality and a push for comparability.
CPAs provide examination (reasonable) or, more often, review (limited) assurance under SSAE against suitable criteria — a growth area; data systems less mature.
Statement of net assets available for benefits, statement of changes, and the actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits + changes. Investments at fair value.
Reports net assets available for benefits (participant account balances); NO actuarial benefit obligation — benefit equals the account balance.
Reports net assets available for benefits and, for defined-benefit-type promises, the benefit obligations.
An employee benefit plan has its own audited financial statements, distinct from the sponsoring employer's pension accounting (FAR Unit 4).

units.title: ISC Unit 1 — IT Governance, General & Application Controls, Systems Development & Data Management

weeks.title: ISC U1·W1 — IT Governance, COBIT & the IT Environment (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — who controls the systems

The Information Systems and Controls (ISC) discipline tests how an organization governs, secures, and controls the technology that produces its financial and operational data. Meridian Building Group runs its job-cost, payroll, and billing on integrated systems; if those systems are poorly governed, every number they produce is suspect. This week establishes the IT governance frameworks, the structure of the IT function, and the control environment that the rest of the discipline builds on — the systems analogue to the conceptual framework that opens FAR.

IT governance versus IT management

IT governance is the board-and-executive responsibility to ensure technology aligns with business strategy, delivers value, and manages risk — distinct from IT management, which runs day-to-day operations. Governance asks "are we doing the right things, and are risks acceptable?"; management asks "are we doing them well?" Effective governance sets the direction (strategy, risk appetite, investment priorities) and monitors outcomes, while delegating execution. The separation mirrors COSO's governance-and-culture component and is the foundation for everything from access control to SOC reporting.

The COBIT framework

COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies) is the leading framework for governing and managing enterprise IT. It distinguishes governance objectives (evaluate, direct, monitor) from management objectives (plan, build, run, monitor), and organizes IT activities into domains with measurable control objectives. COBIT's principles stress that the governance system should be tailored to the enterprise, cover it end-to-end, and be driven by stakeholder needs. It is the framework most directly tied to the ISC discipline's governance content, complementing COSO (enterprise risk/internal control) and operational frameworks like ITIL.

The control environment for IT

IT controls rest on a sound control environment: the tone set by governance, an organizational structure with clear authority and responsibility, competent personnel, and accountability. A central principle is segregation of incompatible IT duties — separating systems development from computer operations, and both from security administration, so that no one can write code, move it to production, and run it without independent checks. Where the organization is too small to fully separate duties, compensating controls (management review of logs and exception reports) substitute. This environment makes the specific general and application controls trustworthy.

Organizing the IT function

A typical IT function separates roles to enforce segregation. Systems analysts and application programmers design and build software; computer operators run production jobs; database administrators (DBAs) control the data structures and access; network and security administrators manage connectivity and protections; and a help desk supports users. The key incompatibility to avoid is letting programmers have access to production data and programs — a programmer who can both write and deploy code can introduce unauthorized changes. Governance assigns these roles and reviews that the separations hold.

IT risk and the frameworks that address it

IT risk spans availability, integrity, confidentiality, and compliance — a system outage, corrupted data, a breach, or a regulatory failure each threatens the business. Several frameworks address it: COBIT (governance/management of IT), COSO (enterprise risk management and internal control), ITIL (IT service management), the NIST cybersecurity framework, and ISO/IEC 27001 (information-security management). A mature organization maps its controls to one or more frameworks so that risks are identified, owned, and monitored rather than addressed ad hoc.

Governance bodies and IT strategy

Governance is exercised through structures: the board (or audit committee) oversees IT risk, often informed by an IT steering committee that prioritizes investments and aligns projects with strategy. An IT strategic plan translates business goals into a technology roadmap, and policies (acceptable use, security, change management) set the rules of the road. These structures ensure that major decisions — adopting a new ERP, moving to the cloud, investing in analytics — are made deliberately, with risk and value weighed, rather than left to technical staff alone.

Governing emerging technology

New technologies stretch governance. Cloud computing shifts infrastructure to third parties, making vendor and SOC-report oversight (covered later in this discipline) essential. Artificial intelligence and automation raise questions of model risk, bias, and explainability. Robotic process automation (RPA) and APIs change how data flows between systems. The governance response is the same in principle: define ownership, assess risk, set controls and monitoring, and keep the technology aligned with strategy and risk appetite — the discipline's recurring theme that control follows from governance.

Comparing the major frameworks

Because the frameworks overlap, knowing each one's focus prevents confusion. COBIT governs and manages enterprise IT end-to-end. COSO's frameworks address internal control and enterprise risk management broadly, with IT as one element. ITIL is operational — it structures IT service management (incident, problem, and change processes). The NIST Cybersecurity Framework organizes security around identify, protect, detect, respond, recover. ISO/IEC 27001 certifies an information-security management system. A useful mental model: COBIT and COSO sit at the governance level, ITIL at the service level, and NIST/ISO at the security level — and a mature organization draws on several at once rather than treating them as competitors.

Outsourcing and third-party governance

Governance does not stop at the organization's walls. When MBG outsources hosting, payroll, or an application to a service organization, it remains accountable for the controls over its data even though it does not operate them. Governance therefore extends to vendor management: due diligence before engagement, contractual control requirements and service-level agreements, and ongoing monitoring — including obtaining and reading the provider's SOC reports (the focus of the next ISC unit). The principle is that responsibility cannot be outsourced: the organization must govern the risk wherever its data lives, including in the cloud and across its supply chain.

Monitoring and continuous improvement

Governance is not a one-time design — it requires monitoring. The board and steering committee track IT performance against objectives using metrics (system availability, project delivery, incident counts, audit findings), review the results of internal and external assessments, and direct remediation of deficiencies. Frameworks like COBIT build in a monitor domain precisely so that the governance system evaluates and improves itself over time. This continuous loop — direct, do, monitor, correct — is what keeps IT aligned with the business as both the technology and the strategy change.

CMA bridge

The CMA program treated MBG's systems as the source of its management data; ISC governs whether those systems can be trusted. The segregation of development from operations is exactly what lets a CFO rely on a system-generated WIP or payroll number — governance is what turns raw system output into reliable information.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish IT governance (board/executive: align, value, risk — evaluate/direct/monitor) from IT management (run operations).
  2. Apply COBIT (governance vs management objectives; tailored, end-to-end, stakeholder-driven) alongside COSO, ITIL, NIST, and ISO 27001.
  3. Enforce the control environment: segregate systems development, operations, and security; keep programmers out of production; use compensating controls when small.
  4. Govern through structures (board/audit committee, IT steering committee, strategic plan, policies) — including for cloud, AI, and RPA.

Recap: IT governance is the board-and-executive duty to align technology with strategy, deliver value, and manage risk (evaluate/direct/monitor), distinct from day-to-day IT management; COBIT is the leading IT-governance framework, complemented by COSO, ITIL, NIST, and ISO 27001; a sound control environment segregates systems development, operations, and security (keeping programmers out of production) with compensating controls when duties cannot be split; and governance is exercised through the board, an IT steering committee, a strategic plan, and policies that extend to emerging technology like cloud, AI, and RPA.

flashcards.back: Governance (board/executive): align IT with strategy, deliver value, manage risk — evaluate, direct, monitor. Management: plan, build, run day-to-day operations.

Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies — leading framework for governing/managing enterprise IT; separates governance (EDM) from management objectives; tailored, end-to-end, stakeholder-driven.
Separate systems development from computer operations from security administration. Critical: keep programmers OUT of production data/programs.
COBIT (govern/manage IT), COSO (ERM/internal control), ITIL (service management), NIST (cybersecurity), ISO/IEC 27001 (information security management).
Controls the database structure and access — an incompatible duty to combine with application programming or operations.
Governance body that prioritizes IT investments and aligns projects with business strategy; reports up to the board/audit committee.
When duties cannot be fully segregated, management review of system logs and exception reports substitutes for separation.
Availability, integrity, confidentiality, and compliance — addressed by mapping controls to a recognized framework with clear ownership and monitoring.

choices: Aligning IT with strategy and managing risk (evaluate/direct/monitor)
questions.explain: Governance is the board/executive responsibility to align IT with strategy, deliver value, and manage risk; management runs operations.

questions.q: COBIT is best described as a framework for:
questions.explain: COBIT governs and manages enterprise IT, separating governance from management objectives.

questions.q: The most critical IT segregation of duties keeps:
choices: Programmers out of production data and programs
questions.explain: A programmer with production access could deploy unauthorized code, so development and operations must be separated.

questions.q: Which framework focuses specifically on information-security management?
questions.explain: ISO/IEC 27001 is the information-security management standard; ITIL is service management; COBIT governs IT broadly.

questions.q: When a small company cannot fully segregate IT duties, it should rely on:
choices: Compensating controls such as management review of logs
questions.explain: Compensating controls (review of logs/exception reports) substitute when duties cannot be separated.

questions.q: An IT steering committee primarily:
choices: Prioritizes IT investments and aligns projects with strategy
questions.explain: The steering committee is a governance body aligning IT investment with business strategy.

weeks.title: ISC U1·W2 — IT General Controls & Application Controls in Depth (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the two layers of IT control

Within the governed IT environment from Week 1 sit two layers of control: IT general controls (ITGCs) that govern the whole environment, and application controls that operate inside a specific process. AUD Unit 3 introduced these from the auditor's chair; ISC examines them from the systems-and-controls designer's chair — deeper, with the access, change, and processing mechanics that make Meridian Building Group's data complete, accurate, and authorized. This week is the technical core of the discipline.

The four ITGC domains

ITGCs fall into four domains. Access to programs and data (logical and physical security) restricts who can see and change what. Program change management controls how software is modified, tested, and approved before production. Program development governs acquiring and implementing new systems. Computer operations covers job scheduling, backup, and recovery. These pervasive controls are the foundation: if any is weak, the application controls that depend on it cannot be relied upon — a programmer with uncontrolled production access can defeat any automated edit check.

Access control — authentication

Access control begins with authentication — proving identity through something you know (a password), have (a token or phone), or are (a biometric). Combining factors yields multi-factor authentication (MFA), far stronger than a password alone. Strong authentication policies (password complexity, rotation, lockout after failed attempts) and protected credential storage are the first line of defense. Authentication answers "who are you?" before the system decides what you may do.

Access control — authorization and accountability

After authentication comes authorization — what the authenticated user may do — governed by the principle of least privilege (grant only the access needed for the role) and implemented through role-based access control (RBAC). Privileged (administrator) access is tightly restricted and monitored. Finally, accountability requires logging of who did what and when, with logs reviewed for anomalies. The trio — authentication, authorization, accountability — is the backbone of logical security, and weaknesses here are the most common and serious IT control deficiencies.

Physical access and environmental controls

Logical controls mean little if someone can walk to a server. Physical access controls — badge readers, locked data centers, visitor logs, cameras — protect the hardware, while environmental controls (fire suppression, climate control, uninterruptible power) protect against non-malicious threats. For cloud-hosted systems these controls shift to the provider and are evidenced through its SOC reports. Physical and environmental controls complete the access picture: the data must be safe from both unauthorized users and physical harm.

Change management and program development

Change management ensures software changes are authorized, tested, approved, and documented before reaching production, with development, test, and production environments kept separate and migration performed by someone other than the developer. Emergency changes follow an expedited but still-controlled path with after-the-fact review. Program development applies the same discipline to new systems through the systems development life cycle (next week). Together they prevent unauthorized or untested code — the change that silently breaks a control or corrupts data — from entering live systems.

Application controls by stage

Application controls ensure a specific process produces complete, accurate, authorized results, classified by stage. Input controls validate data at entry — edit checks, field/format checks, check digits, validity and limit/reasonableness tests, and self-checking of key fields. Processing controls ensure correct handling — batch totals, hash totals, run-to-run reconciliations, and sequence checks. Output controls govern the results — distribution restrictions, output reconciliation, and error reporting. A well-designed application catches a bad transaction at input rather than discovering it in the financial statements.

Classifying controls

Controls are also classified by function and nature. By function: preventive (stop an error before it happens — an edit check), detective (find an error that occurred — a reconciliation), and corrective (fix it — a backup restore). By nature: manual versus automated. The strongest control environments favor preventive, automated controls (consistent and hard to bypass) backed by detective controls that catch what slips through. Mapping each control to its type helps a designer or auditor see whether a process is genuinely protected or merely appears to be.

The CIA triad

Information security is organized around the CIA triad — confidentiality (only authorized parties can read the data), integrity (the data is accurate and unaltered), and availability (the data and systems are accessible when needed). Every control maps to one or more of these objectives: encryption protects confidentiality, hash totals and input edits protect integrity, and backups and redundancy protect availability. The triad gives a designer a checklist — a control that strengthens confidentiality may do nothing for availability — and it frames the security, confidentiality, and privacy content the ISC discipline tests in depth.

Network and boundary controls

Beyond user access, controls protect the perimeter and the data in transit. Firewalls filter traffic between networks; intrusion detection/prevention systems watch for and block attacks; network segmentation and a demilitarized zone (DMZ) isolate public-facing systems from internal ones; and encryption protects data both in transit (TLS) and at rest. Endpoint protections (anti-malware, device management) defend the many access points a modern organization exposes. These boundary controls are general controls in the broadest sense — they protect the environment within which every application and its data operate.

Backup, recovery, and operations controls

The fourth ITGC domain — computer operations — keeps systems running and recoverable. Backups are taken on a defined schedule, stored offsite (or in a separate cloud region), and periodically tested by restoring them, because an untested backup is only a hope. Job scheduling and monitoring ensure batch processes run completely and in order, and incident management logs and resolves failures. A documented disaster-recovery plan defines recovery-time and recovery-point objectives, and capacity monitoring keeps systems available before demand outstrips resources. These operations controls protect availability and integrity: when a server fails or data is corrupted, a tested backup and a recovery procedure are what stand between a brief disruption and a catastrophe — the corrective controls behind the preventive and detective ones.

CMA bridge

When MBG's system rejects a job-cost entry with an invalid cost code, that is an input control doing its job; when month-end batch totals reconcile, that is a processing control. The CFO's confidence in system-generated reports rests on exactly these general and application controls — the difference between data that is trustworthy and data that merely exists.

Practice and recap

  1. Know the four ITGC domains: access to programs/data, change management, program development, computer operations.
  2. Apply access control: authentication (know/have/are, MFA), authorization (least privilege, RBAC), accountability (logging), plus physical/environmental controls.
  3. Enforce change management: authorize/test/approve, separate dev/test/production, migrate via someone other than the developer.
  4. Classify application controls by stage (input edit/validity/limit checks; processing batch/hash totals/reconciliations; output controls) and by function (preventive/detective/corrective; manual/automated).

Recap: ITGCs span access, change management, development, and operations and make application controls reliable; access control rests on authentication (something you know/have/are, MFA), authorization (least privilege, RBAC), and accountability (logging), backed by physical and environmental controls; change management authorizes, tests, approves, and segregates environments so untested code never reaches production; and application controls operate by stage (input edit/check-digit/limit tests, processing batch/hash totals and reconciliations, output controls) and by function (preventive, detective, corrective), with automated preventive controls the strongest.

flashcards.back: Access to programs and data, program change management, program development, and computer operations. Weak ITGCs undermine the application controls that rely on them.
Something you KNOW (password), HAVE (token/phone), or ARE (biometric). Combining them = multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Authorization grants only the access a role needs (least privilege), implemented via role-based access control; privileged access is restricted and monitored.
Who are you? (authenticate) → what may you do? (authorize) → what did you do? (accountability via logging). The backbone of logical security.
Authorize, test, approve, and document changes; keep dev/test/production separate; migrate to production via someone other than the developer.
Input (edit/format/check-digit/validity/limit checks), Processing (batch/hash totals, reconciliations, sequence checks), Output (distribution, reconciliation, error reports).
Preventive (stop before — edit check), Detective (find after — reconciliation), Corrective (fix — backup restore). Plus manual vs automated.
Preventive + automated controls (consistent, hard to bypass), backed by detective controls to catch what slips through.

questions.q: A check digit appended to an account number is a(n):
questions.explain: Check digits validate data at entry — an input application control.

questions.q: Multi-factor authentication combines:
choices: Two or more of: something you know, have, or are
questions.explain: MFA combines factors of different types (know/have/are), far stronger than a single password.

questions.q: The principle of least privilege means:
choices: Granting only the access a role requires
questions.explain: Least privilege limits each user to the minimum access needed for their role.

questions.q: Good change management requires that production migration be performed by:
choices: Someone other than the developer who wrote the change
questions.explain: Separating development from production migration prevents unauthorized or untested code from going live.

questions.q: Batch totals reconciled before and after processing are a(n):
questions.explain: Batch and hash totals reconciled across processing are processing controls.

questions.q: A reconciliation that detects an error after it has occurred is a:
questions.explain: Detective controls find errors that occurred; preventive controls stop them beforehand.

questions.q: If IT general controls over access are weak, the auditor or designer should:
choices: Not rely on automated application controls without further work
questions.explain: Application controls depend on ITGCs; weak access control undermines reliance on automated controls.

weeks.title: ISC U1·W3 — Systems Development & Change Management (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — building and changing systems safely

New systems and changes to existing ones are where risk concentrates: a poorly built ERP or an untested change can corrupt data, break controls, or halt operations. The systems development life cycle (SDLC) and disciplined change management govern how Meridian Building Group acquires, builds, tests, and modifies the systems that run its job-cost and billing. This week covers the phases, the testing and conversion strategies, the project governance, and the controls that keep development from becoming the weakest link.

The systems development life cycle

The SDLC structures development into phases: planning (define the need, feasibility, and business case), analysis (gather and document requirements), design (specify the system and controls), development (build or configure), testing, implementation (deploy and convert), and maintenance. Crucially, controls and security must be designed in from the analysis and design phases — bolting them on later is costly and weaker. Each phase produces documentation and approvals, creating an auditable trail of decisions.

Requirements and design

The early phases determine success. Analysis captures what the business needs — functional requirements, data, reports, and the controls the system must enforce — with strong user involvement so the system fits the work. Design translates requirements into specifications: the data model, processes, interfaces, and the input/processing/output controls from Week 2. A choice arises between building custom software, buying a packaged solution, or adopting cloud/SaaS — each with different control and vendor-oversight implications. Getting requirements right is the cheapest place to prevent defects.

Testing

Disciplined testing validates the system before it goes live, in layers: unit testing (individual components), integration testing (components working together), system testing (the whole system against requirements), and user acceptance testing (UAT) — where business users confirm the system meets their needs before approval. Testing uses test data in a non-production environment, never live data without safeguards. Inadequate testing is a leading cause of failed implementations, so the test plan and its sign-offs are key controls in the SDLC.

Implementation and conversion strategies

Going live requires choosing a conversion approach, each trading risk against cost. Parallel conversion runs the old and new systems simultaneously until the new one is proven — safest but most expensive. Pilot conversion deploys to one location or unit first. Phased conversion rolls out in stages by module or function. Direct ("big-bang") cutover switches entirely at once — cheapest but riskiest, since there is no fallback if the new system fails. The choice depends on the system's criticality and the organization's risk tolerance.

Data conversion and migration

Moving data from the old system to the new — data conversion/migration — is a high-risk, often underestimated step. Data must be cleansed (duplicates, errors, inconsistent formats fixed), mapped from old fields to new, migrated, and then reconciled (record counts and control totals tied from source to target) to prove completeness and accuracy. A migration that silently drops or corrupts records carries the error into every future report. Reconciliation and a verified cutover are the controls that make conversion trustworthy.

Development methodologies and project governance

Development follows a methodology. Waterfall moves sequentially through the phases with heavy upfront documentation — predictable but inflexible. Agile develops iteratively in short cycles (sprints) with continuous user feedback — adaptive but requiring discipline to keep controls and documentation current. Either way, project governance — a sponsor, defined scope, budget and schedule tracking, risk management, and steering-committee oversight — keeps the project aligned and prevents the scope creep and cost overruns that sink IT projects. Governance is what turns a methodology into a controlled outcome.

Change management and post-implementation

Once live, the system enters maintenance, where change management (Week 2) governs every modification — authorized, tested in a separate environment, approved, documented, and migrated by someone other than the developer, with version control tracking what changed. A post-implementation review evaluates whether the system met its objectives and budget and captures lessons learned. Patch management keeps software current against vulnerabilities. These ongoing controls ensure the system stays reliable and secure long after go-live — development discipline does not end at implementation.

Documentation and system flowcharts

Throughout the SDLC, documentation is both a control and a deliverable: requirements specifications, design documents, test plans and results, user manuals, and operations runbooks. System and data-flow documentation — flowcharts, data-flow diagrams, and entity-relationship diagrams — lets analysts, users, and auditors understand how data moves and where controls sit. Strong documentation supports the experienced-auditor standard from AUD (someone with no prior connection can understand the system), enables maintenance, and reduces dependence on the original developers. A system no one but its author understands is itself a risk.

Acquiring versus building, and vendor selection

Many organizations buy rather than build. Acquiring software follows its own disciplined process: define requirements, issue a request for proposal (RFP), evaluate vendors on functionality, cost, support, and financial stability, and assess the controls — including the vendor's SOC report for a hosted solution. The contract should specify control responsibilities, data ownership, and exit terms. Whether built or bought, the same governance applies: the system must meet requirements, enforce controls, and be implemented and converted under the disciplines covered this week — the source of the software changes the procurement steps, not the control objectives.

Feasibility, the business case, and outsourced development

Before building, the planning phase establishes feasibility — technical, operational, economic (cost-benefit), and scheduling — and a business case that justifies the investment and defines success criteria; a steering-committee gate at each phase decides whether to proceed, revise, or cancel before more is spent. Skipping this is how organizations build systems no one needed. When development itself is outsourced to a vendor or offshore team, the organization retains responsibility for requirements, acceptance testing, and control design, and must manage the added risks of code quality, intellectual property, and data security in the vendor's hands. Governance over the project does not transfer with the coding work — the organization still owns the outcome and its controls.

CMA bridge

When MBG implements a new job-cost or ERP system, the conversion strategy and the data-migration reconciliation decide whether the CFO can trust the opening balances. A botched migration corrupts the very WIP and cost data the CMA program analyzes — which is why the SDLC's testing and reconciliation controls matter directly to the finance function.

Practice and recap

  1. Sequence the SDLC (planning → analysis → design → development → testing → implementation → maintenance) and design controls in from the start.
  2. Test in layers (unit, integration, system, UAT) using test data in a non-production environment.
  3. Choose a conversion strategy by risk: parallel (safest), pilot, phased, direct cutover (riskiest); reconcile data migration source-to-target.
  4. Govern projects (sponsor, scope, budget, risk) under waterfall or agile; apply change management, version control, and post-implementation review in maintenance.

Recap: the SDLC runs from planning and analysis through design, development, testing, implementation, and maintenance, with controls designed in early; testing proceeds in layers (unit, integration, system, UAT) on non-production data; conversion strategies trade risk for cost — parallel is safest, direct cutover riskiest — and data migration must be cleansed, mapped, and reconciled source-to-target; and disciplined project governance, version control, post-implementation review, and ongoing change/patch management keep the system reliable after go-live.

flashcards.back: Planning → analysis → design → development → testing → implementation → maintenance. Controls and security must be designed in from analysis/design, not bolted on later.
Unit (components) → integration (components together) → system (whole vs requirements) → user acceptance testing (UAT, business users approve). Use test data in a non-production environment.
Parallel (run both — safest, costliest) → pilot (one site) → phased (by module) → direct/big-bang cutover (switch at once — cheapest, riskiest, no fallback).
Cleanse, map old→new fields, migrate, then RECONCILE record counts/control totals source-to-target to prove completeness and accuracy.
Waterfall: sequential, heavy upfront docs, predictable but inflexible. Agile: iterative sprints with continuous user feedback, adaptive but needs discipline for controls/docs.
Custom build, packaged software, or cloud/SaaS — each with different control design and vendor-oversight (SOC report) implications.
After go-live, evaluate whether the system met objectives/budget and capture lessons learned; patch management keeps software current against vulnerabilities.
Sponsor, defined scope, budget/schedule tracking, risk management, steering-committee oversight — prevents scope creep and overruns.
