weeks.title: ISC U1·W4 — Data Management, Databases & the Data Life Cycle (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — data as the asset

Behind every system is data — and for a discipline named Information Systems and Controls, how data is structured, moved, governed, and protected is central. Meridian Building Group's job-cost, payroll, and billing data must be accurate, consistent, and available across systems. This week covers data governance, the relational database that organizes the data, the ETL and warehousing that move it for analysis, and the data life cycle that governs it from capture to destruction.

Data governance and data quality

Data governance assigns ownership and accountability for data — who defines it, who maintains it, and who may use it — and establishes a single source of truth so the same item means the same thing everywhere. Its goal is data quality, measured on dimensions including completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, timeliness, and uniqueness. Master data management (MDM) maintains consistent core entities (customers, vendors, items) across systems. Poor governance produces the duplicated, inconsistent data that corrupts every downstream report and analysis.

The relational database

Most business data lives in a relational database managed by a database management system (DBMS). Data is organized into tables (relations) of rows (records) and columns (fields). A primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key links a row to a related table, enforcing referential integrity (a job-cost record cannot reference a job that does not exist). Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. This structure lets one fact be stored once and related across the database — the efficiency and integrity that flat files lack.

Querying and integrity constraints

Data is retrieved and manipulated with SQL (Structured Query Language) — SELECT to query, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to change data — and the DBMS enforces integrity constraints: entity integrity (a non-null, unique primary key), referential integrity (valid foreign keys), and domain constraints (values within allowed ranges/types). These database-level controls complement the application input controls from Week 2: even if an application bug tries to write bad data, the database can reject a record that violates a constraint, protecting the integrity of the stored data.

Transactional versus analytical systems

Systems are tuned for different jobs. OLTP (online transaction processing) systems handle high volumes of day-to-day transactions — entering job costs, processing payroll — optimized for fast, reliable writes. OLAP (online analytical processing) systems support analysis and reporting over large historical datasets, optimized for complex reads. Running heavy analytics directly against the transactional system would slow operations, so data is typically copied to a separate analytical environment — which is where ETL and the data warehouse come in.

ETL, warehouses, and lakes

ETL — extract, transform, load — is the process of pulling data from source systems, transforming it (cleansing, standardizing, conforming), and loading it into a target for analysis. The target is often a data warehouse — an integrated, subject-oriented store of historical data — with smaller data marts serving specific functions. A data lake instead stores raw structured and unstructured data for flexible later use. The controls that matter here are the same as any data movement: reconciliation from source to target and validation that the transformation did not distort the data.

The data life cycle

Data is governed across a life cycle: capture/creation (with input controls), maintenance/storage (with access controls and backups), use (with authorization and logging), archival (retaining data no longer active but needed), and destruction/purging (securely disposing of data per retention policy). Each stage has its controls and its risks — a breach is most likely where data is stored or transmitted, and improper destruction can both leak information and violate retention requirements. Managing the whole life cycle, not just live data, is the discipline of data stewardship.

Data analytics and the controls connection

Governed, integrated data enables analytics — the descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analysis from BAR Unit 3 — and the ISC angle is that analytics are only as trustworthy as the data and the controls behind them. Continuous monitoring uses analytics over full populations to flag control exceptions in near real time. The discipline's throughline holds: well-governed data, structured in a sound database, moved through controlled ETL, and protected across its life cycle, is what makes both the financial statements and the analytics on top of them reliable.

Big data and emerging data architectures

Modern data extends beyond tidy relational tables. Big data is often described by the volume, velocity, and variety of information — including unstructured data (documents, images, sensor feeds) that relational databases handle poorly. NoSQL databases and data lakes store this flexible data, and cloud platforms provide the scale to process it. These architectures expand what analytics can do but raise the same governance questions in sharper form: where does the data come from, who owns it, is it accurate, and how is it secured? The technology changes; the data-governance obligations do not.

Data privacy and protection

Some data carries legal obligations. Personal and sensitive information is subject to privacy regulations that constrain how it is collected, used, shared, retained, and destroyed — the ISC discipline's privacy domain. Protecting it relies on the controls already covered (access control, encryption, life-cycle management) plus data classification (labeling data by sensitivity so the right controls apply) and data minimization (collecting and keeping only what is needed). A breach of regulated data brings both reputational and legal consequences, which is why privacy is governed as rigorously as financial-reporting integrity — the next unit develops it fully.

Backup, retention, and the integrity of the data store

Protecting the data store ties the data life cycle to operations. Backups and recovery procedures preserve data against loss or corruption; a retention schedule dictates how long each data type is kept to meet legal and business needs before secure destruction. Database controls — transaction logging, concurrency control so simultaneous updates do not collide, and checkpoints for recovery — preserve integrity within the DBMS itself. Emerging architectures add options: blockchain / distributed ledgers provide tamper-evident, append-only records useful where multiple parties need a shared, trusted history. Whatever the store, the objective is constant — data that is accurate, available, and protected across its whole life.

CMA bridge

The CMA program's dashboards and the auditor's data analytics both draw on MBG's database; ISC ensures that data is governed, normalized, and reconciled as it moves. The single-source-of-truth principle is exactly what lets the WIP figure in the finance report match the one in the operations system — data integrity is the foundation under every number.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply data governance + MDM for a single source of truth and data quality (completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, timeliness, uniqueness).
  2. Use the relational model: tables/rows/columns, primary and foreign keys, referential integrity, normalization, SQL, integrity constraints.
  3. Distinguish OLTP (transactions) from OLAP (analysis); move data via ETL into a warehouse/marts (or a data lake), reconciling source-to-target.
  4. Govern the data life cycle (capture → maintain → use → archive → destroy), each with its controls; enable trustworthy analytics and continuous monitoring.

Recap: data governance and master data management deliver a single source of truth and measurable data quality; the relational database structures data into keyed, normalized tables enforcing entity and referential integrity, queried with SQL; OLTP systems handle transactions while OLAP/analytics run on data moved through ETL into warehouses, marts, or lakes with source-to-target reconciliation; and the data life cycle — capture, maintain, use, archive, destroy — is governed with controls at each stage so the data underpinning the statements and the analytics stays reliable.

flashcards.back: Governance assigns data ownership/accountability for a single source of truth; master data management keeps core entities (customers, vendors, items) consistent across systems.
Completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, timeliness, uniqueness.
Primary key uniquely identifies a row (entity integrity); foreign key links to another table (referential integrity — can't reference a record that doesn't exist).
Entity integrity (unique non-null PK), referential integrity (valid FKs), domain constraints (allowed values/types). Database-level controls beyond application input controls.
OLTP = high-volume day-to-day transaction processing (fast writes). OLAP = analytical processing over large historical data (complex reads). Separate them so analytics don't slow operations.
Extract from sources → Transform (cleanse/standardize/conform) → Load into a warehouse/mart. Control: reconcile source-to-target; validate the transformation.
Data warehouse: integrated, subject-oriented historical store (with data marts for functions). Data lake: raw structured + unstructured data for flexible later use.
Capture/create → maintain/store → use → archive → destroy/purge. Each stage has its own controls and risks (breach likeliest in storage/transmission; secure disposal per retention policy).

questions.q: A foreign key in a relational database enforces:
choices: Referential integrity (a valid link to another table)
questions.explain: A foreign key links to a primary key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.

questions.q: Normalization of a relational database primarily:
choices: Reduces data redundancy and update anomalies
questions.explain: Normalization organizes tables to minimize redundancy and the anomalies it causes.

questions.q: OLTP systems are optimized for:
questions.explain: OLTP handles fast, reliable transaction writes; OLAP handles analytical reads.

questions.q: The 'T' in ETL stands for:
questions.explain: ETL = Extract, Transform, Load; the transform step cleanses and conforms data.

questions.q: A key control over any data migration or ETL load is to:
questions.explain: Source-to-target reconciliation proves the data moved completely and accurately.

questions.q: Master data management (MDM) ensures:
questions.explain: MDM maintains a consistent single version of core data entities across systems.

questions.q: Securely purging data at the end of its life cycle protects against:
questions.explain: Improper destruction can leak sensitive data and breach retention requirements.

units.title: ISC Unit 2 — SOC Engagements, Trust Services Criteria, Cybersecurity & Business Continuity

weeks.title: ISC U2·W1 — SOC Engagements: SOC 1, SOC 2 & SOC 3 (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — assurance over someone else's controls

When Meridian Building Group outsources payroll, hosting, or an application, the controls over its data sit at the service organization — yet MBG remains accountable. System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports are how a service organization gives its customers assurance over those controls, examined by an independent service auditor. AUD Unit 3 met SOC reports from the user auditor's side; this ISC unit examines them from the inside — the types of SOC engagement, the parties, and what each report does and does not provide.

Why SOC reports exist

Outsourcing transfers operation of a control to a third party but not responsibility for it. A user organization cannot practically send its auditors into every vendor, and the vendor cannot host dozens of separate customer audits. The SOC report solves this: the service organization engages one service auditor to examine its controls and issue a report its many customers (and their auditors) can rely on. It is the efficient, standardized answer to "can I trust the controls at my vendor?" — the assurance backbone of a cloud-and-outsourcing economy.

SOC 1 — controls relevant to financial reporting

A SOC 1 report addresses controls at a service organization that are relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) — for example, a payroll processor's controls over calculating and recording pay. It is performed under the attestation standards (AT-C 320), is restricted in use to the service organization, its user entities, and their auditors, and is precisely the report a user auditor obtains to rely on the service organization's controls (AUD Unit 3). SOC 1 answers the financial-statement-audit question: do the vendor's controls support the numbers that flow into my books?

SOC 2 — the trust services criteria

A SOC 2 report addresses controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy — the Trust Services Criteria (covered in depth next week) — rather than financial reporting. It serves a broader set of stakeholders (customers, regulators, business partners) who care about how a vendor protects systems and data, and like SOC 1 it is restricted in use to parties with sufficient knowledge of the system. SOC 2 is the report a company requests when evaluating a cloud provider's security posture — the dominant report in vendor-risk management.

SOC 3 — general use

A SOC 3 report covers the same Trust Services Criteria as SOC 2 but is a general-use, summary report: it provides the auditor's opinion and a short description without the detailed description of controls and tests that make SOC 2 restricted. Because it omits the sensitive detail, a SOC 3 can be freely distributed — posted on a website or shared in marketing as a seal of assurance. The trade-off is depth: SOC 3 tells the public "an independent auditor examined our security controls," while SOC 2 gives a knowledgeable user the evidence to evaluate them.

Type 1 versus Type 2

SOC 1 and SOC 2 each come in two types, the same distinction as in AUD Unit 3. A Type 1 report opines on whether the controls are suitably designed at a point in time. A Type 2 report goes further, opining on whether the controls were operating effectively over a period (typically six to twelve months) and including the auditor's tests of controls and the results. Only a Type 2 report supports a user's reliance on the operating effectiveness of the controls — a Type 1 confirms the design but not that the controls actually worked.

The parties to a SOC engagement

A SOC engagement involves defined roles. The service organization operates the system and makes a written assertion about its controls. The service auditor (an independent CPA firm) examines and reports. The user entity is the customer relying on the report, and its user auditor may use the report in the financial-statement audit. When the service organization itself relies on a subservice organization (e.g., a SaaS vendor hosted on a cloud provider), the report uses either the carve-out method (excluding the subservice org's controls, noting them) or the inclusive method (covering them) — a distinction users must understand to know what the report actually covers.

Complementary user-entity controls

A SOC report almost always assumes the user organization performs certain controls itself — the complementary user-entity controls (CUECs). For example, a payroll provider's controls work only if the user reviews and approves the payroll register and restricts who can submit changes. The report lists these CUECs, and the user's reliance on the service org's controls is conditional on performing them. A user that reads a clean SOC report but ignores the CUECs has a false sense of security — the assurance is a shared responsibility, not a transfer of it.

What a SOC report contains, and the SOC family

A SOC report follows a consistent structure worth knowing. It opens with the service auditor's opinion (unqualified/clean, or qualified by identified control exceptions), followed by management's written assertion about the system and the suitability of its controls, and a description of the system — its boundaries, infrastructure, software, people, data, and procedures. A Type 2 report then adds the service auditor's tests of controls and the results, the detailed evidence a knowledgeable user reads to judge operating effectiveness and the complementary user-entity controls. Beyond the SOC 1/2/3 trio, the AICPA also offers a SOC for Cybersecurity (an entity-wide cyber-risk-management examination, general use) and SOC for Supply Chain — the same examination model extended to new subject matter as assurance needs expand. Reading any SOC report therefore begins with checking its type (1 vs 2), its category coverage, and its opinion before placing reliance on it.

CMA bridge

When MBG moves payroll or job-cost hosting to a vendor, the CFO should obtain and read the vendor's SOC 1 Type 2 (for the financial-reporting controls) or SOC 2 (for security) — and confirm MBG performs the complementary user-entity controls. This is the practical vendor-risk discipline behind the outsourcing decisions a finance function makes constantly.

Practice and recap

  1. Match the report to the need: SOC 1 = controls over user ICFR (financial reporting); SOC 2 = Trust Services Criteria (security/availability/processing integrity/confidentiality/privacy); SOC 3 = general-use summary of SOC 2 subject matter.
  2. Distinguish Type 1 (design at a point in time) from Type 2 (operating effectiveness over a period, with tests + results); only Type 2 supports reliance on operating effectiveness.
  3. Identify the parties: service organization (assertion), service auditor, user entity, user auditor, subservice organization (carve-out vs inclusive).
  4. Recognize complementary user-entity controls (CUECs) — reliance is conditional on the user performing them.

Recap: SOC reports give a service organization's customers independent assurance over its controls — SOC 1 covers controls relevant to user financial reporting (restricted use), SOC 2 covers the Trust Services Criteria for broader stakeholders (restricted use), and SOC 3 is a general-use summary of the SOC 2 subject matter; SOC 1 and SOC 2 come as Type 1 (design at a point) or Type 2 (operating effectiveness over a period, with tests), and only Type 2 supports reliance on effectiveness; the engagement involves the service organization, service auditor, user entity and its auditor, and any subservice organization (carve-out or inclusive), with complementary user-entity controls making the assurance a shared responsibility.

flashcards.back: SOC 1: controls relevant to user ICFR (financial reporting). SOC 2: Trust Services Criteria (security/availability/processing integrity/confidentiality/privacy). SOC 3: general-use summary of SOC 2 subject matter (no detail).

flashcards.front: SOC 1/2 restricted vs SOC 3 general use
flashcards.back: SOC 1 and SOC 2 are restricted to parties with knowledge of the system; SOC 3 omits the detailed description/tests so it can be distributed freely (a public seal).
Type 1: suitability of design at a point in time. Type 2: operating effectiveness over a period (6–12 mo) + tests and results. Only Type 2 supports reliance on operating effectiveness.
Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy. Security is the baseline 'common criteria'; the others are added as relevant.
Service organization (makes the assertion), service auditor (examines/reports), user entity (relies), user auditor (may use it in the audit), subservice organization (vendor's vendor).
For a subservice organization: carve-out excludes its controls from the report (notes them); inclusive covers them. Affects what the report actually assures.
Controls the SOC report assumes the USER performs (e.g., review the payroll register). Reliance on the service org's controls is conditional on performing the CUECs.

flashcards.front: Which SOC for a cloud vendor's security?
flashcards.back: SOC 2 (Trust Services Criteria), typically Type 2, for vendor-risk evaluation; SOC 1 is for controls affecting the user's financial reporting.

questions.q: A SOC 1 report addresses controls relevant to:
choices: User entities' internal control over financial reporting
questions.explain: SOC 1 covers controls at a service organization relevant to user ICFR.

questions.q: Which report uses the Trust Services Criteria and is restricted to knowledgeable users?
questions.explain: SOC 2 reports on the Trust Services Criteria and is restricted; SOC 3 is the general-use summary.

questions.q: A SOC 3 report differs from SOC 2 in that it is:
choices: General use, without the detailed description and tests
questions.explain: SOC 3 covers the same subject matter but omits the detail, so it can be freely distributed.

questions.q: Only which type of SOC report supports reliance on operating effectiveness?
questions.explain: Type 2 tests operating effectiveness over a period; Type 1 only opines on design at a point in time.

questions.q: The party that makes the written assertion about its controls is the:
questions.explain: The service organization asserts about its controls; the service auditor examines and reports.

questions.q: Excluding a subservice organization's controls from the report (noting them) is the:
questions.explain: Carve-out excludes the subservice org's controls; the inclusive method covers them.

choices: Controls the user organization must perform for the service org's controls to be effective

weeks.title: ISC U2·W2 — The Trust Services Criteria: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality & Privacy (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — what a SOC 2 actually measures

A SOC 2 report is only as meaningful as the criteria it tests against. Those are the Trust Services Criteria (TSC) — five categories that define what it means for a system to be trustworthy: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy. This week works through each, the relationships among them, and the distinction the exam loves to test — confidentiality versus privacy. These criteria are the substance of the ISC discipline's security domain and the yardstick by which any service organization's controls are judged.

Security — the common criteria

Security is the foundational category, also called the common criteria, and it is required in every SOC 2 engagement. It addresses protection of the system against unauthorized access — both logical and physical — covering the access controls, boundary protections (firewalls, encryption), change management, and monitoring from ISC Unit 1. Because the other four categories all depend on a secure system, Security underlies them: there is no meaningful availability, integrity, confidentiality, or privacy without it. A SOC 2 that includes only Security still says something important; one that omits it is impossible.

Availability

Availability addresses whether the system is available for operation and use as committed or agreed — the uptime and performance a service-level agreement promises. It is not about functionality or usability; it is about access. The relevant controls include capacity and performance monitoring, environmental protections, backup and recovery, and the business continuity and disaster recovery plans (covered in Week 4) that keep the system reachable through disruptions. A cloud customer that depends on a provider being up chooses a SOC 2 that includes the Availability category.

Processing Integrity

Processing Integrity addresses whether system processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized — in short, whether the system does what it is supposed to do, correctly. It maps directly to the application controls from ISC Unit 1 (input, processing, and output controls): data is validated on entry, processed without error, and produced completely and on time. Importantly, processing integrity concerns the processing, not the underlying data's correctness if bad data was supplied — "garbage in" is the user's problem, but the system must not corrupt good data. It is the criterion a payment processor or a calculation engine must meet.

Confidentiality

Confidentiality addresses whether information designated as confidential is protected as committed — encompassing trade secrets, business plans, intellectual property, and any sensitive business information a contract or policy marks confidential. Controls include encryption, restricted access, and proper retention and disposal. Confidentiality applies to any sensitive information, regardless of whether it concerns people — a merger plan or a proprietary algorithm is confidential business data. This breadth is exactly what distinguishes it from the next, narrower category.

Privacy — and how it differs from confidentiality

Privacy addresses the collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal of personal information in conformity with the entity's privacy notice and established privacy principles. The key exam distinction: privacy applies specifically to personal information about individuals (names, Social Security numbers, health and financial data), while confidentiality applies to any sensitive information, personal or not. Privacy is also broader in scope of obligation — it covers the full life cycle of personal data and an individual's rights (notice, choice, access), reflecting privacy regulations. A trade secret is confidential; a customer's medical record is both confidential and a privacy matter.

How the criteria combine in an engagement

A service organization chooses which TSC categories its SOC 2 covers, based on what it commits to customers — Security is mandatory, and the others are added as relevant (a hosting provider adds Availability; a health-data processor adds Confidentiality and Privacy). Within each category, the controls are evaluated against points of focus that illustrate what meeting the criterion looks like. The result is a tailored report: two SOC 2s can cover different category sets, so a user must check which criteria a given report actually addresses before relying on it for a particular concern.

The criteria as a control framework

Beyond SOC reporting, the Trust Services Criteria function as a practical framework for designing and assessing controls over any system. They translate the abstract goals of ISC Unit 1 — govern, secure, control — into testable objectives an organization can build toward and an auditor can examine. Mastering the five categories, the mandatory role of Security, and the confidentiality-versus-privacy line gives a candidate the vocabulary the ISC discipline is built on and the lens through which modern systems assurance is performed.

The common criteria and points of focus

The five categories share a backbone: the common criteria (the Security category) are organized like COSO's components — control environment, communication and information, risk assessment, monitoring, and control activities — adapted to information systems. Each criterion is accompanied by points of focus: illustrative attributes that help the organization and the auditor judge whether the criterion is met (for example, points of focus under Security describe boundary protection, identity management, and threat detection). The points of focus are not a checklist to satisfy line by line; they are guidance for exercising judgment about whether the underlying objective is achieved.

Mapping controls to the criteria

In practice, a service organization maps its actual controls to each selected criterion to demonstrate coverage — a single control (multi-factor authentication, say) may support several criteria (Security and, by protecting access to personal data, Privacy). Gaps in the mapping reveal criteria with no supporting control, which the organization must remediate before the examination. This mapping discipline mirrors the skill graph applied to learning: relate each concrete control to the objective it serves, so that coverage — and gaps — become visible. An auditor likewise traces from each criterion to the control and the evidence that it is met, so an unsupported criterion cannot hide.

CMA bridge

When MBG selects a cloud vendor for sensitive payroll and employee data, the relevant SOC 2 should cover Security (always), Availability (the system must be up), Confidentiality (protect the business data), and Privacy (protect employees' personal information). Knowing which criteria matter for which data lets the CFO ask the vendor for the right report.

Practice and recap

  1. Know the five TSC: Security (mandatory common criteria), Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy.
  2. Security underlies all others (protection from unauthorized access); Availability = system available as committed (uptime/DR); Processing Integrity = complete/valid/accurate/timely/authorized processing.
  3. Distinguish Confidentiality (ANY sensitive information) from Privacy (PERSONAL information about individuals, full life cycle + rights, per the privacy notice).
  4. A service org chooses which categories its SOC 2 covers (Security required); check which criteria a report addresses before relying on it.

Recap: the Trust Services Criteria define a trustworthy system across five categories — Security (the mandatory common criteria protecting against unauthorized access and underlying all others), Availability (the system is up as committed), Processing Integrity (processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized), Confidentiality (any designated sensitive information is protected), and Privacy (personal information is handled across its life cycle per the privacy notice); the exam line is that confidentiality covers any sensitive data while privacy is specifically about individuals' personal information; and a SOC 2 covers whichever categories the service organization selects, with Security always required.

flashcards.back: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy. Security is the mandatory 'common criteria'; the rest are added as relevant.
Protection of the system against unauthorized (logical + physical) access. Required in every SOC 2; underlies all the other categories.
The system is available for operation and use as committed/agreed (uptime, SLA). About access, NOT functionality. Controls: capacity monitoring, backup/recovery, BCP/DR.
System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized — the system processes correctly. Maps to input/processing/output application controls. (Doesn't fix bad input data.)
Information DESIGNATED confidential (trade secrets, IP, business plans — any sensitive info, personal or not) is protected via encryption, access limits, proper disposal.
Personal information about individuals is collected/used/retained/disclosed/disposed per the entity's privacy notice + principles, including individual rights. Specific to people.
Confidentiality = ANY sensitive information. Privacy = specifically PERSONAL information about individuals (full life cycle + rights/regulations).
The service organization selects which categories its SOC 2 covers (Security always required); a user must check WHICH criteria a report addresses before relying on it.

questions.q: Which Trust Services category is required in every SOC 2 engagement?
questions.explain: Security (the common criteria) is mandatory and underlies the other categories.

questions.q: The Availability criterion concerns whether the system is:
choices: Available for operation and use as committed
questions.explain: Availability is about access/uptime as committed — not functionality or usability.

questions.q: Processing Integrity means system processing is:
choices: Complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized
questions.explain: Processing Integrity addresses correct, complete, authorized processing — mapping to application controls.

questions.q: The key difference between Confidentiality and Privacy is that Privacy applies to:
questions.explain: Privacy is specific to individuals' personal information; confidentiality covers any sensitive information.

questions.q: A trade secret or a proprietary algorithm is protected under which criterion?
questions.explain: Sensitive business information (not about individuals) falls under Confidentiality.

questions.q: Who selects which Trust Services categories a SOC 2 will cover?
choices: The service organization (with Security always required)
questions.explain: The service organization chooses the categories based on its commitments; Security is mandatory.

questions.q: Privacy controls address personal information across its:
choices: Collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal
questions.explain: Privacy covers the full life cycle of personal information per the privacy notice and principles.

weeks.title: ISC U2·W3 — Cybersecurity: Threats, Defenses & Incident Response (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — defending the systems that hold the numbers

The Security criterion is only as strong as the defenses behind it. A breach can corrupt Meridian Building Group's data, halt operations, trigger liabilities, and destroy trust — so understanding threats, the layered defenses that counter them, and the incident-response process when defenses fail is core to the ISC discipline. This week builds the cybersecurity vocabulary and the response framework an accountant must know to assess, and help govern, an organization's protection of its information.

Threats, vulnerabilities, and risk

Three terms anchor the field. A threat is a potential cause of harm (a hacker, malware, a natural disaster). A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat can exploit (an unpatched server, a weak password, an untrained employee). Risk is the combination — the likelihood a threat exploits a vulnerability and the resulting impact. Security management is therefore risk management: identify assets, assess threats and vulnerabilities, and apply controls that reduce risk to an acceptable level. You cannot eliminate threats, but you can reduce vulnerabilities and limit impact.

Common attack types

Candidates should recognize the major attack types. Malware includes viruses (attach to files), worms (self-propagate across networks), trojans (disguised as legitimate software), and ransomware (encrypts data and demands payment). Phishing and broader social engineering manipulate people into revealing credentials or granting access — the most common entry point. Denial-of-service (DoS/DDoS) attacks overwhelm a system to make it unavailable. SQL injection and other application attacks exploit poorly validated input, while man-in-the-middle attacks intercept communications. An advanced persistent threat (APT) is a stealthy, prolonged intrusion.

Defense in depth

No single control stops every attack, so security uses defense in depth — layered controls so that if one fails, others still protect the asset. Layers span the perimeter (firewalls, intrusion prevention), the network (segmentation, monitoring), the endpoint (anti-malware, device management), the application (input validation, secure coding), and the data (encryption, access control), all wrapped in people controls (security awareness training). The layered model reflects the reality that the human layer is often the weakest, which is why training and phishing simulations matter as much as firewalls.

Preventive, detective, and corrective security controls

Security controls map to the same functions from ISC Unit 1. Preventive controls stop attacks: multi-factor authentication, encryption, firewalls, least-privilege access, and prompt patch management (closing known vulnerabilities). Detective controls find attacks in progress or after: intrusion detection systems, logging, and security information and event management (SIEM) tools that aggregate and correlate logs to flag anomalies. Corrective controls limit damage and restore operations: incident response, backups, and recovery procedures. A strong program balances all three — prevention reduces incidents, detection catches what gets through, and correction limits the harm.

The incident-response life cycle

When an incident occurs, a disciplined incident-response process limits damage. A common life cycle runs: preparation (a plan, a trained team, tools), identification/detection (recognizing an incident occurred), containment (isolating affected systems to stop spread), eradication (removing the threat — malware, compromised accounts), recovery (restoring systems from clean backups and confirming normal operation), and lessons learned (a post-incident review to improve defenses). Speed in containment is decisive — the difference between an isolated incident and an enterprise-wide breach is often how fast the team isolates the first compromised system.

Frameworks and proactive testing

Organizations structure cybersecurity with frameworks, most prominently the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, organized around five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — a memorable map of a complete program. Proactively, vulnerability management scans for and remediates weaknesses, and penetration testing (ethical hacking) simulates real attacks to find gaps before adversaries do. A SOC 2 examination will look for exactly these practices — a documented framework, vulnerability management, and tested incident response — as evidence that the Security criterion is met.

Governance, people, and the accountant's role

Cybersecurity is ultimately a governance matter (ISC Unit 1): the board oversees cyber risk, management owns the program, and everyone is a control through security-aware behavior. The accountant's role is not to be a hacker but to assess whether the organization has identified its cyber risks, implemented layered controls, and can respond to an incident — and to understand the financial-statement consequences of a breach (contingent liabilities, asset impairment, disclosure, going-concern). Cyber risk has become a financial risk, which is why it sits squarely within the ISC discipline and the CFO's purview.

Identity, access, and the zero-trust model

Because stolen credentials are behind so many breaches, identity is a primary battleground. Attacks include password cracking, credential stuffing (reusing leaked passwords), and privilege escalation (gaining rights beyond those granted); phishing variants include spear phishing (targeted), whaling (executives), and vishing/smishing (voice and SMS). Defenses center on multi-factor authentication, strong password policies, and prompt deprovisioning of departed users. The modern architectural response is zero trust — "never trust, always verify" — which abandons the assumption that anything inside the network perimeter is safe and instead authenticates and authorizes every request based on identity and context, with microsegmentation and least-privilege access as building blocks.

Encryption and data protection

Encryption is the workhorse of data protection, rendering data unreadable without a key. Data is encrypted at rest (in storage) and in transit (moving across networks, via TLS). Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (fast, for bulk data); asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a public/private key pair and underpins secure key exchange and digital signatures. Hashing, by contrast, is a one-way transformation used to verify integrity and to store passwords — not to be reversed. The security of encryption depends on key management — generating, storing, rotating, and protecting keys — because a leaked key defeats the strongest algorithm. Encryption supports the Confidentiality and Privacy criteria and is a control an examiner expects to see over sensitive data. Together with continuous monitoring and timely patching, encryption forms the core of a credible Security posture. Defenders also segment networks and keep offline backups so that even a successful intrusion is contained and recoverable rather than catastrophic.

CMA bridge

A ransomware attack that locks MBG's job-cost system is simultaneously an operations crisis and a financial event — lost productivity, recovery cost, possible ransom, and disclosure. The CFO who understands defense in depth and incident response can both reduce the likelihood and manage the financial fallout, connecting cybersecurity directly to the finance function.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish threat (potential harm), vulnerability (exploitable weakness), and risk (likelihood × impact); security = risk management.
  2. Recognize attack types: malware (virus/worm/trojan/ransomware), phishing/social engineering, DoS/DDoS, SQL injection, MITM, APT.
  3. Apply defense in depth (layered: perimeter/network/endpoint/application/data/people) and preventive (MFA/encryption/patching), detective (IDS/SIEM/logging), corrective (IR/backups) controls.
  4. Run the incident-response life cycle (prepare → identify → contain → eradicate → recover → lessons learned); use NIST CSF (Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover), vulnerability management, and penetration testing.

Recap: cybersecurity manages the risk that threats exploit vulnerabilities — countered by defense in depth across perimeter, network, endpoint, application, data, and people layers, and by preventive (MFA, encryption, patching), detective (IDS, SIEM, logging), and corrective (incident response, backups) controls; when defenses fail, the incident-response life cycle (preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned) limits damage, with fast containment decisive; and the NIST framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), vulnerability management, and penetration testing structure a program whose failures are now genuine financial-statement events.

Virus (attaches to files), worm (self-propagates), trojan (disguised), ransomware (encrypts data, demands payment).
Manipulating people into revealing credentials or granting access — the most common entry point. The human layer is often the weakest.

Layered controls so if one fails others protect the asset: perimeter (firewall/IPS), network (segmentation), endpoint (anti-malware), application (input validation), data (encryption), people (training).
Preventive: MFA, encryption, firewall, patching. Detective: IDS, logging, SIEM. Corrective: incident response, backups, recovery.
Preparation → Identification/detection → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons learned. Fast containment is decisive.
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
Vulnerability management: scan for and remediate weaknesses. Penetration testing (ethical hacking): simulate real attacks to find gaps before adversaries do.

questions.explain: Risk combines the probability of a threat exploiting a vulnerability with the resulting impact.

questions.q: Ransomware is malware that:
questions.explain: Ransomware encrypts a victim's data and demands payment for the key.

choices: Layering multiple controls so one failure doesn't expose the asset
Relying on a single strong firewall

questions.q: A SIEM tool is primarily a:
choices: Detective control that aggregates and correlates logs
questions.explain: SIEM aggregates and analyzes log/event data to detect anomalies — a detective control.

questions.q: In incident response, isolating affected systems to stop the spread is:
questions.explain: Containment isolates compromised systems; eradication then removes the threat and recovery restores operations.

questions.explain: NIST CSF: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

choices: Simulating real attacks to find gaps before adversaries do

weeks.title: ISC U2·W4 — Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery & Resilience (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — staying in business when systems fail

The Availability criterion ultimately depends on the ability to keep operating through disruption — a server failure, a ransomware attack, a flood, a regional outage. Business continuity and disaster recovery planning is how an organization prepares to survive these events with minimal damage. This final ISC week covers the difference between the two, the analysis that prioritizes recovery, the key objectives (RTO and RPO), the backup and recovery-site strategies, and the testing that turns a plan on paper into genuine resilience for Meridian Building Group.

Business continuity versus disaster recovery

The two terms are related but distinct. Business continuity planning (BCP) is the broad discipline of keeping the whole business operating during and after a disruption — people, facilities, processes, and communications, not just technology. Disaster recovery (DR) is the subset focused on restoring IT systems and data after a disruptive event. DR answers "how do we get the systems back?"; BCP answers the larger "how does the business keep running — and keep serving customers and meeting obligations — while we do?" A complete program needs both.

The business impact analysis

Planning starts with a business impact analysis (BIA), which identifies the organization's critical business processes and the impact of their disruption over time — financial, operational, legal, and reputational. The BIA determines each process's maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) — how long it can be unavailable before the damage becomes unacceptable — and the resources each depends on. By ranking processes from most to least critical, the BIA drives prioritization: recovery effort and investment go first to the processes whose loss would hurt most, rather than treating every system as equally urgent.

RTO and RPO — the two key objectives

Two objectives quantify the recovery requirement. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the target time to restore a system after a disruption — how quickly it must be back. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss, expressed as a point in time — how much recent data the organization can afford to lose, which drives backup frequency. Example: an RPO of one hour means backups must occur at least hourly so that no more than an hour of data is lost; an RTO of four hours means the recovery solution must restore service within four hours. Tighter objectives cost more, so they are set per process based on the BIA.

Backup strategies

Backups are the foundation of recovery. A full backup copies all data (slow but simple to restore); an incremental backup copies only data changed since the last backup (fast to take, slower to restore); a differential backup copies data changed since the last full backup (a middle ground). The widely cited 3-2-1 rule — three copies of data, on two different media, with one offsite — guards against localized loss. Critically, backups must be stored offsite (or in a separate cloud region) and tested by restoring them: an untested backup is an assumption, not a control.

Recovery sites and redundancy

To meet aggressive RTOs, organizations maintain alternate recovery sites. A hot site is fully equipped and continuously updated, enabling near-immediate failover — fastest and most expensive. A warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs data loading and setup — moderate cost and recovery time. A cold site is just space and infrastructure, requiring everything to be installed — cheapest but slowest. Cloud-based DR increasingly replaces physical sites with on-demand recovery capacity. Within systems, redundancy — failover clusters, redundant power and network, and RAID for disks — provides high availability so a single component failure does not cause an outage at all.

Testing the plan

A plan that is never tested will fail when needed. Organizations test BCP/DR at increasing levels of rigor: a tabletop exercise (the team walks through the plan in a meeting), a simulation/walkthrough (executing parts in a test environment), and a full interruption test (actually failing over to the recovery site — the most realistic and most disruptive). Testing reveals gaps — outdated contact lists, backups that will not restore, dependencies no one documented — and keeps the plan current as systems change. Regular testing, not the existence of a binder, is what produces real recoverability.

From recovery to resilience

Modern practice extends beyond recovering after a failure toward resilience — designing systems and processes to withstand and adapt to disruption with minimal interruption in the first place. Resilience combines high availability, redundancy, distributed cloud architectures, and a tested response capability so that disruptions are absorbed rather than survived. For the accountant, the assurance question is whether the organization has analyzed its critical processes (BIA), set and can meet its RTO/RPO, maintains tested backups and recovery capability, and has rehearsed its response — the controls that make the Availability criterion, and the going-concern assumption behind it, credible.

People, communication, and crisis management

Technology recovery is only half of continuity; the human and communication side is the other. A plan designates a crisis-management team and roles, maintains current contact lists and call trees, and defines how the organization communicates with employees, customers, suppliers, and regulators during a disruption. It addresses alternate work arrangements (remote work, alternate facilities) for events — a pandemic, a fire, a building loss — that affect people and places rather than just systems. Plans stay current through assigned ownership and review after every test or significant system change. A technically flawless recovery still fails if no one knows their role or how to reach customers, which is why BCP reaches well beyond the data center.

Risk transfer and the cost of downtime

Finally, continuity planning weighs risk transfer: cyber-insurance and business-interruption insurance shift part of the financial impact of a disruption to an insurer, complementing — not replacing — the recovery controls. The investment in recovery capability is set against the cost of downtime — lost revenue, contractual penalties, and reputational harm per hour of outage — which makes BCP/DR a cost-benefit decision the CFO co-owns rather than a purely technical one.

CMA bridge

If a disaster takes MBG's systems offline mid-project, the BCP/DR plan determines whether the company bills, makes payroll, and keeps jobs moving or grinds to a halt. The RTO/RPO decisions are financial decisions — how much to invest in recovery capability against the cost of downtime — squarely the kind of risk-versus-cost judgment a CFO makes.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish BCP (keep the whole business operating) from DR (restore IT systems and data — a subset of BCP).
  2. Use the business impact analysis to identify critical processes and maximum tolerable downtime, driving prioritization.
  3. Set RTO (target restore time) and RPO (max acceptable data loss → backup frequency); apply backup strategies (full/incremental/differential, 3-2-1, offsite, tested).
  4. Choose recovery sites (hot/warm/cold or cloud) and redundancy (failover, RAID) by RTO; test the plan (tabletop → simulation → full interruption) for genuine resilience.

Recap: business continuity keeps the whole organization operating through disruption while disaster recovery restores its IT systems; a business impact analysis ranks critical processes by maximum tolerable downtime, setting each system's recovery time objective (how fast to restore) and recovery point objective (how much data loss is acceptable, driving backup frequency); recovery rests on tested backups (full/incremental/differential, the 3-2-1 rule, offsite), on hot/warm/cold or cloud recovery sites and redundancy chosen to meet the RTO, and on regular testing (tabletop, simulation, full interruption) — all aimed at resilience that absorbs disruption rather than merely surviving it.

questions.q: Disaster recovery (DR) is best described as:
choices: Restoring IT systems and data — a subset of business continuity
questions.explain: DR focuses on restoring IT; BCP is the broader discipline of keeping the whole business operating.

questions.q: The recovery point objective (RPO) defines:
choices: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss
The target time to restore a system
The cost of a hot site
questions.explain: RPO is the acceptable data loss (a point in time), which drives backup frequency; RTO is the restore-time target.

questions.q: An RPO of one hour means backups must occur:
questions.explain: To lose no more than an hour of data, backups must run at least every hour.

questions.q: Which recovery site offers the fastest failover at the highest cost?
questions.explain: A hot site is fully equipped and continuously updated for near-immediate failover.

questions.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule means:
choices: 3 copies, on 2 media types, with 1 offsite
questions.explain: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with at least 1 stored offsite.

questions.q: A business impact analysis primarily determines:
choices: Critical processes and their maximum tolerable downtime
questions.explain: The BIA ranks critical processes and their tolerable downtime to prioritize recovery.

questions.q: The most realistic (and most disruptive) way to test a DR plan is a:
questions.explain: A full interruption test actually fails over to the recovery site — the most realistic validation.
